problems.title: A pillbox fixes the normal jump at a charged sheet
problems.objective: Use a guided Gaussian pillbox to obtain the signed normal-field jump, then apply isolated-sheet symmetry and audit the resulting field magnitude.
problems.statement: An infinite sheet at $z=0$ in vacuum carries uniform surface charge $\sigma=+4.00\ \mathrm{nC\,m^{-2}}$. Let $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf z}$ point from $z<0$ to $z>0$, with one-sided fields $\mathbf E_-$ and $\mathbf E_+$. The field is finite away from the sheet, and no external field is applied. (a) A thin Gaussian pillbox has top outward normal $+\hat{\mathbf n}$ and bottom outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf n}$. Use Gauss's law to derive $\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf E_+-\mathbf E_-)=\sigma/\epsilon_0$. (b) For this isolated sheet, symmetry gives $\mathbf E_+=-\mathbf E_-$ and the fields are normal to the sheet. Determine both vectors. (c) Evaluate their magnitude using $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$, and check the sign and SI units.
permittedResults: Vacuum Gauss law, $\oint_S\mathbf E\cdot d\mathbf a=Q_{\mathrm{enc}}/\epsilon_0$.
For an isolated uniform sheet, reflection symmetry makes the two fields equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and normal to the sheet.
problems.strategy: Write the signed flux through the two flat faces before invoking symmetry. Use the jump first, then split it equally only because the isolated-sheet symmetry has been supplied.
hints: The bottom contribution is $A\mathbf E_-\cdot(-\hat{\mathbf n})$.
Set $\mathbf E_+=E_0\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf E_-=-E_0\hat{\mathbf n}$.
For positive $\sigma$, both fields must point away from the sheet.
problems.solution:
The side flux vanishes as the pillbox height tends to zero. The two flat faces give
$$A\mathbf E_+\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}-A\mathbf E_-\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=\frac{\sigma A}{\epsilon_0},$$
so
$$\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf E_+-\mathbf E_-)=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}.$$
For the isolated sheet, write $\mathbf E_+=E_0\hat{\mathbf n}$ and $\mathbf E_-=-E_0\hat{\mathbf n}$. The jump condition gives $2E_0=\sigma/\epsilon_0$, hence
$$\mathbf E_+=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\hat{\mathbf z},\qquad \mathbf E_-=-\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Numerically,
$$E_0=\frac{4.00\times10^{-9}}{2(8.8541878128\times10^{-12})}=2.26\times10^2\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}.$$
Thus $\mathbf E_+=+(226\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\mathbf E_-=-(226\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}})\hat{\mathbf z}$. These directions point away from a positive sheet. Also $[\sigma/\epsilon_0]=(\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}})/(\mathrm{C\,V^{-1}m^{-1}})=\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$.
rubricCriteria: Uses opposite outward normals to obtain $\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf E_+-\mathbf E_-)=\sigma/\epsilon_0$.
Invokes isolated-sheet symmetry only after deriving the jump and obtains the correct two vectors.
Reports $226\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ with correct directions and units.

commonErrors.description: Uses the declared interface normal on both pillbox faces.
commonErrors.consequence: The face fluxes are added instead of subtracted, so the jump sign is wrong.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the full jump magnitude to each one-sided field.
commonErrors.consequence: Misses the factor of two imposed by the equal-and-opposite symmetry.

problems.flawedProof: Both pillbox faces use $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, so $E_{+z}+E_{-z}=\sigma/\epsilon_0$. Symmetry then makes each field have magnitude $\sigma/\epsilon_0$, giving $452\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ on each side.

problems.title: A sheet-current jump fixes two one-sided magnetic fields
problems.objective: Derive the signed tangential magnetic-field jump from an oriented Amperian rectangle, then use one supplied one-sided field to determine the other.
problems.statement:
At $z=0$, an infinite sheet carries $\mathbf K=12.0\,\hat{\mathbf x}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. Immediately below it,
$$\mathbf B_-=(4.00\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
A narrow rectangular Amperian surface lies in the yz plane, has long sides of length L parallel to $\hat{\mathbf y}$, and straddles the sheet. Choose its surface normal $+\hat{\mathbf x}$, so the induced boundary orientation runs along $-\hat{\mathbf y}$ on the top segment and $+\hat{\mathbf y}$ on the bottom segment. Assume the short-side contributions vanish with the rectangle height. (a) Apply $\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0 I_{\rm enc}$ and take the zero-height limit to derive the signed relation between $B_{+y}$ and $B_{-y}$. Re-express it as $\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)=\mu_0\mathbf K$. (b) Find $\mathbf B_+$ using $\mu_0=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}}$. (c) Reverse both the surface normal and boundary traversal and show that the physical jump relation is unchanged. Check SI units.
permittedResults: The magnetostatic integral law $\oint_C\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=\mu_0 I_{\rm enc}$.
The magnetic field remains finite on each side as the loop height tends to zero.
problems.strategy: Write the two long-side circulation terms using the declared traversal before inserting numbers. The oriented current through the yz surface is the sheet current times the intersection length.
hints: The top contribution is $-B_{+y}L$ and the bottom contribution is $+B_{-y}L$.
The sheet current crosses the $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ surface with $I_{\rm enc}=KL$.
Numerically, $\mu_0K=15.0796\ \mu\mathrm T$.
problems.solution:
With the stated $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ orientation, the two surviving long-side terms give
$$\oint\mathbf B\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell
=-B_{+y}L+B_{-y}L.$$
The sheet current crosses the surface in its positive-normal direction, so $I_{\rm enc}=KL$. Ampere's law yields
$$B_{-y}-B_{+y}=\mu_0K,$$
or
$$B_{+y}-B_{-y}=-\mu_0K.$$
Because $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=-\hat{\mathbf x}$, this is exactly
$$\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf B_+-\mathbf B_-)=\mu_0K\hat{\mathbf x}=\mu_0\mathbf K.$$

The jump magnitude is
$$\mu_0K=(4\pi\times10^{-7})(12.0)\ \mathrm T
=1.50796\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm T
=15.0796\ \mu\mathrm T.$$
Therefore
$$B_{+y}=4.00\ \mu\mathrm T-15.0796\ \mu\mathrm T
=-11.0796\ \mu\mathrm T,$$
so
$$\boxed{\mathbf B_+=-(11.1\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}.}$$
The given lower field is $\mathbf B_-=(4.00\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}$.

If the surface normal is reversed, the boundary traversal reverses, making the circulation $B_{+y}L-B_{-y}L$; the oriented enclosed current also becomes $-KL$. Multiplying both sides by $-1$ recovers the same jump. Finally,
$$[\mu_0K]=(\mathrm{T\,m\,A^{-1}})(\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}})=\mathrm T,$$
as required.
rubricCriteria: Uses the declared loop orientation to obtain the two long-side terms with opposite signs.
Derives the vector jump and computes $\mathbf B_+=-(11.1\ \mu\mathrm T)\hat{\mathbf y}$.
Shows that reversing both orientations preserves the relation and verifies the SI units.

commonErrors.description: Traverses the top segment along positive y while retaining the positive-x surface normal.
commonErrors.consequence: Reverses the magnetic jump and obtains the wrong upper-field direction.

commonErrors.description: Treats the surface-current density K as the enclosed current without multiplying by L.
commonErrors.consequence: Leaves unmatched length dimensions in Ampere's law and an invalid field magnitude.

problems.flawedProof: For normal $+\hat{\mathbf x}$, take both long sides along $+\hat{\mathbf y}$. Then $(B_{+y}-B_{-y})L=\mu_0KL$, so $B_{+y}=4.00+15.08=19.08\ \mu\mathrm T$. The loop orientation does not affect this result.

problems.title: A field jump becomes a delta-function charge density
problems.objective: Use a supplied distributional derivative to recover the sheet charge from its discontinuous electric field and verify the result by a Gaussian slab.
problems.statement:
A stationary sheet at $z=0$ has field
$$\mathbf E(z)=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\operatorname{sgn}(z)\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Use the distributional identity $d\,\operatorname{sgn}(z)/dz=2\delta(z)$. (a) Compute $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E$ distributionally and determine $\rho(\mathbf r)$ from Gauss's law. (b) Independently integrate Gauss's law over a slab of face area $A$ spanning the sheet. (c) State the SI units of $\delta(z)$ and $\rho$, and explain why differentiating only at $z\ne0$ misses the charge.
permittedResults: $d\,\operatorname{sgn}(z)/dz=2\delta(z)$.
$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho/\epsilon_0$.
The delta distribution has unit integral across any interval containing the origin.
problems.strategy: Differentiate only the scalar coefficient of the fixed unit vector, then compare the resulting distribution with Gauss's law. Use the slab as a sign and normalization check.
hints: $\partial_z E_z=(\sigma/2\epsilon_0)(2\delta(z))$.
The slab's top and bottom outward normals are opposite.
A one-dimensional delta function has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$.
problems.solution:
Distributionally,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\frac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}\frac{d}{dz}\operatorname{sgn}(z)=\frac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}\delta(z).$$
Gauss's law therefore gives
$$\rho(\mathbf r)=\sigma\delta(z).$$
For a slab of face area $A$, the field is $+\sigma\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\epsilon_0)$ on the top face and $-\sigma\hat{\mathbf z}/(2\epsilon_0)$ on the bottom. Each dot product with its outward normal is positive, so the total flux is $\sigma A/\epsilon_0$. The enclosed charge is
$$\int_V\rho\,dV=\sigma A\int_{-a}^{a}\delta(z)\,dz=\sigma A,$$
which gives the same flux. Since $\int\delta(z)\,dz$ is dimensionless, $[\delta]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}$ and $[\rho]=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$. Pointwise differentiation away from the jump gives zero and omits the singular source.
rubricCriteria: Obtains $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=(\sigma/\epsilon_0)\delta(z)$ and $\rho=\sigma\delta(z)$.
Matches the distributional charge to the slab flux $\sigma A/\epsilon_0$ with correct face orientations.
States the correct units and explains the failure of an away-from-sheet calculation.

commonErrors.description: Uses $d\,\operatorname{sgn}/dz=\delta$ instead of $2\delta$.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces only half of the sheet charge.

commonErrors.description: Subtracts the bottom-face flux even though both its field and outward normal reverse.
commonErrors.consequence: Incorrectly makes the slab flux vanish.

problems.flawedProof: The field is constant for $z>0$ and for $z<0$, so its divergence is zero everywhere. Therefore Gauss's law gives $\rho=0$.

problems.title: Four macroscopic interface conditions share one normal convention
problems.objective: Apply the four supplied macroscopic jump conditions to a compact oblique interface datum while keeping free sources, constitutive laws, and signs distinct.
problems.statement:
At $z=0$, medium 1 lies below and medium 2 above, with $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Let $\mathbf D_i=\epsilon_i\mathbf E_i$ and $\mathbf B_i=\mu_i\mathbf H_i$, where $\epsilon_1=2\epsilon_0$, $\epsilon_2=4\epsilon_0$, $\mu_1=\mu_0$, and $\mu_2=2\mu_0$. Use
$$\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf D_2-\mathbf D_1)=\sigma_f,\quad \hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\mathbf B_2-\mathbf B_1)=0,$$
$$\hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf E_2-\mathbf E_1)=\mathbf0,\quad \hat{\mathbf n}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_f.$$
Given
$$\mathbf E_1=(3\hat{\mathbf x}+2\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}},\quad \mathbf H_1=(2\hat{\mathbf y}-4\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
$$\sigma_f=4\epsilon_0(10^3\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}),\qquad \mathbf K_f=\hat{\mathbf x}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
(a) determine $\mathbf E_2$ and $\mathbf H_2$; (b) verify all four jumps; (c) explain why $\sigma_f$ and $\mathbf K_f$ are free, not total microscopic, sources here.
permittedResults: The four jump conditions displayed in the statement.
For tangential $\mathbf K_f$, $\mathbf H_{2\parallel}-\mathbf H_{1\parallel}=\mathbf K_f\times\hat{\mathbf n}$.
$\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$ in each medium.
problems.strategy: Copy the tangential electric field first. Use the normal D jump for the remaining electric component. Then use the tangential H increment and normal B continuity.
hints: $4\epsilon_0E_{2z}-2\epsilon_0E_{1z}=\sigma_f$.
$\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf z}=-\hat{\mathbf y}$.
Normal B continuity gives $2\mu_0H_{2z}=\mu_0H_{1z}$.
problems.solution:
Tangential electric continuity gives $E_{2x}=3\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}}$. The normal D condition gives
$$4\epsilon_0E_{2z}-2\epsilon_0(2\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}})=4\epsilon_0(1\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}}),$$
so $E_{2z}=2\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}}$ and
$$\mathbf E_2=(3\hat{\mathbf x}+2\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}}.$$
For H,
$$\mathbf H_{2\parallel}-\mathbf H_{1\parallel}=\mathbf K_f\times\hat{\mathbf n}=-\hat{\mathbf y}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
so $H_{2y}=1\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$. Normal B continuity gives $2\mu_0H_{2z}=\mu_0(-4\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}})$, hence $H_{2z}=-2\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$ and
$$\mathbf H_2=(\hat{\mathbf y}-2\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The normal D difference equals $\sigma_f$, the normal B components are both $-4\mu_0\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, tangential E is unchanged, and
$$\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\hat{\mathbf x}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}=\mathbf K_f.$$
The sources are free quantities because polarization and magnetization are already absorbed into $\mathbf D,\mathbf H,\epsilon_i,$ and $\mu_i$.
rubricCriteria: Obtains $\mathbf E_2=(3\hat{\mathbf x}+2\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{kV\,m^{-1}}$.
Obtains $\mathbf H_2=(\hat{\mathbf y}-2\hat{\mathbf z})\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$ with the correct sign.
Verifies all four jumps and correctly identifies the free-source convention.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf K_f$ instead of $\mathbf K_f\times\hat{\mathbf n}$ for the tangential H increment.
commonErrors.consequence: Raises rather than lowers the y component of H.

commonErrors.description: Uses E rather than D in the normal electric jump.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignores the different permittivities.

problems.flawedProof: All components of E and H are continuous unless a magnetic monopole is present. Therefore $\mathbf E_2=\mathbf E_1$ and $\mathbf H_2=\mathbf H_1$ regardless of the free sources.

problems.title: A changing sheet charge requires surface-current divergence
problems.objective: Derive the surface continuity equation from an oriented planar control region and construct a current compatible with a prescribed sinusoidal sheet charge.
problems.statement:
A fixed sheet at $z=0$ carries surface charge $\sigma_s(x,t)$ and tangential current $\mathbf K_s(x,t)$, with no bulk current crossing the sheet. For any planar region $D$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_D\sigma_s\,dA=-\oint_{\partial D}\mathbf K_s\cdot\hat{\mathbf m}\,d\ell,$$
where $\hat{\mathbf m}$ is the outward in-plane normal. (a) Use the planar divergence theorem to derive the local surface continuity equation. (b) For $\sigma_s=A\cos(kx)\cos(\omega t)$, construct one periodic current of the form $K_x(x,t)\hat{\mathbf x}$. (c) Show that adding a spatially uniform $K_0(t)\hat{\mathbf y}$ changes neither the charge evolution nor the units.
permittedResults: The integral conservation law displayed in the statement.
The planar divergence theorem.
$A$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, $k$ has units $\mathrm{m^{-1}}$, and $\omega$ has units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
problems.strategy: Localize the integral balance, differentiate the prescribed charge, and integrate the required current divergence once with respect to x.
hints: The local sign is $\partial_t\sigma_s+\boldsymbol\nabla_\parallel\cdot\mathbf K_s=0$.
Try $K_x\propto\sin(kx)\sin(\omega t)$.
A spatially uniform tangential current has zero surface divergence.
problems.solution:
The divergence theorem and arbitrary D give
$$\partial_t\sigma_s+\boldsymbol\nabla_\parallel\cdot\mathbf K_s=0.$$
Here
$$\partial_t\sigma_s=-A\omega\cos(kx)\sin(\omega t),$$
so a compatible current is
$$\mathbf K_s=\frac{A\omega}{k}\sin(kx)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Its x derivative cancels $\partial_t\sigma_s$. Adding $K_0(t)\hat{\mathbf y}$ changes no divergence because it is spatially uniform, so the charge evolution does not determine the current uniquely. Finally,
$$[A\omega/k]=(\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}})(\mathrm{s^{-1}})/(\mathrm{m^{-1}})=\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
rubricCriteria: Derives $\partial_t\sigma_s+\boldsymbol\nabla_\parallel\cdot\mathbf K_s=0$ with the correct sign.
Constructs $(A\omega/k)\sin(kx)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}$ and verifies it.
Identifies a valid divergence-free addition and checks units.

commonErrors.description: Reverses the sign between charge accumulation and outward current.
commonErrors.consequence: Constructs a current that reinforces rather than balances the charge change.

commonErrors.description: Claims that the divergence uniquely fixes both current components.
commonErrors.consequence: Excludes valid divergence-free additions.

problems.flawedProof: Outward current increases the charge inside D, so $\partial_t\sigma_s-\boldsymbol\nabla_\parallel\cdot\mathbf K_s=0$. This makes the compatible current the negative of the stated one.

problems.title: Ampere-Maxwell enforces the continuity equation
problems.objective: Take one divergence to derive charge continuity, then verify the consistency condition on a simple time-dependent charge-current pair.
problems.statement:
In vacuum,
$$\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E,\qquad \boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho/\epsilon_0.$$
(a) Take the divergence of the first equation and use the second to derive local charge continuity. (b) Let
$$\rho(x,t)=\rho_0e^{-t/\tau}\cos(kx),\qquad \mathbf J(x,t)=\frac{\rho_0}{k\tau}e^{-t/\tau}\sin(kx)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Verify continuity directly. (c) Check SI units and explain why a pair that violates continuity cannot satisfy both displayed Maxwell equations.
permittedResults: The divergence of a curl is zero.
Spatial and temporal derivatives commute for the stated smooth fields.
$\rho$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$.
problems.strategy: Apply divergence before substituting Gauss's law. For the example, compute the time derivative and x derivative separately and compare signs.
hints: $0=\mu_0\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E)$.
$\partial_x\sin(kx)=k\cos(kx)$.
Both continuity terms have units of current per volume.
problems.solution:
Taking divergence gives
$$0=\mu_0\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E)=\mu_0(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\partial_t\rho).$$
Therefore $\partial_t\rho+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$. For the proposed pair,
$$\partial_t\rho=-\frac{\rho_0}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}\cos(kx),\qquad
\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=\frac{\rho_0}{\tau}e^{-t/\tau}\cos(kx),$$
so the sum vanishes. Since $[\rho_0/(k\tau)]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, J has the correct units. A violating pair would make the divergence of the right-hand side of Ampere-Maxwell nonzero while the divergence of its left-hand side is identically zero.
rubricCriteria: Uses divergence of a curl and Gauss's law to obtain continuity with the correct sign.
Differentiates the proposed pair and verifies exact cancellation.
Checks J units and states the consistency consequence.

commonErrors.description: Drops the displacement-current term before taking the divergence.
commonErrors.consequence: Incorrectly concludes that all currents must be divergence-free.

commonErrors.description: Misses the factor k when differentiating the sine.
commonErrors.consequence: The example then appears to violate continuity.

problems.flawedProof: Because the divergence of a curl is zero, Ampere's law gives $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$. Gauss's law is unrelated, so charge may vary arbitrarily.

problems.title: A changing coaxial voltage produces the same displacement current at every radius
problems.objective: Derive the coaxial electric field and integrate its displacement current across a radial cut, exposing the cancellation that makes the total current radius independent.
problems.statement: A vacuum coaxial capacitor has conductor radii $a<b$ and active length $\ell$, with negligible end effects. The voltage is $V(t)=\Phi(a,t)-\Phi(b,t)$. (a) Use cylindrical symmetry and the voltage integral to obtain $\mathbf E(r,t)$ for $a<r<b$. (b) Find $\mathbf J_D=\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E$ and integrate it through the cylindrical cut at radius $r_0$, whose normal is $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ and area element is $r_0\,d\phi\,dz$. Show that the result does not depend on $r_0$. (c) Evaluate the current and $J_D(r_0)$ for $a=1.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, $b=4.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, $\ell=0.500\ \mathrm m$, $r_0=2.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, and $\dot V=2.50\times10^6\ \mathrm{V\,s^{-1}}$, using $\epsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$.
permittedResults: $\mathbf J_D=\partial_t\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E$ in vacuum.
$V(t)=-\int_b^a\mathbf E\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell$.
Cylindrical cut area element at fixed radius is $r,dphi,dz$.
problems.strategy: First determine the 1/r field coefficient from the voltage. In the flux integral, keep the 1/r field factor beside the r from the area element.
hints: $\mathbf E=V(t)\hat{\mathbf r}/[r\ln(b/a)]$.
Integrate over a full azimuth and the active length.
Radius independence follows before any numbers are inserted.
problems.solution:
Cylindrical symmetry gives $\mathbf E=C(t)\hat{\mathbf r}/r$. The voltage condition yields
$$V(t)=\int_a^b E_r\,dr=C(t)\ln(b/a),$$
so
$$\mathbf E(r,t)=\frac{V(t)}{r\ln(b/a)}\hat{\mathbf r},\qquad
\mathbf J_D=\frac{\epsilon_0\dot V(t)}{r\ln(b/a)}\hat{\mathbf r}.$$
Across the cut at $r_0$,
$$I_D=\int_0^\ell\int_0^{2\pi}\frac{\epsilon_0\dot V}{r_0\ln(b/a)}r_0\,d\phi\,dz
=\frac{2\pi\epsilon_0\ell\dot V}{\ln(b/a)},$$
which is independent of $r_0$. With the stated values, $\ln(b/a)=\ln4$,
$$I_D=5.02\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm A=50.2\ \mu\mathrm A,$$
and
$$J_D(2.00\ \mathrm{mm})=7.98\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}.$$
The signs are positive along $+\hat{\mathbf r}$ because $\dot V>0$.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\mathbf E=V\hat{\mathbf r}/[r\ln(b/a)]$.
Integrates the displacement current with the cylindrical area factor and demonstrates radius independence.
Reports $50.2\ \mu\mathrm A$ and $7.98\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$ with correct signs and units.

commonErrors.description: Uses a uniform parallel-plate electric field in the coaxial gap.
commonErrors.consequence: Loses both the logarithm and radius cancellation.

commonErrors.description: Uses a flat area element instead of the cylindrical factor r.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces a current that spuriously depends on radius.

problems.flawedProof: The voltage drops uniformly across the radial gap, so $E=V/(b-a)$. Multiplying $\epsilon_0\dot E$ by $2\pi r_0\ell$ makes the current proportional to $r_0$.

problems.title: One radial current formula cannot satisfy continuity both inside and outside a decaying sphere
problems.objective: Audit a tempting global radial-current ansatz, then construct the correct piecewise current and verify its boundary flux against total charge loss.
problems.statement:
A sphere of radius $R$ contains
$$\rho(r,t)=\rho_0e^{-t/\tau}\quad (r<R),\qquad \rho=0\quad (r>R),$$
with no surface charge at $r=R$. A proposed current is $\mathbf J_p=\alpha(t)r\hat{\mathbf r}$ for all $r$. (a) Use $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot[f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}]=r^{-2}\partial_r(r^2f)$ to show that no single $\alpha(t)$ works both inside and outside. (b) Construct a current that is regular at $r=0$, satisfies continuity in both regions, and has continuous normal current at $R$. (c) Compare its outward boundary flux with $-dQ/dt$ for the total enclosed charge.
permittedResults: $\partial_t\rho+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0$.
$\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot[f(r)\hat{\mathbf r}]=r^{-2}\partial_r(r^2f)$.
No surface charge accumulation requires normal current continuity across the fixed boundary.
problems.strategy: Determine the coefficient demanded inside, compare it with the exterior requirement, then use a divergence-free inverse-square exterior current matched to the boundary value.
hints: Inside, $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot(\alpha r\hat{\mathbf r})=3\alpha$.
Outside, a divergence-free radial field has the form $C(t)\hat{\mathbf r}/r^2$.
problems.solution:
Inside the sphere, continuity requires
$$-\frac{\rho}{\tau}+3\alpha=0,\qquad \alpha=\frac{\rho}{3\tau}.$$
Outside, $\partial_t\rho=0$, so the same global ansatz would require $3\alpha=0$. These conditions are incompatible while $\rho\ne0$.

A regular interior current is
$$\mathbf J_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{\rho(t)r}{3\tau}\hat{\mathbf r}.$$
The divergence-free exterior form matched at $r=R$ is
$$\mathbf J_{\mathrm{out}}=\frac{\rho(t)R^3}{3\tau r^2}\hat{\mathbf r}.$$
Both give $J_r(R)=\rho(t)R/(3\tau)$, so no surface charge is created. The outward flux is
$$4\pi R^2J_r(R)=\frac{4\pi R^3\rho(t)}{3\tau}=\frac{Q(t)}{\tau}=-\frac{dQ}{dt},$$
because $Q(t)=4\pi R^3\rho(t)/3$.
rubricCriteria: Shows that the global linear ansatz demands incompatible interior and exterior coefficients.
Constructs the regular linear interior current and matched inverse-square exterior current.
Verifies boundary continuity and matches outward flux to total charge loss.

commonErrors.description: Checks continuity only inside the charged region.
commonErrors.consequence: Mistakenly accepts a global current whose exterior divergence is nonzero.

commonErrors.description: Sets the exterior current to zero without allowing surface accumulation.
commonErrors.consequence: Creates a discontinuity in normal current.

problems.flawedProof: Choosing $\alpha=\rho/(3\tau)$ satisfies continuity inside, so it is valid everywhere. A nonzero current divergence outside is harmless because $\rho=0$.

problems.title: Maxwell evolution preserves initially satisfied Gauss constraints
problems.objective: Derive the time evolution of electric and magnetic Gauss residuals and identify exactly how a continuity defect drives electric-constraint drift.
problems.statement:
Suppose the vacuum curl equations hold and define
$$C_E=\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E-\rho/\epsilon_0,\qquad C_B=\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf B.$$
(a) Use the two curl equations to derive $\partial_tC_B=0$ and
$$\partial_tC_E=-\frac{\partial_t\rho+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J}{\epsilon_0}.$$
(b) Conclude what happens when continuity holds and both constraints vanish initially. (c) As a defect check, take $\mathbf E=\mathbf B=\mathbf J=\mathbf0$ and $\rho=s_0t$ with constant $s_0$. Verify the curl equations, compute $C_E(t)$, and audit the units.
permittedResults: The divergence of a curl is zero.
The vacuum Maxwell curl equations.
Spatial and temporal derivatives commute for the stated smooth fields.
problems.strategy: Take divergence of each curl equation and solve for the time derivative of the corresponding residual. Treat the defect example as a direct substitution.
hints: Faraday's law gives $\partial_t(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf B)=0$.
Use the divergence of Ampere-Maxwell to replace the time derivative of div E.
For the example, $C_E=-s_0t/\epsilon_0$.
problems.solution:
Taking divergence of Faraday's law gives
$$\partial_tC_B=-\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot(\boldsymbol\nabla\times\mathbf E)=0.$$
Taking divergence of Ampere-Maxwell gives
$$0=\mu_0\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\mu_0\epsilon_0\partial_t(\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf E),$$
so
$$\partial_tC_E=-\frac{\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf J+\partial_t\rho}{\epsilon_0}.$$
If continuity holds, both time derivatives vanish. Constraints that are zero initially remain zero.

For $\mathbf E=\mathbf B=\mathbf J=\mathbf0$ and $\rho=s_0t$, both curl equations read $0=0$, but continuity has defect $s_0$. The residual is
$$C_E(t)=-\frac{s_0t}{\epsilon_0}.$$
Since $[s_0]=\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}s^{-1}}$, $[s_0/\epsilon_0]=\mathrm{V\,m^{-2}s^{-1}}$, the correct unit for $\partial_tC_E$.
rubricCriteria: Derives both residual evolution equations using divergence of a curl.
Correctly concludes preservation under continuity and initially satisfied constraints.
Verifies the defect example and its units.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the Gauss constraints propagate without using continuity.
commonErrors.consequence: Misses the required source-consistency condition.

commonErrors.description: Writes $\partial_tC_E=+s/\epsilon_0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Predicts drift with the wrong sign.

problems.flawedProof: The divergence of every field is automatically zero because the divergence of a curl is zero. Hence both constraints remain zero even when continuity fails.

problems.title: A moving interface uses current relative to the moving faces
problems.objective: Derive the planar moving-interface charge balance from relative face fluxes and apply it to a numerical sign audit.
problems.statement:
A planar interface moves along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ with speed $u$. Let $[f]=f_+-f_-$, and let $\sigma_s$ and tangential $\mathbf K_s$ be measured on the interface. Charge crossing a face moving with velocity $u\hat{\mathbf z}$ is measured by $(\mathbf J-\rho u\hat{\mathbf z})\cdot\mathbf N$. (a) Apply this rule to the upper and lower faces of a thin moving pillbox and derive
$$\partial_t\sigma_s+\boldsymbol\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K_s+[\mathbf J\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}]-u[\rho]=0.$$
(b) Evaluate $\partial_t\sigma_s$ when $u=2.00\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\rho_-=1.00\ \mu\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, $\rho_+=4.00\ \mu\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}$, $J_{-z}=3.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, $J_{+z}=9.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$, and $\boldsymbol\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K_s=-1.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$. (c) Check the stationary-interface limit and SI units.
permittedResults: The relative-flux rule displayed in the statement.
The planar surface divergence theorem.
problems.strategy: Write the outward relative flux on each face separately. Sum the two face terms and tangential side outflow before solving the numerical balance.
hints: The upper-face term is $J_{+z}-u\rho_+$.
The lower-face term is $-J_{-z}+u\rho_-$.
Here $u[\rho]=6.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.
problems.solution:
The upper outward relative flux is $J_{+z}-u\rho_+$ and the lower is $-J_{-z}+u\rho_-$. Their sum is $[\mathbf J\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}]-u[\rho]$. Adding tangential side outflow and charge accumulation gives
$$\partial_t\sigma_s+\boldsymbol\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K_s+[\mathbf J\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}]-u[\rho]=0.$$
For the data,
$$[\mathbf J\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}]=6.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}},\qquad
u[\rho]=6.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}.$$
Therefore
$$\partial_t\sigma_s=-(-1.00)-6.00+6.00=+1.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}.$$
When $u=0$, the standard fixed-interface law remains. Every term has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$ because $u\rho$ has units $(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})(\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}})=\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.
rubricCriteria: Combines the two oriented relative face fluxes to obtain the correct jump law.
Computes $\partial_t\sigma_s=+1.00\ \mu\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.
Recovers the stationary limit and checks all units.

commonErrors.description: Uses laboratory current rather than current relative to moving faces.
commonErrors.consequence: Omits the $-u[\rho]$ term.

commonErrors.description: Writes $+u[\rho]$ for the stated jump convention.
commonErrors.consequence: Reverses the swept-charge effect.

problems.flawedProof: Interface motion changes only position, so the face fluxes are $J_{+z}$ and $-J_{-z}$. The balance contains no density-jump term.

problems.title: Vacuum field energy bounds the local Poynting flux
problems.objective: Prove the sharp vacuum inequality between energy density and energy-flux magnitude, characterize equality, and distinguish steady through-flow from accumulation.
problems.statement:
In vacuum,
$$u=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0},\qquad
\mathbf S=\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0},\qquad
c=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}.$$
(a) Prove the pointwise bound $|\mathbf S|\le cu$ using only a cross-product bound and a two-variable square inequality. (b) Determine all equality conditions. (c) Apply the result to uniform static fields $\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=B_0\hat{\mathbf y}$ in a rectangular box. Find the signed flux through both z faces, show the net outward flux is zero, and explain why a nonzero S does not imply changing u. Include SI-unit and zero-field checks.
permittedResults: $|\mathbf E\times\mathbf B|\le EB$, with equality exactly for perpendicular nonzero fields.
$2xy\le x^2+y^2$ for nonnegative x and y, with equality exactly when $x=y$.
$\partial_tu+\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-\mathbf J\cdot\mathbf E$.
problems.strategy: Scale E and B so the two terms of u become two squared variables. Apply the cross-product and arithmetic-geometric inequalities separately, retaining both equality conditions.
hints: Set $x=\sqrt{\epsilon_0}E$ and $y=B/\sqrt{\mu_0}$.
Then $|\mathbf S|\le cxy$ and $u=(x^2+y^2)/2$.
For the box, use opposite outward normals on its two z faces.
problems.solution:
The cross-product bound gives
$$|\mathbf S|\le\frac{EB}{\mu_0}.$$
With $x=\sqrt{\epsilon_0}E$ and $y=B/\sqrt{\mu_0}$,
$$\frac{EB}{\mu_0}=cxy,\qquad u=\frac{x^2+y^2}{2}.$$
Since $xy\le(x^2+y^2)/2$,
$$\boxed{|\mathbf S|\le cu}.$$
For nonzero fields, equality requires both $\mathbf E\perp\mathbf B$ and $x=y$, or
$$\frac EB=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}=c.$$
The zero fields also saturate the bound trivially.

For the uniform crossed fields,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{E_0B_0}{\mu_0}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
If each z face has area A, the upper signed outward flux is $+E_0B_0A/\mu_0$ and the lower signed outward flux is its negative. The net flux and $\boldsymbol\nabla\cdot\mathbf S$ are zero, so a source-free static box has $\partial_tu=0$: energy enters one face at exactly the rate it leaves the other. The units are $[u]=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ and $[cu]=\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}=[S]$. If either field vanishes, S vanishes while the remaining field energy stays nonnegative.
rubricCriteria: Derives the sharp inequality $|\mathbf S|\le cu$ with both required inequalities.
Identifies perpendicular fields with $E/B=c$ as the nontrivial equality case.
Computes both signed box fluxes, explains their cancellation, and checks units and limits.

commonErrors.description: Applies the scalar inequality without first bounding the cross-product magnitude.
commonErrors.consequence: Claims equality for parallel fields even though their Poynting vector vanishes.

commonErrors.description: Counts only the upper box face.
commonErrors.consequence: Mistakes steady energy through-flow for net loss or accumulation.

problems.flawedProof: Because $2EB\le E^2+B^2$, one always has $|\mathbf S|\le u$. Equality holds whenever E and B have equal numerical values, regardless of units or their relative direction.

problems.title: Building a linear dielectric field costs one half of E dot D
problems.objective: Integrate quasistatic source work for a parallel-plate dielectric and recover the linear energy density with its factor of one half.
problems.statement:
A homogeneous linear dielectric fills a parallel-plate capacitor of plate area $A$ and separation $\ell$, with fringing neglected. The plates are charged quasistatically from zero to $\pm Q$. At an intermediate charge $q$, $D=q/A$, $E=D/\epsilon$, and $V=E\ell$. (a) Starting from $dW=V\,dq$, integrate the source work to the final charge. (b) Divide by the dielectric volume and show
$$w=\frac{D^2}{2\epsilon}=\frac12\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D=\frac12\epsilon E^2.$$
(c) Check SI units and the limits $Q\to0$ and $\epsilon\to\epsilon_0$.
permittedResults: $dW=V\,dq$ for quasistatic charging.
$D=q/A$, $E=D/\epsilon$, and $V=E\ell$.
The dielectric volume is $A\ell$.
problems.strategy: Express the instantaneous voltage as a linear function of intermediate charge before integrating. Divide by volume only after the integral.
hints: $V(q)=q\ell/(\epsilon A)$.
The factor one half comes from integrating q from zero to Q.
Use $D=Q/A$ in the final density.
problems.solution:
At intermediate charge q,
$$V(q)=\frac{q\ell}{\epsilon A}.$$
Therefore
$$W=\int_0^QV(q)\,dq=\frac{\ell}{\epsilon A}\int_0^Qq\,dq
=\frac{Q^2\ell}{2\epsilon A}.$$
Dividing by $A\ell$ gives
$$w=\frac{Q^2}{2\epsilon A^2}=\frac{D^2}{2\epsilon}
=\frac12ED=\frac12\epsilon E^2.$$
The one half records the linear rise of voltage during charging; using only final voltage would double the work. Since $ED$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, the units are correct. The energy vanishes as $Q\to0$, and $\epsilon=\epsilon_0$ recovers the vacuum result.
rubricCriteria: Expresses V as a function of intermediate charge and integrates from zero to Q.
Obtains all equivalent linear energy-density forms with factor one half.
Explains the factor, checks units, and verifies both limits.

commonErrors.description: Uses the final voltage throughout charging.
commonErrors.consequence: Predicts twice the correct work.

commonErrors.description: Divides work by area but not separation.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces energy per area instead of per volume.

problems.flawedProof: The final source work is $QV$. Dividing by volume gives $w=D^2/\epsilon$, with no factor one half.

problems.title: Magnetic energy density depends on the constitutive path
problems.objective: Derive reversible magnetic energy as a constitutive line integral, evaluate it for linear and weakly nonlinear media, and construct a quantitative counterexample to the claim that magnetic energy density is always one-half of $\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H$.
problems.statement: A homogeneous magnetic specimen fills an ideal toroid of mean path length $\ell$, cross-sectional area $A$, and volume $\mathcal V=A\ell$. A tightly wound coil has $N$ turns and carries current $I$. Leakage flux, resistance, hysteresis, eddy currents, magnetostriction, and electric-field energy are neglected. The medium is local, quasistatic, and reversible, and the reference state $\mathbf B=\mathbf 0$ has zero magnetic energy. (a) Starting from Ampere's law and Faraday's law, derive the incremental source work per unit volume and show that $du=\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B$. State the condition under which the corresponding line integral defines a state function. (b) For collinear fields, evaluate $u(B)$ first for $B=\mu H$ with constant positive $\mu$, and then for the reversible weakly nonlinear law $H(B)=B/\mu+\gamma B^3$, where $\gamma>0$. (c) Compare the nonlinear result with $BH/2$ and identify precisely why the latter expression is not universal. (d) Use $\mu=2.50\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, $\gamma=100\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}\,T^{-3}}$, and $B=0.800\ \mathrm T$ to calculate $H$, the correct energy density, and $BH/2$. Include an SI-dimensional check and a linear-medium limit.
permittedResults: Ampere's law for an ideal toroid, $H\ell=NI$
Faraday's law, including the opposing sign of the induced emf
Electrical source power $P=IV$
For a lossless quasistatic process, source work equals the increase of reversible stored energy
problems.strategy: Use the toroid as an explicit work-measuring device: express the source voltage through the changing flux and eliminate $I$ using Ampere's law. Then integrate $H$ with respect to $B$, rather than inserting the endpoint values into a linear-medium formula. Compare the nonlinear integral term by term with $BH/2$ and finish with dimensional and zero-nonlinearity checks.
hints: Choose the source-voltage sign so that it opposes the winding's induced emf. With $\Phi=AB$, express $IV_s$ entirely in terms of $H$, $\dot B$, and $A\ell$.

After dividing the source power by the specimen volume, integrate along the reversible constitutive loading curve from $\mathbf 0$ to the final $\mathbf B$. For a vector medium, ask when this line integral is path independent.
For the cubic law, integrate the linear and cubic terms separately. In $BH/2$, the endpoint cubic term receives a different numerical coefficient from the integrated cubic term.
problems.solution:
For positive current and increasing flux, the winding's induced emf is $-N\,d\Phi/dt$. The external source must therefore provide the opposing terminal voltage $V_s=+N\,d\Phi/dt$. Since $\Phi=AB$ and Ampere's law gives $I=H\ell/N$, the source power is
$$P_s=IV_s=\frac{H\ell}{N}NA\frac{dB}{dt}=A\ell H\frac{dB}{dt}=\mathcal V H\frac{dB}{dt}.$$
The assumed reversible, lossless process stores all of this work, so
$$\frac{du}{dt}=H\frac{dB}{dt},\qquad du=H\,dB.$$
Independent ideal windings can vary Cartesian components separately, giving the vector form
$$du=\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B.$$
With zero energy at $\mathbf B=\mathbf 0$, the stored energy density is therefore
$$u(\mathbf B)=\int_{\mathcal C:\,\mathbf 0\to\mathbf B}\mathbf H(\mathbf B')\cdot d\mathbf B'.$$
For this to be a state function in a multicomponent medium, the differential must be exact. In a smooth simply connected constitutive domain this requires $\partial H_i/\partial B_j=\partial H_j/\partial B_i$. A hysteretic loop with nonzero $\oint\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B$ would instead represent dissipation and is excluded by reversibility.

For the linear collinear law $H=B/\mu$,
$$u(B)=\int_0^B\frac{B'}{\mu}\,dB'=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}=\frac{BH}{2}.$$
Thus $BH/2$ is valid here because $H$ is proportional to $B$ throughout the loading process.

For the nonlinear law,
$$u(B)=\int_0^B\left(\frac{B'}{\mu}+\gamma B'^3\right)dB'=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}+\frac{\gamma B^4}{4}.$$
In contrast, using only endpoint values gives
$$\frac{BH}{2}=\frac{B}{2}\left(\frac{B}{\mu}+\gamma B^3\right)=\frac{B^2}{2\mu}+\frac{\gamma B^4}{2}.$$
It consequently overestimates the energy by $\gamma B^4/4$. Geometrically, the energy is the area under the constitutive curve $H(B')$, whereas $BH/2$ is the triangular area appropriate only to a straight line through the origin. Equivalently, integration by parts gives $\int_0^B H\,dB'=BH-\int_0^H B\,dH'$, and the two integrals are equal only under additional constitutive restrictions.

For the stated data,
$$H=\frac{0.800}{2.50\times10^{-3}}+100(0.800)^3=320+51.2=371.2\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The correct energy density is
$$u=\frac{(0.800)^2}{2(2.50\times10^{-3})}+\frac{100(0.800)^4}{4}=128+10.24=138.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$
The endpoint expression instead gives
$$\frac{BH}{2}=\frac{(0.800)(371.2)}{2}=148.48\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}},$$
which is $10.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$ too large. Dimensionally, $BH$ has units $\mathrm{T\,A\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $\gamma B^4$ has the same units because $[\gamma]=\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}\,T^{-3}}$. Finally, as $\gamma\to0$, both expressions reduce to $B^2/(2\mu)$, providing the linear-medium check.
rubricCriteria: Derives $du=\mathbf H\cdot d\mathbf B$ from the toroidal source-work calculation with the correct Faraday-law sign and states the exact-differential requirement for reversible vector constitutive behavior.
Correctly integrates both constitutive laws and explicitly demonstrates that the nonlinear coefficient in $BH/2$ differs from the coefficient in $\int H\,dB$.
Obtains $H=371.2\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $u=138.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and $BH/2=148.48\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, with valid dimensional and $\gamma\to0$ checks.

commonErrors.description: Assumes $u=BH/2$ for the cubic constitutive law without integrating along the loading curve.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonlinear contribution is assigned the coefficient $1/2$ instead of $1/4$, overestimating the stated energy density by $10.24\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

commonErrors.description: Integrates $B\,dH$ while labeling the result as the source-supplied magnetic energy $\int H\,dB$.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculation produces magnetic coenergy rather than the requested stored energy; the two coincide for the linear law but differ for the nonlinear law.

problems.flawedProof: The final fields completely determine the magnetic energy, so their average during turn-on is always one-half of the final product. Hence $u=BH/2$ for any reversible material. With $B=0.800\ \mathrm T$, the constitutive law gives $H=371.2\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, and therefore $u=(0.800)(371.2)/2=148.48\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

problems.title: A dielectric insertion changes which agency pays the energy bill
problems.objective: Derive the force and complete energy ledger for quasistatic dielectric insertion under fixed-free-charge and fixed-voltage constraints, including the battery contribution that reconciles opposite changes in stored electrical energy.
problems.statement: Two rectangular conducting plates occupy $0<X<L$, $0<y<w$, and the planes $z=0$ and $z=d$. The upper plate at $z=d$ is positive, so the gap field points approximately in the $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ direction; the gap-facing normals of the upper and lower plates are $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, respectively. A lossless linear dielectric slab of relative permittivity $\kappa>1$ fills the full gap and width and is inserted from the $X<0$ side. Let $x\in[0,L]$ be its overlap length, with $+x$ defined inward. Neglect fringing, edge stress, gravity, and kinetic energy, and assume quasistatic motion. Vacuum occupies the uncovered part. (a) Derive the overlap-dependent capacitance $C(x)$ from the normal displacement field. (b) Starting from quasistatic energy conservation, derive the electrical force $F_x$ separately when free charge $Q$ is fixed and when voltage $V=\phi_{\rm upper}-\phi_{\rm lower}$ is fixed by an ideal battery. Use positive battery work to mean energy delivered by the battery to the capacitor-mechanical system. (c) For each constraint, state the signs of the field-energy change, battery work, electromagnetic work on the slab, and external-agent work. Explain why both constraints pull the slab inward even though the derivatives of stored field energy have opposite signs. (d) Use $L=0.100\ \mathrm m$, $w=0.0500\ \mathrm m$, $d=1.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, $\kappa=4.00$, and $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. At $x_0=0.0400\ \mathrm m$, take $V_0=500\ \mathrm V$ and $Q_0=C(x_0)V_0$. Calculate the initial inward force under either constraint. Then move the slab to $x_1=0.0600\ \mathrm m$ and give complete finite energy ledgers for an isolated capacitor with fixed $Q_0$ and for a capacitor held at fixed $V_0$. Include a limiting or independent check.
permittedResults: The constitutive laws $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E$ in vacuum and $\mathbf D=\kappa\epsilon_0\mathbf E$ in the dielectric
The capacitance definition $C=Q/V$
Quasistatic energy conservation and electrical work $V\,dQ$ at a source terminal
Conductors in electrostatic equilibrium are equipotentials
problems.strategy: Treat the vacuum-filled and dielectric-filled plate areas as parallel regions sharing the same voltage drop. Derive the stored electrical energy by quasistatically charging the capacitor at fixed overlap. Then apply one signed energy balance, $dU=\delta W_{\rm bat}-F_xdx$, first with $dQ=0$ and then with $dV=0$. For the numerical ledger, compute endpoint capacitances before evaluating each energy transfer.
hints: Because both side-by-side regions span the same plate separation, they have the same voltage drop and field magnitude. Add their free charges on the upper plate to obtain $C(x)$.
Use $U(Q,x)=\int_0^Q(q/C(x))\,dq$. For an infinitesimal inward displacement, the field does $F_xdx$ of mechanical work, so write an energy balance with that term leaving the electrical subsystem.
At fixed voltage, $dQ=V\,dC$ and the battery delivers $VdQ$. Compare this source work with the change of $CV^2/2$ before assigning the remainder to mechanical work.
problems.solution:
Ignoring fringing, the magnitude of the field in each side-by-side region is $E=V/d$. The vacuum area is $A_v=w(L-x)$ and the dielectric area is $A_d=wx$. On the positive upper plate, the magnitudes of the normal displacement fields are $D_v=\epsilon_0V/d$ and $D_d=\kappa\epsilon_0V/d$. Thus the total positive free charge is
$$Q=D_vA_v+D_dA_d=\frac{\epsilon_0wV}{d}\big[(L-x)+\kappa x\big].$$
Therefore
$$C(x)=\frac{Q}{V}=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}\big[L+(\kappa-1)x\big],\qquad C'(x)=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}(\kappa-1)>0.$$
The two regions act in parallel because they share the same conductor potentials.

At fixed $x$, quasistatically assembling charge gives
$$U(Q,x)=\int_0^Q\frac{q}{C(x)}\,dq=\frac{Q^2}{2C(x)}=\frac12C(x)V^2.$$
This reversible electrical storage includes the dielectric's polarization energy. If the slab advances by $dx>0$, the electromagnetic field does mechanical work $F_xdx$. With positive $\delta W_{\rm bat}$ defined as work delivered by the battery, energy conservation is
$$dU=\delta W_{\rm bat}-F_xdx.$$

For an isolated capacitor, $dQ=0$ and $\delta W_{\rm bat}=0$. Hence
$$F_x=-\left(\frac{\partial U}{\partial x}\right)_Q=\frac{Q^2}{2C^2}C'(x)>0.$$
The field energy decreases, the field does positive work on the inward-moving slab, and a quasistatic external agent does $dW_{\rm ext}=-F_xdx<0$, meaning that it absorbs energy.

At fixed voltage, $Q=CV$, so $dQ=VdC$. The battery work is
$$\delta W_{\rm bat}=VdQ=V^2dC.$$
Meanwhile,
$$dU=d\left(\frac12CV^2\right)=\frac12V^2dC.$$
Substitution into the energy balance gives
$$F_xdx=V^2dC-\frac12V^2dC=\frac12V^2dC,$$
so
$$F_x=\frac12V^2C'(x)>0.$$
Although the stored electrical energy now increases, the battery supplies twice that increase; the other half becomes positive mechanical work. Equivalently, the battery's internal energy changes by $dU_{\rm bat}=-V^2dC$, and $-d(U+U_{\rm bat})/dx=V^2C'/2$. The apparently outward result from $-dU/dx$ at fixed $V$ is therefore invalid because $U$ alone omits the voltage-maintaining agency.

Numerically,
$$\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}=4.4270939064\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}},\qquad C'=1.32812817192\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}.$$
At $x_0=0.0400\ \mathrm m$,
$$C_0=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}(0.100+3(0.0400))=9.73960659408\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm F=97.3961\ \mathrm{pF},$$
so
$$Q_0=C_0V_0=4.86980329704\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm C=48.6980\ \mathrm{nC}.$$
Because $Q_0/C_0=V_0$, both constraints give the same initial force:
$$F_x(x_0)=\frac12V_0^2C'=1.6601602149\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm N=166.016\ \mu\mathrm N,$$
directed inward. This equality is an independent check: force is determined by the instantaneous electrical state, even though the subsequent constraint changes its evolution.

At $x_1=0.0600\ \mathrm m$,
$$C_1=\frac{\epsilon_0w}{d}(0.100+3(0.0600))=1.23958629379\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm F=123.959\ \mathrm{pF}.$$
For fixed $Q_0$, the endpoint energies are
$$U_0=\frac{Q_0^2}{2C_0}=12.1745\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad U_1=\frac{Q_0^2}{2C_1}=9.56569\ \mu\mathrm J.$$
Thus
$$\Delta U=-2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad W_{\rm bat}=0,
\qquad W_{\rm em}=+2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad W_{\rm ext}=-2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J.$$
The voltage falls to $Q_0/C_1=392.857\ \mathrm V$, so the inward force decreases during insertion.

For fixed $V_0$, the capacitance change is $\Delta C=2.65625634384\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm F$. Therefore
$$\Delta U=\frac12V_0^2\Delta C=+3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J,$$
$$W_{\rm bat}=V_0^2\Delta C=+6.64064\ \mu\mathrm J,$$
$$W_{\rm em}=W_{\rm bat}-\Delta U=+3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J,
\qquad W_{\rm ext}=-3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J.$$
The mechanical result also equals $F_x(x_1-x_0)$ because $C'$ and the fixed-voltage force are constant. Finally, if $\kappa\to1$, then $C'\to0$ and both force formulas vanish, as required when insertion does not change the medium.
rubricCriteria: Derives $C(x)=\epsilon_0w[L+(\kappa-1)x]/d$ from the two displacement-field regions and uses the inward coordinate so that $C'(x)>0$.
Uses the signed balance $dU=\delta W_{\rm bat}-F_xdx$ to obtain the correct fixed-charge and fixed-voltage forces, explicitly accounting for $VdQ$ battery work and all agency signs.

Correctly computes the $166.016\ \mu\mathrm N$ initial inward force and both finite ledgers, including $-2.60882\ \mu\mathrm J$ fixed-charge field-energy change and the fixed-voltage split of $6.64064\ \mu\mathrm J$ battery work into $3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J$ field energy and $3.32032\ \mu\mathrm J$ mechanical work.

commonErrors.description: At fixed voltage, applies $F_x=-(\partial U/\partial x)_V$ to $U=CV^2/2$ while omitting the ideal battery from the energy ledger.
commonErrors.consequence: Because $C'(x)>0$, this predicts an erroneous outward force even though the battery supplies enough energy for both increased storage and inward mechanical work.

commonErrors.description: Assigns battery work the sign $-VdQ$ even though the problem defines positive battery work as energy delivered to the capacitor-mechanical system.
commonErrors.consequence: The fixed-voltage ledger fails energy conservation or incorrectly assigns the battery as absorbing energy while charge enters its positive-terminal plate.

problems.flawedProof: At fixed charge, $U=Q^2/(2C)$ decreases as the slab enters, so $F_x=-dU/dx=Q^2C'/(2C^2)>0$. At fixed voltage, however, $U=CV^2/2$ increases, and therefore $F_x=-dU/dx=-V^2C'/2<0$. For the stated data this gives $F_x=-166.016\ \mu\mathrm N$, so a voltage-controlled capacitor pushes the dielectric outward while an isolated capacitor pulls it inward.

problems.title: Polarization work separates field storage from material heating
problems.objective: Derive the macroscopic local energy balance, separate vacuum field storage from power transferred to polarization and magnetization, and use a prescribed polarization lag to distinguish cyclic material absorption from a universal material state energy.
problems.statement:
Work in a fixed, stationary macroscopic region in SI units. All fields are differentiable, and there are no moving boundaries. The macroscopic Maxwell equations are
$$\nabla\times\mathbf H=\mathbf J_f+\partial_t\mathbf D,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Here $\mathbf J_f$ is free-current density. Use the decompositions
$$\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P,\qquad \mathbf B=\mu_0(\mathbf H+\mathbf M),$$
without assuming linearity, passivity, or an evolution law for $\mathbf P$ or $\mathbf M$.

(a) Starting directly from Maxwell's equations, derive a local energy balance containing $\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B$.

(b) Split this balance into a vacuum storage density, an electromagnetic energy-flux density, and power densities transferred to free current, polarization, and magnetization. Explain why the latter terms are not automatically instantaneous heating rates or derivatives of positive material energies.

(c) In a right-handed Cartesian frame, consider the prescribed, spatially local periodic response
$$\mathbf E(t)=E_0\cos(\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf P(t)=P_0\cos(\omega t-\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf x},$$
with $\mathbf M=0$, $E_0=2.00\times10^4\ \mathrm{V/m}$, $P_0=3.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}$, $f=\omega/(2\pi)=1.00\ \mathrm{kHz}$, and $\delta=30.0^\circ$. This is a prescribed lag; do not assume a Debye or any other relaxation model. Find the instantaneous polarization power density, its cycle average, and the work transferred per unit volume per cycle.

(d) Use the closed cycle in the $(E,P)$ plane to show why $\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P$ cannot generally equal the time derivative of a single-valued universal material energy. Check the limits $\delta=0$ and $\delta<0$.
permittedResults:
The vector identity $
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf H)=\mathbf H\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf H)$ may be used.
For a periodic function of period $T$, its cycle average is $\langle q\rangle=T^{-1}\int_0^T q(t)\,dt$.
No pre-established macroscopic Poynting theorem or material energy formula may be quoted.
problems.strategy: Dot the Ampere-Maxwell equation with $\mathbf E$ and Faraday's law with $\mathbf H$, then use the divergence identity with careful signs. Insert the definitions of $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf B$ only after obtaining the unsplit balance. For the lag example, compute $\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf P}$ directly and relate its cycle integral to the oriented area enclosed in the $(E,P)$ plane.
hints: Combine $\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf H)$ and $\mathbf H\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)$ so that they become the divergence of $\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$.

After substituting $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P$, recognize $\epsilon_0\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf E}$ as a total time derivative, but do not make the same assumption about $\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf P}$.
For the periodic example, use $\sin a\cos b=\tfrac12[\sin(a+b)+\sin(a-b)]$ and compare $\int_0^T E\dot P\,dt$ with $\oint E\,dP$.
problems.solution:
Dotting the Ampere-Maxwell equation with $\mathbf E$ gives
$$\mathbf E\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf H)=\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D.$$
Dotting Faraday's law with $\mathbf H$ gives
$$\mathbf H\cdot(\nabla\times\mathbf E)=-\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
The stated vector identity therefore yields
$$\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E-\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D-\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Thus the unsplit local balance is
$$\boxed{\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D+\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E.}$$
A positive divergence represents net electromagnetic energy leaving a small volume.

Using the specified decompositions,
$$\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf D=\partial_t\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}\right)+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P,$$
$$\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf B=\partial_t\left(\frac{\mu_0H^2}{2}\right)+\mu_0\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf M.$$
Define, for this bookkeeping convention,
$$u_{\mathrm v}=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{\mu_0H^2}{2},\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H.$$
The balance becomes
$$\boxed{\partial_tu_{\mathrm v}+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=-p_{\mathrm{mat}},}$$
where
$$\boxed{p_{\mathrm{mat}}=\mathbf J_f\cdot\mathbf E+\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P+\mu_0\mathbf H\cdot\partial_t\mathbf M.}$$
Every term has units $\mathrm{W/m^3}$; for example, $(\mathrm{V/m})(\mathrm{C/(m^2s)})=\mathrm{W/m^3}$. Positive $p_{\mathrm{mat}}$ is electromagnetic power transferred to the non-vacuum sector under this allocation. It can temporarily become reversible internal, mechanical, or chemical energy rather than heat. Only with additional constitutive and thermodynamic assumptions may part or all of it be identified as heating.

For the prescribed polarization, let $\theta=\omega t$. Then
$$\partial_t\mathbf P=-\omega P_0\sin(\theta-\delta)\,\hat{\mathbf x},$$
so the polarization power density is
$$p_P(t)=\mathbf E\cdot\partial_t\mathbf P=-\omega E_0P_0\cos\theta\sin(\theta-\delta).$$
Equivalently,
$$\boxed{p_P(t)=\frac{\omega E_0P_0}{2}\left[\sin\delta-\sin(2\omega t-\delta)\right].}$$
It is not generally positive at every instant. The oscillatory term averages to zero, giving
$$\boxed{\langle p_P\rangle=\frac{\omega E_0P_0}{2}\sin\delta.}$$
Here $\omega=2\pi(1.00\times10^3)\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $E_0P_0=6.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$. Therefore
$$\boxed{\langle p_P\rangle=94.2\ \mathrm{W/m^3}.}$$
The period is $T=1.00\ \mathrm{ms}$, so the work transferred per unit volume per cycle is
$$W_P=\int_0^T p_P\,dt=\pi E_0P_0\sin\delta,$$
$$\boxed{W_P=9.42\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3\ per\ cycle}.}$$
In a periodic steady material state with no mechanical, chemical, or other exported energy, this positive net transfer must ultimately appear as heat. The prescribed-lag model by itself establishes only net material absorption.

Since $dP=\dot P\,dt$,
$$W_P=\oint E\,dP=\pi E_0P_0\sin\delta.$$
For $\delta\ne0$ this closed-path integral is nonzero. If $E\dot P$ were the total derivative of a single-valued material state energy, its integral around every closed state-space path would have to vanish. Hence no such universal energy exists for an arbitrary lagging polarization.

As a limiting check, when $\delta=0$, $P=(P_0/E_0)E$ and
$$E\dot P=\partial_t\left(\frac{P_0}{2E_0}E^2\right),$$
so the cycle work vanishes and reversible storage is possible. For $\delta<0$, $\langle p_P\rangle<0$; the prescribed medium is active over a cycle and returns energy to the electromagnetic field. Thus positivity cannot be asserted without a passivity assumption.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives the signed local balance from the two curl equations and identifies $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$.
Correctly separates $u_{\mathrm v}$ from all three material-transfer terms and explains why polarization work is not universally instantaneous heat or a positive state energy.
Correctly obtains the lagged-response power, $94.2\ \mathrm{W/m^3}$ average, $9.42\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$ cycle work, and the closed-loop and phase-limit checks.

commonErrors.description: Using the cross-product divergence identity with the two curl terms interchanged or with the wrong overall sign.
commonErrors.consequence: The Poynting-flux divergence acquires the wrong sign, so outward energy flow is incorrectly interpreted as energy entering the volume.

commonErrors.description: Assuming $\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf P}=\tfrac12\partial_t(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf P)$ for an arbitrary polarization history.
commonErrors.consequence: The nonzero lag-cycle work is incorrectly forced to vanish, erasing material absorption and the distinction between reversible storage and dissipation.

problems.flawedProof: After writing $\mathbf D=\epsilon_0\mathbf E+\mathbf P$, define the polarization energy as $u_P=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf P/2$. Then $\mathbf E\cdot\dot{\mathbf P}=\dot u_P$ for any material, so its integral over a period is zero because $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf P$ return to their initial values. Therefore the prescribed phase lag cannot transfer net energy to the material.

problems.title: Maxwell stress gives the pressure on a conducting surface
problems.objective: Derive the vacuum Maxwell stress tensor from local momentum balance, evaluate its traction on a conducting surface, and determine the net direction when electric and magnetic pressures compete.
problems.statement:
A stationary planar conductor occupies $z<0$ and vacuum occupies $z>0$. Let the unit normal pointing outward from the conductor into vacuum be $\hat{\mathbf n}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Immediately outside the conductor,
$$\mathbf E=E_n\hat{\mathbf n},\qquad \mathbf B=\mathbf B_t,\qquad \mathbf B_t\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0,$$
where $B_t=|\mathbf B_t|$. Assume the fields immediately inside are negligible, so the requested force is due to the one-sided exterior fields. Use SI units and the vacuum Maxwell equations.

(a) Starting from the vacuum Lorentz force density $\mathbf f=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B$, derive the momentum balance
$$\mathbf f=\nabla\cdot\mathbf T-\partial_t\mathbf g$$
by finding the Maxwell stress tensor $\mathbf T$ and field momentum density $\mathbf g$.

(b) Use a vanishingly thin pillbox to show that the electromagnetic force per unit area on the conductor is $\mathbf t=\mathbf T_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$. Evaluate this traction for the stated one-sided fields, identifying the electric outward pressure and magnetic inward pressure.

(c) Take $E_n=6.00\times10^7\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $B_t=0.180\ \mathrm T$. Using $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$ and $\mu_0=1.25663706212\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H/m}$, calculate both pressures and the net traction, including its direction.

(d) Check the result independently using the induced surface charge and surface current, with the force evaluated using the average of the fields on the two sides. Also state the equality condition at which the net normal pressure vanishes.
permittedResults: The vacuum Maxwell equations and the Lorentz force density $\mathbf f=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B$ may be used.

The dyadic identity $
abla\cdot(\mathbf a\mathbf a-	frac12a^2\mathbf I)=\mathbf a(
abla\cdot\mathbf a)-\mathbf a	imes(
abla	imes\mathbf a)$ may be used.
The Maxwell stress tensor itself may not be quoted without derivation.
problems.strategy: Rewrite the electric and magnetic parts of the Lorentz force as divergences of dyadics, retaining the time derivative generated by the displacement current. Once the stress tensor is obtained, apply it directly to the declared outward normal. For the independent check, infer the surface sources from field jumps and use half of each discontinuous exterior field as the field acting on its own surface source.
hints: Substitute $\rho=\epsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf J=\mu_0^{-1}\nabla\times\mathbf B-\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E$ into the Lorentz force density.
The remaining time-dependent terms combine through $\partial_t(\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)$.
When calculating $\mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$, use $\mathbf E\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=E_n$ but $\mathbf B_t\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0$; this difference determines the opposite pressure signs.
problems.solution:
In vacuum,
$$\rho=\epsilon_0\nabla\cdot\mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf J=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\nabla\times\mathbf B-\epsilon_0\partial_t\mathbf E.$$
The dyadic identity and Faraday's law give
$$\nabla\cdot\left[\epsilon_0\left(\mathbf E\mathbf E-\frac12E^2\mathbf I\right)\right]
=\rho\mathbf E-\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times(\nabla\times\mathbf E)
=\rho\mathbf E+\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\partial_t\mathbf B.$$
Because $\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$,
$$\nabla\cdot\left[\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\mathbf B\mathbf B-\frac12B^2\mathbf I\right)\right]
=\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B.$$
Ampere-Maxwell's law then gives
$$\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\nabla\times\mathbf B)\times\mathbf B
=\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0(\partial_t\mathbf E)\times\mathbf B.$$
Adding the two equations produces
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf T=\rho\mathbf E+\mathbf J\times\mathbf B+\epsilon_0\partial_t(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B).$$
Consequently,
$$\boxed{\mathbf f=\nabla\cdot\mathbf T-\partial_t\mathbf g,}$$
with
$$\boxed{\mathbf T=\epsilon_0\left(\mathbf E\mathbf E-\frac12E^2\mathbf I\right)+\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\mathbf B\mathbf B-\frac12B^2\mathbf I\right),}$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B.}$$
Both parts of $\mathbf T$ have units of pressure: $\epsilon_0E^2$ and $B^2/\mu_0$ are in $\mathrm{N/m^2}$.

Integrate the momentum balance over a thin pillbox containing the interface. As its thickness tends to zero, the finite field-momentum term vanishes with the volume. The inner-face stress is zero by assumption, while the exterior face has outward pillbox normal $\hat{\mathbf n}$. Thus the force per unit area on the conductor is
$$\mathbf t=\mathbf T_{\mathrm{out}}\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
For the normal electric field,
$$\left(\mathbf E\mathbf E-\frac12E^2\mathbf I\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}
=\frac12E_n^2\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
For the tangential magnetic field, $\mathbf B_t\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}=0$, so
$$\left(\mathbf B_t\mathbf B_t-\frac12B_t^2\mathbf I\right)\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}
=-\frac12B_t^2\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\mathbf t=\left(\frac{\epsilon_0E_n^2}{2}-\frac{B_t^2}{2\mu_0}\right)\hat{\mathbf n}.}$$
The electric pressure
$$\boxed{p_E=\frac{\epsilon_0E_n^2}{2}}$$
is outward, toward the vacuum. The magnetic pressure
$$\boxed{p_B=\frac{B_t^2}{2\mu_0}}$$
is inward, into the conductor.

Numerically,
$$p_E=\frac{(8.8541878128\times10^{-12})(6.00\times10^7)^2}{2}
=1.59375\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}=15.94\ \mathrm{kPa},$$
while
$$p_B=\frac{(0.180)^2}{2(1.25663706212\times10^{-6})}
=1.28916\times10^4\ \mathrm{Pa}=12.89\ \mathrm{kPa}.$$
Hence
$$\boxed{\mathbf t=(3.05\times10^3\ \mathrm{Pa})\hat{\mathbf n}.}$$
The net pressure is $3.05\ \mathrm{kPa}$ outward from the conductor into the vacuum.

For an independent surface-source check, the electric boundary condition gives
$$\sigma=\epsilon_0E_n.$$
The electric field acting on the surface charge excludes its singular self-field and equals the average of the two limiting fields, $\mathbf E_{\mathrm{avg}}=E_n\hat{\mathbf n}/2$. Therefore
$$\frac{\mathbf F_E}{A}=\sigma\mathbf E_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{\epsilon_0E_n^2}{2}\hat{\mathbf n}.$$
The magnetic boundary condition gives the surface current
$$\mathbf K=\hat{\mathbf n}\times\frac{\mathbf B_t}{\mu_0}.$$
Using $\mathbf B_{\mathrm{avg}}=\mathbf B_t/2$,
$$\frac{\mathbf F_B}{A}=\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{avg}}
=\frac{(\hat{\mathbf n}\times\mathbf B_t)\times\mathbf B_t}{2\mu_0}
=-\frac{B_t^2}{2\mu_0}\hat{\mathbf n},$$
which independently confirms both signs and factors of one-half.

The net pressure vanishes when
$$\epsilon_0E_n^2=\frac{B_t^2}{\mu_0},$$
or
$$\boxed{|E_n|=cB_t,\qquad c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}}.}$$
For the numerical fields, $cB_t\approx5.40\times10^7\ \mathrm{V/m}<|E_n|$, consistently predicting an outward net traction. If nonzero fields existed inside the conductor, the required traction would instead be the stress jump $(\mathbf T_{\mathrm{out}}-\mathbf T_{\mathrm{in}})\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives both the vacuum Maxwell stress tensor and $\mathbf g=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ from Maxwell's equations and the Lorentz force density.
Correctly applies the declared outward normal to obtain electric outward pressure $\epsilon_0E_n^2/2$ and magnetic inward pressure $B_t^2/(2\mu_0)$.
Correctly computes $15.94\ \mathrm{kPa}$ electric, $12.89\ \mathrm{kPa}$ magnetic, and $3.05\ \mathrm{kPa}$ net outward, with a valid surface-source or equality-condition check.

commonErrors.description: Treating the magnetic energy density $B_t^2/(2\mu_0)$ as an outward isotropic pressure without evaluating the tensor traction.
commonErrors.consequence: The magnetic contribution receives the wrong sign, and the two pressures are incorrectly added rather than opposed.

commonErrors.description: Using $-\hat{\mathbf n}$ as the conductor's outward normal or applying the vacuum pillbox normal inconsistently.
commonErrors.consequence: The final physical direction is reversed even if the pressure magnitudes are calculated correctly.

problems.flawedProof: The electric and magnetic field energy densities are both positive, so each must push outward on the conductor. Thus the total pressure is $p=\epsilon_0E_n^2/2+B_t^2/(2\mu_0)=15.94\ \mathrm{kPa}+12.89\ \mathrm{kPa}=28.83\ \mathrm{kPa}$ outward. The tensor orientation is unnecessary because energy density is already pressure.

problems.title: Stress and energy agree on the force pulling a dielectric wedge
problems.objective: Derive the fixed-voltage insertion force on a dielectric wedge by an energy ledger that includes battery work, reproduce it with macroscopic Maxwell stress, and verify the agreement numerically and dimensionally.
problems.statement:
Two long, perfectly conducting parallel plates occupy $0<x<L$, $0<y<w$, at $z=0$ and $z=d$. The lower plate is maintained at potential $V$ and the upper plate at zero, so the principal field points along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. A rigid linear, homogeneous, isotropic dielectric wedge has relative permittivity $\epsilon_r$ and fills the entire gap over the footprint $0<x'<x$, $0<y<w$; its active portion has constant width $w$, while any remote taper lies outside the capacitor. Vacuum fills the remaining footprint. The wedge is translated quasistatically in the $+\hat{\mathbf x}$ direction by increasing $x$. Assume $d\ll w,L$, that the dielectric nose and both plate ends are separated by several gap widths, and that electrostriction, gravity, friction, and position-dependent external fringe capacitance are negligible. Local fringing near the dielectric nose may transmit force but must lie inside the stress control surface. The voltage is held fixed by an ideal battery. This is electrostatics, so no phasor convention is used.

(a) Derive $C(x)$ directly from the plate charge. Use a battery-field-mechanical energy ledger to show why the force is $+d(CV^2/2)/dx$, rather than the negative derivative of the stored field energy at fixed voltage.

(b) Enclose the dielectric nose with a rectangular control surface. Its rear face lies in the uniform dielectric region with outward normal $-\hat{\mathbf x}$, and its front face lies in the uniform vacuum region with outward normal $+\hat{\mathbf x}$. Evaluate the $x$-directed Maxwell-stress traction on these faces and show that it gives the same force. Explain why the other faces do not contribute to the lateral force under the stated approximation.

(c) For $L=0.400\,\mathrm{m}$, $x=0.150\,\mathrm{m}$, $w=0.0800\,\mathrm{m}$, $d=2.00\,\mathrm{mm}$, $\epsilon_r=4.20$, and $V=500\,\mathrm{V}$, calculate the force. Independently check it using the energy-density difference, audit its SI dimensions, and state two limiting checks.
permittedResults: In a linear isotropic dielectric, $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ with $\epsilon=\epsilon_r\epsilon_0$, and the electrostatic energy density is $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$.
The macroscopic electrostatic stress tensor for a rigid linear isotropic medium with electrostriction neglected is $T_{ij}=E_iD_j-\delta_{ij}(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D)/2$.
For quasistatic charge $dQ$ delivered by an ideal source at voltage $V$, the source supplies energy $V\,dQ$.
problems.strategy: Treat the dielectric-filled and vacuum-filled footprints as parallel regions sharing the same plate voltage. First derive their free plate charges and hence $C(x)$. At fixed voltage, distinguish battery work from the change in field energy. For the independent stress calculation, place the control faces in uniform regions so that only the difference between dielectric and vacuum normal stresses remains.
hints: Both side-by-side regions have field magnitude $V/d$. Integrate $\mathbf D\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}$ over the lower plate separately over areas $wx$ and $w(L-x)$.
During an increment $dx$ at fixed $V$, use $dQ=V\,dC$ and compare the battery work $V\,dQ$ with $d(CV^2/2)$. The difference is mechanical work done by the field.
On either control face normal to $\hat{\mathbf x}$, the field has no $x$ component, so $T_{xx}=-\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$. Carefully include the opposite outward normals of the front and rear faces.
problems.solution:
The leading parallel-plate field is
$$\mathbf E=\frac{V}{d}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The dielectric and vacuum regions share this voltage because both touch the same conducting plates. The free charge on the lower plate is therefore
$$Q(x)=\int \mathbf D\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}\,dA
=\epsilon\frac{V}{d}wx+\epsilon_0\frac{V}{d}w(L-x).$$
Thus
$$C(x)=\frac{Q}{V}=\frac{w}{d}\left[\epsilon_0L+(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)x\right],$$
so
$$\frac{dC}{dx}=\frac{w}{d}(\epsilon-\epsilon_0).$$

The field energy follows by integrating $u=\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D/2$ over both volumes:
$$U_{\mathrm f}=\frac12\epsilon E^2wxd+\frac12\epsilon_0E^2w(L-x)d
=\frac12C(x)V^2.$$
At fixed $V$, an increment $dC$ requires $dQ=V\,dC$. The battery supplies
$$dW_{\mathrm b}=V\,dQ=V^2dC,$$
while the field-energy increase is
$$dU_{\mathrm f}=\frac12V^2dC.$$
Energy conservation in the quasistatic process gives $dW_{\mathrm b}=dU_{\mathrm f}+dW_{\mathrm{mech}}$, where $dW_{\mathrm{mech}}$ is work done by the electric field on the wedge. Hence
$$dW_{\mathrm{mech}}=\frac12V^2dC,$$
and the insertion force is
$$F_x=\frac{dW_{\mathrm{mech}}}{dx}=\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac12CV^2\right)
=\frac12(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\frac{w}{d}V^2>0.$$
Equivalently, the fixed-voltage mechanical potential is $U_{\mathrm f}-VQ=-CV^2/2$, whose negative derivative gives the same positive force.

For the stress calculation, define
$$u_{\mathrm d}=\frac12\epsilon E^2,\qquad u_0=\frac12\epsilon_0E^2.$$
Because $E_x=0$, the normal stress on a face perpendicular to $\hat{\mathbf x}$ is $T_{xx}=-u$. On the rear dielectric face, whose outward normal is $-\hat{\mathbf x}$, the $x$ traction is
$$\left(\mathbf T_{\mathrm d}\cdot(-\hat{\mathbf x})\right)_x=+u_{\mathrm d}.$$
On the front vacuum face, whose outward normal is $+\hat{\mathbf x}$, it is
$$\left(\mathbf T_0\cdot\hat{\mathbf x}\right)_x=-u_0.$$
Each face has area $wd$, so the net stress force is
$$F_x=(u_{\mathrm d}-u_0)wd
=\frac12(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\left(\frac{V}{d}\right)^2wd
=\frac12(\epsilon-\epsilon_0)\frac{w}{d}V^2.$$
This agrees with the energy result. The faces normal to $\hat{\mathbf y}$ have no $x$ traction in the uniform approximation. On surfaces immediately adjacent to ideal conductors, the tangential component $E_x$ vanishes, so $T_{xz}=E_xD_z=0$. The localized nose fringe field is enclosed rather than discarded; placing the front and rear faces in uniform regions makes its integrated effect equal to the stress difference above.

Numerically,
$$\frac{dC}{dx}=\epsilon_0(\epsilon_r-1)\frac{w}{d}
=(8.85419\times10^{-12})(3.20)\frac{0.0800}{0.00200}
=1.13334\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{F/m}.$$
Therefore
$$F_x=\frac12(500)^2(1.13334\times10^{-9})
=1.42\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N,$$
directed into the capacitor. Independently, $E=2.50\times10^5\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and
$$u_{\mathrm d}-u_0=\frac12\epsilon_0(3.20)E^2=0.885\,\mathrm{J/m^3}.$$
Multiplication by $wd=(0.0800)(0.00200)=1.60\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{m^2}$ gives $1.42\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N$. Dimensionally, $V^2(dC/dx)$ has units $\mathrm{V^2F/m}=\mathrm{J/m}=\mathrm N$. The force vanishes when $\epsilon_r\to1$ or $V\to0$, and it is unchanged when the voltage polarity is reversed.
rubricCriteria: Derives $C(x)$ from the two plate-charge integrals and obtains the positive fixed-voltage force only after accounting for both $V\,dQ$ battery work and the field-energy change.
Uses the stated front and rear normals with $T_{xx}=-u$ to obtain $(u_{\mathrm d}-u_0)wd$, and specifically explains the absence of lateral traction from the remaining control faces.
Obtains $F_x=1.42\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm N$ in the insertion direction and supplies a consistent energy-density, dimensional, and limiting check.

commonErrors.description: Treating the fixed-voltage capacitor as an isolated system and writing $F_x=-d(CV^2/2)/dx$ without including the battery energy $V\,dQ$.
commonErrors.consequence: The predicted force has the wrong sign and incorrectly says the dielectric is expelled.

commonErrors.description: Using the dielectric stress or energy density alone instead of subtracting the vacuum traction on the opposite control face.
commonErrors.consequence: The result remains nonzero when $\epsilon_r=1$ and overestimates the physical insertion force.

problems.flawedProof: The capacitor stores $U=C(x)V^2/2$. Since force is always minus the derivative of stored energy, $F_x=-dU/dx=-(V^2/2)(dC/dx)$. Because $dC/dx>0$, the wedge is pushed toward decreasing $x$. Thus a dielectric is expelled from a capacitor held at fixed voltage.

problems.title: An anisotropic polarizable body feels torque without net force
problems.objective: Construct the induced-dipole energy of an anisotropic body, including the one-half factor, and use it to calculate torque, equilibrium orientations, and translational force in a uniform electric field.
problems.statement:
A small neutral body is confined to rotate in the $xy$ plane. Its orthonormal body axes are $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ and $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$, with $\hat{\mathbf e}_1\times\hat{\mathbf e}_2=\hat{\mathbf z}$. It has no permanent dipole and has the linear polarizability tensor
$$\boldsymbol\alpha=\alpha_1\hat{\mathbf e}_1\hat{\mathbf e}_1+\alpha_2\hat{\mathbf e}_2\hat{\mathbf e}_2,$$
where $\alpha_1,\alpha_2>0$. An ideal fixed source produces a static, spatially uniform field
$$\mathbf E=E(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf e}_1+\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf e}_2),$$
where positive $\theta$ is measured from $\hat{\mathbf e}_1$ toward $\hat{\mathbf e}_2$. If the body's laboratory orientation is $\phi$ and the fixed field direction is $\beta$, then $\theta=\beta-\phi$. Treat the body in the electric-dipole approximation, neglect field gradients, higher multipoles, saturation, and interactions with boundaries. No phasors are used.

(a) Model the reversible internal polarization energy along each principal axis and minimize over the induced dipole components. Derive the equilibrium induced dipole and its field-dependent energy, explicitly establishing the factor $1/2$.
