commonErrors.consequence: Misses the independent permeability-to-permittivity ratio.

commonErrors.description: Uses rms formulas with peak-amplitude equations or drops the factor of two.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces inconsistent fields and average intensity.

problems.flawedProof: Both media have refractive index three, so they must have the same speed and impedance. Equal intensity then gives identical E, H, and B amplitudes in the two waves.

problems.title: Electric and magnetic energies are equal in a single traveling wave
problems.objective: Use the plane-wave impedance relation to prove equality of average electric and magnetic energies and verify it numerically.
problems.statement:
A monochromatic plane wave travels in a lossless nondispersive medium. Its peak amplitudes obey $H_0=E_0/\eta$, where $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$. (a) Show that
$$\langle u_E\rangle=\frac{\epsilon E_0^2}{4},\qquad
\langle u_H\rangle=\frac{\mu H_0^2}{4}$$
are equal. (b) Show that $\langle S\rangle=E_0H_0/2=E_0^2/(2\eta)$. (c) Evaluate $H_0$, both energy contributions, total average energy density, and intensity for $\epsilon=4\epsilon_0$, $\mu=\mu_0$, and $E_0=100\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, using $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\eta_0=376.7303137\ \Omega$.
permittedResults: $\langle\cos^2\rangle=1/2$.
$\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$ and $H_0=E_0/\eta$.
$\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$.
problems.strategy: Substitute H0=E0/eta into the magnetic energy before inserting numbers. Keep the peak-to-average factor one half in both energy and flux.
hints: $\mu/\eta^2=\epsilon$.
Here $\eta=\eta_0/2$.
The total energy is twice either equal contribution.
problems.solution:
Using $H_0=E_0/\eta$ and $\eta^2=\mu/\epsilon$,
$$\langle u_H\rangle=\frac{\mu E_0^2}{4\eta^2}
=\frac{\epsilon E_0^2}{4}=\langle u_E\rangle.$$
The in-phase fields also give
$$\langle S\rangle=\frac{E_0H_0}{2}=\frac{E_0^2}{2\eta}.$$
For the stated medium, $\eta=\eta_0/2=188.365\ \Omega$, so
$$H_0=0.530884\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
Each average energy contribution is
$$\langle u_E\rangle=\langle u_H\rangle=8.85419\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}},$$
the total is $1.77084\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, and
$$\langle S\rangle=26.5442\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.$$
All quantities are positive and vanish quadratically with E0.
rubricCriteria: Proves electric-magnetic energy equality using the impedance relation.
Derives the peak-amplitude cycle-averaged Poynting flux.
Reports all numerical field, energy, and intensity values with correct units.

commonErrors.description: Uses peak squared fields without averaging cosine squared.
commonErrors.consequence: Doubles both average energy and intensity.

commonErrors.description: Sets E0 equal to H0 numerically.
commonErrors.consequence: Ignores the dimensional impedance relation.

problems.flawedProof: Because E and H are in phase, their numerical amplitudes are equal. The electric and magnetic energies are therefore equal without any material factors, and the average intensity is $E_0H_0$.

problems.title: Absorption and reflection transfer different momentum for the same incident energy
problems.objective: Derive normal radiation pressure from vacuum field momentum and the Maxwell stress tensor, then reconcile the different absorber and mirror forces with complete energy and momentum ledgers.
problems.statement:
Vacuum fills $z<0$. A planar opaque panel has its illuminated face at $z=0$, with front-face normal $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, and an incident plane wave propagates in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Positive force on the panel is defined along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use real fields $\mathbf E_i=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B_i=(E_0/c)\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}$; equivalently, the phasor convention is $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{i(kz-\omega t)}\}$. The vacuum relations are $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$, $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/\mu_0$, $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$, and
$$T_{ij}=\epsilon_0\left(E_iE_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}E^2\right)+\frac1{\mu_0}\left(B_iB_j-\frac12\delta_{ij}B^2\right).$$
For a control volume around the panel, take the entrance-plane outward normal as $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ and the exit-plane outward normal as $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Assume steady periodic fields, normal incidence, negligible edge diffraction, and a panel held fixed so that mirror recoil-energy corrections are negligible. (a) Derive $I=c\langle u\rangle$, $\langle\mathbf g\rangle=(I/c^2)\hat{\mathbf z}$, and the incident-wave value of $\langle T_{zz}\rangle$. (b) If the reflected and transmitted intensities are $I_r$ and $I_t$, use Maxwell stress and momentum balance to derive the pressure. Specialize to perfect absorption and perfect specular reflection. (c) For an incident pulse of energy $U$, close separate energy and momentum ledgers for the absorber and mirror. Explain why pressure must not be identified with energy density merely because the two have the same SI dimensions. (d) A uniform beam of intensity $1.50\times10^4\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$ illuminates a finite panel of area $6.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ for $20.0\ \mathrm{s}$. Calculate the pressures, forces, intercepted energy, and impulses for perfect absorption and reflection. Use $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
permittedResults: The vacuum momentum balance $\mathbf F_{\mathrm{matter}}=\oint \mathbf T\cdot\hat{\mathbf n}\,dA-d(\int\mathbf g\,dV)/dt$.
The harmonic average $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$.
Energy conservation for a fixed passive panel, with no transmitted field for an opaque panel.
problems.strategy: First derive the energy and momentum densities of one traveling wave. Then evaluate the longitudinal Maxwell stress, including the cancellation of incident-reflected interference terms in $T_{zz}$. Apply the stress integral on the two faces of a control volume, and independently check the result by comparing the initial and final momenta of a finite pulse.
hints: For a transverse vacuum wave, the electric and magnetic terms in $u$ are equal, while both contribute negatively to $T_{zz}$.
On the incident side write $\mathbf E=(E_i+E_r)\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf B=(E_i-E_r)\hat{\mathbf y}/c$; inspect what happens to the cross terms in $T_{zz}$.
In the pulse ledger, reflected energy travels in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, so its momentum has the opposite sign even though its energy remains positive.
problems.solution:
The instantaneous vacuum energy density is
$$u=\frac12\epsilon_0E_i^2+\frac1{2\mu_0}B_i^2=\epsilon_0E_i^2,$$
because $B_i=E_i/c$ and $1/(\mu_0c^2)=\epsilon_0$. Also,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{E_iB_i}{\mu_0}\hat{\mathbf z}=\epsilon_0cE_i^2\hat{\mathbf z}=cu\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Thus
$$I=\langle S_z\rangle=c\langle u\rangle,\qquad \langle\mathbf g\rangle=\frac{\langle\mathbf S\rangle}{c^2}=\frac{I}{c^2}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The longitudinal stress is
$$T_{zz}=-\frac12\epsilon_0E_i^2-\frac1{2\mu_0}B_i^2=-u,$$
so $\langle T_{zz}\rangle=-I/c$.

On the incident side, represent the signed transverse fields as
$$\mathbf E=(E_i+E_r)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf B=\frac{E_i-E_r}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
The minus sign in the reflected magnetic field follows from its propagation in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$. Therefore
$$T_{zz}=-\frac12\epsilon_0(E_i+E_r)^2-\frac1{2\mu_0c^2}(E_i-E_r)^2=-\epsilon_0(E_i^2+E_r^2).$$
The interference terms cancel exactly, giving
$$\langle T_{zz}\rangle_{\mathrm{left}}=-\frac{I_i+I_r}{c}.$$
On the transmitted side, $\langle T_{zz}\rangle_{\mathrm{right}}=-I_t/c$. The time-averaged field-momentum derivative vanishes in steady state. The entrance normal is $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ and the exit normal is $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, so the force per area is
$$p=\frac{F_z}{A}=\frac{I_i+I_r-I_t}{c}.$$
With $R=I_r/I_i$, $T=I_t/I_i$, and absorbed fraction $\mathcal A=1-R-T$,
$$p=\frac{(\mathcal A+2R)I_i}{c}.$$
Hence a perfectly absorbing opaque panel has
$$p_{\mathrm{abs}}=\frac{I_i}{c},$$
while a perfect mirror has
$$p_{\mathrm{refl}}=\frac{2I_i}{c}.$$
The transparent limit $R=0$, $T=1$ gives $p=0$, as required.

For an incident pulse, $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$ implies incident momentum $+U\hat{\mathbf z}/c$. A perfect absorber leaves no outgoing field: the panel-support system receives momentum $+U\hat{\mathbf z}/c$, while the energy $U$ becomes internal energy, principally heat. A fixed perfect mirror returns field energy $U$ but the outgoing field momentum is $-U\hat{\mathbf z}/c$. The mirror-support impulse is therefore
$$\Delta\mathbf p_{\mathrm{matter}}=\frac{U}{c}\hat{\mathbf z}-\left(-\frac{U}{c}\hat{\mathbf z}\right)=\frac{2U}{c}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The ideal fixed mirror does no mechanical work because its displacement is zero; the field retains its energy. For a freely recoiling finite-mass mirror, a small Doppler energy transfer would have to be included.

Although $I/c$, energy density, and pressure all have units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{N\,m^{-2}}$, dimensional agreement does not establish equality. The equality for absorption follows from the stress or momentum flux. Indeed, reflection gives twice the pressure for the same incident energy density.

Numerically, the intercepted power and energy are
$$P=IA=(1.50\times10^4)(6.00\times10^{-2})=9.00\times10^2\ \mathrm W,$$
$$U=P\Delta t=(9.00\times10^2)(20.0)=1.80\times10^4\ \mathrm J.$$
For absorption,
$$p_{\mathrm{abs}}=\frac{1.50\times10^4}{2.99792458\times10^8}=5.00\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{Pa},$$
$$F_{\mathrm{abs}}=pA=3.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm N,\qquad J_{\mathrm{abs}}=F\Delta t=6.00\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{N\,s}=\frac{U}{c}.$$
For reflection,
$$p_{\mathrm{refl}}=1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{Pa},$$
$$F_{\mathrm{refl}}=6.00\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm N,\qquad J_{\mathrm{refl}}=1.20\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{N\,s}=\frac{2U}{c}.$$
The pressure unit check is $(\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}})/(\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})=\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{Pa}$, while the pulse-momentum calculation independently verifies both factors.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives $\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2$, $I=c\langle u\rangle$, and the negative longitudinal stress of a transverse vacuum wave.
Uses the stated control-volume normals to obtain $p=(I_i+I_r-I_t)/c$ and explains the reflected momentum sign that produces the factor of two.
Calculates both finite-panel ledgers with correct SI units and distinguishes stress-based pressure from a dimensional identification with energy density.

commonErrors.description: Treating the reflected pulse momentum as $+U/c$ because its energy is positive, rather than as $-U/c$ because it propagates in $-\hat{\mathbf z}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The mirror is assigned zero or incorrect impulse instead of $2U/c$.

commonErrors.description: Declaring $p=\langle u\rangle$ solely from the shared units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}=\mathrm{Pa}$ and applying that equality to both surface types.
commonErrors.consequence: The Maxwell-stress origin of pressure is lost and absorption is incorrectly predicted to exert the same pressure as reflection.

problems.flawedProof: Since pressure and energy density both have units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$, one may set $p=\langle u\rangle=I/c$ for any illuminated surface. A reflected pulse still has positive energy $U$, so its momentum after reflection is also $+U/c$. Its momentum therefore does not change, and a perfect mirror experiences the same pressure $I/c$ as an absorber.

problems.title: Energy velocity equals phase speed only under declared material assumptions
problems.objective: Prove that averaged electromagnetic energy is transported at the phase speed in an ideal homogeneous medium and identify precisely why the conclusion need not survive dispersion or loss.
problems.statement:
Consider an unbounded, homogeneous, time-independent medium with no free charge or current. Its constitutive laws are local, linear, isotropic, and uncoupled:
$$\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E,\qquad \mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H,$$
where $\epsilon>0$ and $\mu>0$ are real scalar constants independent of frequency. Thus the medium is lossless and nondispersive, with no conductivity or magnetoelectric coupling. A monochromatic plane wave propagates along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ with $\mathbf E$ along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ and $\mathbf H$ along $\hat{\mathbf y}$. Use the phasor convention $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf F}(z)e^{-i\omega t}\}$, with $\widetilde{\mathbf F}\propto e^{ikz}$ and $k>0$. (a) Starting from the source-free Maxwell curl equations, derive the dispersion relation and field-amplitude ratio. (b) Derive the instantaneous Poynting theorem for the declared constitutive model and hence its electromagnetic energy density. (c) Prove that the energy velocity defined by $\mathbf v_E=\langle\mathbf S\rangle/\langle u\rangle$ is
$$\mathbf v_E=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\hat{\mathbf z},$$
and equals the phase-velocity vector. (d) Verify the theorem for $\epsilon=3.00\epsilon_0$, $\mu=1.20\mu_0$, and peak electric amplitude $E_0=100\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ by calculating the impedance, magnetic amplitude, average flux, average energy density, and both velocities. Use $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and $Z_0=376.730\ \Omega$. (e) List the assumptions used and give a specific warning showing which proof step fails in a dispersive or lossy medium, without developing a causality theory.
permittedResults: The source-free curl equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$.

The vector identity $
abla\cdot(\mathbf E	imes\mathbf H)=\mathbf H\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf E)-\mathbf E\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf H)$.
The harmonic average $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$ and the vacuum identity $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$.
problems.strategy: Use the phasor curl equations first to determine $k$ and the wave impedance. Derive rather than assume the appropriate energy density by combining the time-domain curl equations. Then use equality of the cycle-averaged electric and magnetic energies to simplify the flux-to-energy ratio, and audit the theorem by locating the exact constitutive steps that fail with loss or dispersion.
hints: With the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law gives $k\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=\omega\mu\widetilde{\mathbf H}$.
Dot the time-domain Faraday equation with $\mathbf H$, dot the Ampere-Maxwell equation with $\mathbf E$, and use the divergence identity.
After finding $H_0/E_0$, compare $\mu H_0^2$ with $\epsilon E_0^2$ before forming $\langle S\rangle/\langle u\rangle$.
problems.solution:
For phasors proportional to $e^{ikz}$, Faraday's law gives
$$ik\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\mu\widetilde{\mathbf H},$$
so
$$\widetilde{\mathbf H}=\frac{k}{\omega\mu}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}.$$
The Ampere-Maxwell equation gives
$$ik\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}=-i\omega\epsilon\widetilde{\mathbf E}.$$
Substitution, using $\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E})=-\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ for a transverse wave, yields
$$k^2=\omega^2\mu\epsilon.$$
For $k>0$,
$$k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon},\qquad v_p=\frac{\omega}{k}=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}.$$
The field ratio is
$$\frac{E_0}{H_0}=\frac{\omega\mu}{k}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}}\equiv Z,$$
where $Z$ is real because the medium is lossless under the stated model.

To derive the energy density, use the time-domain equations
$$\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\mu\frac{\partial\mathbf H}{\partial t},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf H=\epsilon\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
The divergence identity gives
$$\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=-\mu\mathbf H\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf H}{\partial t}-\epsilon\mathbf E\cdot\frac{\partial\mathbf E}{\partial t}.$$
Because $\epsilon$ and $\mu$ are real, time-independent constants, this becomes
$$\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(\frac12\epsilon E^2+\frac12\mu H^2\right)+\nabla\cdot(\mathbf E\times\mathbf H)=0.$$
Thus
$$u=\frac12\epsilon E^2+\frac12\mu H^2,\qquad \mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H.$$
The real fields may be written
$$\mathbf E=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf H=H_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Therefore
$$\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\frac12E_0H_0\hat{\mathbf z},$$
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac14\epsilon E_0^2+\frac14\mu H_0^2.$$
Since $H_0=E_0\sqrt{\epsilon/\mu}$, the electric and magnetic contributions are equal:
$$\mu H_0^2=\epsilon E_0^2.$$
Consequently,
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac12\epsilon E_0^2,$$
while
$$\langle S\rangle=\frac12E_0^2\sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{\mu}}.$$
Their ratio is
$$\mathbf v_E=\frac{\langle\mathbf S\rangle}{\langle u\rangle}=\frac1{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}\hat{\mathbf z}=v_p\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Its dimensions are $(\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}})/(\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}})=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The vacuum limit $\epsilon=\epsilon_0$, $\mu=\mu_0$ gives $v_E=v_p=c$, providing an independent check.

For the numerical medium,
$$\epsilon=2.65626\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}},\qquad \mu=1.50796\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}.$$
The impedance is
$$Z=Z_0\sqrt{\frac{1.20}{3.00}}=(376.730)\sqrt{0.400}=2.3827\times10^2\ \Omega.$$
Thus
$$H_0=\frac{E_0}{Z}=0.4197\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}.$$
The average flux and energy density are
$$\langle S\rangle=\frac12E_0H_0=20.99\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac12\epsilon E_0^2=1.328\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$
Hence
$$v_E=\frac{20.99}{1.328\times10^{-7}}=1.580\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$
Independently,
$$v_p=\frac{c}{\sqrt{(3.00)(1.20)}}=1.580\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},$$
which verifies the theorem.

The proof used linearity; homogeneity; isotropic scalar $\epsilon$ and $\mu$; local and instantaneous constitutive response; frequency independence; real positive parameters; absence of conductivity, free sources, and magnetoelectric coupling; and propagation away from interfaces. In a dispersive medium, $\mathbf D(t)$ is not generally an instantaneous constant multiple of $\mathbf E(t)$, so $\mathbf E\cdot\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$ cannot be replaced by $\partial(\epsilon E^2/2)/\partial t$. Material degrees of freedom then contribute to stored energy, and energy velocity need not equal phase velocity. In a lossy medium with conductivity $\sigma>0$, Ampere's law contains $\sigma\mathbf E$, and the energy equation acquires $-\sigma E^2$ on its right-hand side. The propagation constant and impedance are then generally complex, so the lossless proof and its velocity equality do not apply.
rubricCriteria: Derives $k^2=\omega^2\mu\epsilon$ and $E_0/H_0=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$ with signs consistent with the declared propagation and phasor convention.
Derives the nondispersive energy density from Maxwell's equations and uses both electric and magnetic contributions to prove $\langle\mathbf S\rangle/\langle u\rangle=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$.
Completes the numerical verification and identifies the precise constitutive or conservation-law step invalidated by dispersion or loss.

commonErrors.description: Using only $\epsilon E^2/2$ as the instantaneous energy density, or only $\epsilon E_0^2/4$ after averaging, while omitting the equal magnetic contribution.
commonErrors.consequence: The calculated energy velocity is twice the phase speed.

commonErrors.description: Applying the real, frequency-independent formulas unchanged when $\epsilon$, $\mu$, or the propagation constant are frequency-dependent or complex.
commonErrors.consequence: The proof ignores material stored energy or dissipation and asserts an energy-velocity equality outside its assumptions.

problems.flawedProof: The average energy density is just the electric part, $\langle u\rangle=\epsilon E_0^2/4$. Since $H_0=E_0\sqrt{\epsilon/\mu}$, the average Poynting flux is $\langle S\rangle=E_0^2\sqrt{\epsilon/\mu}/2$. Therefore $\langle S\rangle/\langle u\rangle=2/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$. This argument uses only the values of $\epsilon$ and $\mu$, so the same expression remains valid if they are frequency-dependent or complex in a lossy material.

problems.title: Impedance and speed determine both permittivity and permeability
problems.objective: Recover both constitutive parameters of a lossless medium from independent speed and impedance measurements, then use the reconstructed parameters to determine wave amplitudes, energy density, and power flow with dimensional and physical checks.
problems.statement: A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, nondispersive, lossless medium fills all space and has real positive permittivity $\epsilon$ and permeability $\mu$. There are no free charges or currents. Use the phasor convention $\mathbf E(\mathbf r,t)=\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf E}(\mathbf r)e^{-i\omega t}\}$. A linearly polarized plane wave travels in the $+z$ direction with $\mathbf E\parallel\hat{\mathbf x}$, so choose $\mathbf H\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}$ and define the positive intrinsic impedance by $\eta=E_0/H_0$. Measurements give $v=2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $\eta=250\ \Omega$, and peak electric-field amplitude $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$. (a) Starting from the source-free Maxwell equations and the constitutive laws, derive $\epsilon=1/(\eta v)$ and $\mu=\eta/v$. (b) Calculate $\epsilon$ and $\mu$. (c) Predict the peak magnetic flux density $B_0$, the cycle-averaged total electromagnetic energy density $\langle u\rangle$, and the cycle-averaged intensity $\langle\mathbf S\rangle$. (d) Audit the SI units and positivity of the inferred parameters, and independently check the intensity using both energy transport and field amplitudes.
permittedResults: The source-free macroscopic Maxwell equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\partial\mathbf D/\partial t$.
The constitutive laws $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$ for the stated medium.
The definitions $u=(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)/2$ and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$, together with $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$.
problems.strategy: Represent the wave by mutually orthogonal electric and magnetic phasors proportional to $e^{ikz}$. Apply both curl equations separately: one expresses $E_0/H_0$ as $\mu v$, while the other expresses it as $1/(\epsilon v)$. After reconstructing the material parameters, exploit the equality of electric and magnetic energy contributions in a traveling lossless plane wave and cross-check $\langle S\rangle$ against $v\langle u\rangle$.
hints: With the stated convention, the phasor curl equations are $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}$ and $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}=-i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf D}$.
For phasors proportional to $e^{ikz}$, use $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}=\hat{\mathbf y}$ and $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=-\hat{\mathbf x}$, then set $v=\omega/k$.
Compute $H_0=E_0/\eta$ and $B_0=\mu H_0$; for the checks, compare $E_0H_0/2$, $v\langle u\rangle$, and $E_0^2/(2\eta)$.
problems.solution:
Take
$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}=E_0e^{ikz}\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf H}=H_0e^{ikz}\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad k>0.$$
Faraday's law gives
$$ikE_0\hat{\mathbf y}=i\omega\mu H_0\hat{\mathbf y},$$
so
$$\eta=\frac{E_0}{H_0}=\frac{\omega\mu}{k}=\mu v.$$
The Ampere-Maxwell equation gives
$$-ikH_0\hat{\mathbf x}=-i\omega\epsilon E_0\hat{\mathbf x},$$
so
$$\eta=\frac{E_0}{H_0}=\frac{k}{\omega\epsilon}=\frac{1}{\epsilon v}.$$
Solving these two independently derived relations yields
$$\boxed{\epsilon=\frac{1}{\eta v}},\qquad \boxed{\mu=\frac{\eta}{v}}.$$
Numerically,
$$\epsilon=\frac{1}{(250\ \Omega)(2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}})}=2.00\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}},$$
$$\mu=\frac{250\ \Omega}{2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}=1.25\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}.$$
The magnetic-field amplitudes are
$$H_0=\frac{E_0}{\eta}=0.480\ \mathrm{A\,m^{-1}},$$
$$B_0=\mu H_0=\frac{E_0}{v}=6.00\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm T.$$
The magnetic field points along $+\hat{\mathbf y}$, so the power flow is along $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=+\hat{\mathbf z}$. For the real sinusoidal fields, the averaged electric contribution is $\epsilon E_0^2/4$. From $B_0=E_0/v$ and $v^2=1/(\mu\epsilon)$, the averaged magnetic contribution is also $\epsilon E_0^2/4$. Hence
$$\langle u\rangle=\frac{\epsilon E_0^2}{2}=\frac{(2.00\times10^{-11})(120)^2}{2}=1.44\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}.$$
The averaged Poynting vector is
$$\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\frac{E_0H_0}{2}\hat{\mathbf z}=\frac{E_0^2}{2\eta}\hat{\mathbf z}=28.8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
The SI audits are
$$[\epsilon]=\frac{1}{\Omega(\mathrm{m/s})}=\frac{\mathrm s}{\Omega\,\mathrm m}=\mathrm{F/m},\qquad [\mu]=\frac{\Omega}{\mathrm{m/s}}=\frac{\Omega\,\mathrm s}{\mathrm m}=\mathrm{H/m},$$
$$[B_0]=\frac{\mathrm{V/m}}{\mathrm{m/s}}=\mathrm{V\,s/m^2}=\mathrm T,$$
and $E_0^2/\eta$ has units $\mathrm{W/m^2}$. Since the measured $v$ and the magnitude-defined $\eta$ are positive, both reconstructed constitutive parameters are positive, as assumed for this passive lossless medium. Reconstructing the measurements gives
$$\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}}=2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\epsilon}}=250\ \Omega.$$
Finally, the independent energy-transport check is
$$v\langle u\rangle=(2.00\times10^8)(1.44\times10^{-7})=28.8\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
which agrees with $E_0H_0/2$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly applies both phasor curl equations with the stated orientation to derive $\eta=\mu v=1/(\epsilon v)$ and hence both constitutive parameters.
Correctly obtains $\epsilon$, $\mu$, $H_0$, $B_0$, $\langle u\rangle$, and the directed intensity with peak rather than RMS amplitudes.
Explicitly verifies SI dimensions, positive material parameters, equal averaged electric and magnetic energies, and agreement between $v\langle u\rangle$ and $E_0H_0/2$.

commonErrors.description: Treats intrinsic impedance as $E_0/B_0$ rather than $E_0/H_0$.
commonErrors.consequence: Produces a dimensionally invalid magnetic-flux amplitude and destroys the distinction between ohms and wave speed.

commonErrors.description: Interchanges the solutions for the constitutive parameters, writing $\epsilon=\eta/v$ and $\mu=1/(\eta v)$.
commonErrors.consequence: Assigns permeability units to the claimed permittivity and permittivity units to the claimed permeability.

problems.flawedProof:
The wave impedance compares the electric and magnetic flux-density amplitudes, so $\eta=E_0/B_0$. Therefore
$$B_0=\frac{120}{250}=0.480\ \mathrm T.$$
The magnetic amplitude is thus obtained directly from the measured impedance, and no factor involving the wave speed is required.

problems.title: A standing wave offsets electric and magnetic nodes by a quarter wavelength
problems.objective: Construct an electromagnetic standing wave from two counterpropagating vacuum waves, track the propagation-dependent magnetic-field sign, and reconcile zero average power flow with spatially uniform average energy density and local energy exchange.
problems.statement: Vacuum fills all space, with no charges, currents, or boundaries. Let $\epsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$ be positive constants and $c=1/\sqrt{\mu_0\epsilon_0}$. Use Cartesian coordinates with the component waves propagating along $+z$ and $-z$, both linearly polarized along $\hat{\mathbf x}$ and each having peak electric amplitude $E_0$. Adopt $\mathbf E=\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{-i\omega t}\}$, let $k=\omega/c$, and take the ideal monochromatic fields to extend over all $z\in\mathbb R$. (a) Derive the magnetic phasor of each traveling component from Faraday's law, including its sign. (b) Superpose the components and derive real expressions for $\mathbf E(z,t)$ and $\mathbf B(z,t)$. (c) Locate all spatial electric and magnetic nodes and antinodes, and establish their quarter-wavelength offset. (d) Calculate the instantaneous and cycle-averaged Poynting vectors. (e) Calculate the instantaneous total energy density, verify local energy conservation, and show that its cycle average is spatially uniform and equals the sum of the averaged energies of the two traveling waves.
permittedResults: The vacuum equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu_0\epsilon_0\,\partial\mathbf E/\partial t$.
The vacuum definitions $\mathbf S=(1/\mu_0)\mathbf E\times\mathbf B$ and $u=\epsilon_0E^2/2+B^2/(2\mu_0)$.
The relations $\cos(a-b)+\cos(a+b)=2\cos a\cos b$, $\cos(a-b)-\cos(a+b)=2\sin a\sin b$, and $\langle\sin(2\omega t)\rangle=0$.
problems.strategy: Label the propagation direction by $s=\pm1$ and apply phasor Faraday's law before superposition; this makes the required reversal of the magnetic field explicit. After obtaining the standing fields, read nodes from their spatial envelopes. Compute the Poynting vector and energy density without averaging prematurely, then verify the one-dimensional Poynting balance and average only at the end.
hints: For $\widetilde{\mathbf E}_s=E_0e^{iskz}\hat{\mathbf x}$, evaluate $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_s$ and compare it with $i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}_s$.
Add the two real electric fields but subtract their magnetic cosine factors; the resulting electric and magnetic standing-wave envelopes involve $\cos(kz)$ and $\sin(kz)$, respectively.
Express the final results using double angles. The local conservation check reduces to $\partial u/\partial t+\partial S_z/\partial z=0$ with $\omega=ck$.
problems.solution:
For a propagation label $s=+1$ or $-1$, write
$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}_s=E_0e^{iskz}\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Phasor Faraday's law is $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_s=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}_s$. Since
$$\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_s=iskE_0e^{iskz}\hat{\mathbf y},$$
it follows that
$$\widetilde{\mathbf B}_s=s\frac{k}{\omega}E_0e^{iskz}\hat{\mathbf y}=s\frac{E_0}{c}e^{iskz}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Thus the $-z$ wave must have the opposite magnetic direction. The real component fields are
$$\mathbf E_+=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf B_+=\frac{E_0}{c}\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y},$$
$$\mathbf E_-=E_0\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf B_-=-\frac{E_0}{c}\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Their sums are
$$\boxed{\mathbf E(z,t)=2E_0\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}},$$
$$\boxed{\mathbf B(z,t)=\frac{2E_0}{c}\sin(kz)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}}.$$
With $\lambda=2\pi/k$, electric nodes satisfy $\cos(kz)=0$ and electric antinodes satisfy $|\cos(kz)|=1$:
$$z_{E,\mathrm{node}}=\frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{4},\qquad z_{E,\mathrm{antinode}}=\frac{n\lambda}{2},\qquad n\in\mathbb Z.$$
Magnetic nodes and antinodes satisfy $\sin(kz)=0$ and $|\sin(kz)|=1$:
$$z_{B,\mathrm{node}}=\frac{n\lambda}{2},\qquad z_{B,\mathrm{antinode}}=\frac{(2n+1)\lambda}{4}.$$
Every electric antinode is a magnetic node and conversely; the nearest electric and magnetic nodes are separated by $\lambda/4$.

The instantaneous Poynting vector is
$$\mathbf S=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\mathbf E\times\mathbf B=\frac{E_0^2}{\mu_0c}\sin(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\mathbf 0}.$$
Although there is no net cycle-averaged transport, $S_z$ reverses every quarter cycle and transfers energy locally between neighboring electric and magnetic antinodes.

The electric and magnetic energy densities are
$$u_E=2\epsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(kz)\cos^2(\omega t),$$
$$u_B=\frac{2E_0^2}{\mu_0c^2}\sin^2(kz)\sin^2(\omega t)=2\epsilon_0E_0^2\sin^2(kz)\sin^2(\omega t).$$
Their sum can be written
$$\boxed{u(z,t)=\epsilon_0E_0^2\left[1+\cos(2kz)\cos(2\omega t)\right]}.$$
The local conservation law follows directly:
$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=-2\omega\epsilon_0E_0^2\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t),$$
while, using $1/(\mu_0c)=\epsilon_0c$ and $ck=\omega$,
$$\frac{\partial S_z}{\partial z}=2\omega\epsilon_0E_0^2\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t).$$
Hence $\partial u/\partial t+\partial S_z/\partial z=0$. Averaging the energy gives
$$\langle u_E\rangle=\epsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(kz),\qquad \langle u_B\rangle=\epsilon_0E_0^2\sin^2(kz),$$
so
$$\boxed{\langle u\rangle=\epsilon_0E_0^2},$$
independent of position. Each original traveling wave has averaged total energy density $\epsilon_0E_0^2/2$, so their sum supplies the same result. Dimensionally, $E_0/c$ has units $\mathrm T$, $E_0^2/(\mu_0c)$ has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, and $\epsilon_0E_0^2$ has units $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the propagation-dependent sign $\widetilde{\mathbf B}_s=s(E_0/c)e^{iskz}\hat{\mathbf y}$ and obtains the correct real standing-wave fields.
Correctly identifies the complete electric and magnetic node and antinode sets and demonstrates the $\lambda/4$ displacement.
Computes the instantaneous Poynting vector and energy density, proves zero cycle-averaged flux and local Poynting balance, and verifies the uniform averaged total energy.

commonErrors.description: Assigns the same $+\hat{\mathbf y}$ magnetic direction to both counterpropagating waves.
commonErrors.consequence: Makes electric and magnetic nodes coincide and produces a spurious nonzero average power flux instead of a standing wave.

commonErrors.description: Averages $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ before forming quadratic energy quantities.
commonErrors.consequence: Incorrectly concludes that the standing wave has zero average energy because both field averages vanish.

problems.flawedProof:
Both waves have positive amplitude and electric polarization $\hat{\mathbf x}$, so assign both magnetic fields to $+\hat{\mathbf y}$. Then
$$\mathbf B=\frac{E_0}{c}\left[\cos(kz-\omega t)+\cos(kz+\omega t)\right]\hat{\mathbf y}=\frac{2E_0}{c}\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Thus $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B$ have the same nodes, and
$$\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\frac{2E_0^2}{\mu_0c}\cos^2(kz)\hat{\mathbf z},$$
so the superposed field carries steady positive power.

problems.title: Reactive Poynting flow reverses twice per cycle
problems.objective: Prove pointwise energy conservation in an equal-amplitude electromagnetic standing wave and distinguish vanishing time-averaged transport from nonzero instantaneous reactive flow.
problems.statement:
Use a right-handed Cartesian system with propagation along $z$ and polarization along $x$. A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, lossless medium fills all space and obeys $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, where $\epsilon$ and $\mu$ are positive constants. There are no free charges, currents, interfaces, or boundaries in the domain. Define $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$, $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$, $k=\omega/v$, and $T=2\pi/\omega$. Positive flux is measured through a plane $z=\mathrm{constant}$ with unit normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Phasors, when used, follow $\mathbf E=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{-i\omega t})$.

Two coherent waves of equal peak electric amplitude $E_0$ have real electric fields
$$\mathbf E_+=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf E_-=E_0\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
(a) Derive the corresponding magnetic fields from Faraday's law, including the sign of the backward-wave field, and superpose the waves.
(b) Compute the instantaneous Poynting vector $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$, the electromagnetic energy density $u=(\epsilon E^2+B^2/\mu)/2$, and $\partial_tu$.
(c) Verify the source-free local Poynting theorem $\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=0$ pointwise.
(d) Find all spatial and temporal locations where $|\mathbf S|$ is maximal, specify its direction there, and determine its time average. Explain precisely how often the instantaneous flow changes direction, without inferring that zero average flux means zero instantaneous flux.
permittedResults: The source-free Maxwell curl equations $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\partial_t\mathbf D$.
The definitions $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$ and $u=(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)/2$.
Standard trigonometric product-to-sum identities and the time average of a sinusoid over an integer number of periods.
problems.strategy: First use the wave-vector direction in Faraday's law to fix the opposite magnetic-field signs. Reduce the superposed fields to standing-wave products, then calculate $u$, $\partial_tu$, and $\partial_zS_z$ independently. Finally maximize the separated spatial and temporal sine factors and compare instantaneous and averaged transport.
hints: With the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law gives $\widetilde{\mathbf B}=(1/\omega)\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}$; the wave vectors are $+k\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $-k\hat{\mathbf z}$.
After superposition, use the sum and difference of cosines. The electric and magnetic standing-wave factors are shifted by one-quarter wavelength and one-quarter period.
Write $S_z$ as a product of $\sin(2kz)$ and $\sin(2\omega t)$. When checking conservation, reduce the material constants with $k/\eta=\epsilon\omega$ before comparing terms.
problems.solution:
For a monochromatic phasor, Faraday's law becomes $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}$. For the forward wave, $\mathbf k_+=k\hat{\mathbf z}$, so
$$\widetilde{\mathbf B}_+=\frac{1}{\omega}\mathbf k_+\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_+=\frac{E_0}{v}e^{ikz}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
For the backward wave, $\mathbf k_-=-k\hat{\mathbf z}$, giving the essential sign reversal
$$\widetilde{\mathbf B}_-=\frac{1}{\omega}\mathbf k_-\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}_-=-\frac{E_0}{v}e^{-ikz}\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Thus the real magnetic fields are
$$\mathbf B_+=\frac{E_0}{v}\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf B_-=-\frac{E_0}{v}\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Superposition and the sum-difference identities give
$$\mathbf E=2E_0\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},$$
$$\mathbf B=\frac{2E_0}{v}\sin(kz)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
Because $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu$ and $\mu v=\eta$, the instantaneous Poynting vector is
$$\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H
=\frac{4E_0^2}{\eta}\cos(kz)\sin(kz)\cos(\omega t)\sin(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z},$$
so
$$\boxed{\mathbf S(z,t)=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}\sin(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z}}.$$
Its SI dimensions are $(\mathrm{V/m})^2/\Omega=\mathrm{W/m^2}$.

The electric contribution to the energy density is
$$\frac{\epsilon E^2}{2}=2\epsilon E_0^2\cos^2(kz)\cos^2(\omega t).$$
Since $1/(\mu v^2)=\epsilon$, the magnetic contribution is
$$\frac{B^2}{2\mu}=2\epsilon E_0^2\sin^2(kz)\sin^2(\omega t).$$
Therefore
$$u=2\epsilon E_0^2\left[\cos^2(kz)\cos^2(\omega t)+\sin^2(kz)\sin^2(\omega t)\right],$$
and differentiation gives
$$\boxed{\partial_tu=-2\epsilon\omega E_0^2\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)}.$$
The divergence is purely longitudinal:
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=\partial_zS_z=\frac{2kE_0^2}{\eta}\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t).$$
Using $1/\eta=\epsilon v$ and $k=\omega/v$ gives $k/\eta=\epsilon\omega$, hence
$$\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=2\epsilon\omega E_0^2\cos(2kz)\sin(2\omega t)=-\partial_tu.$$
Thus $\partial_tu+\nabla\cdot\mathbf S=0$ at every $z$ and $t$.

The magnitude reaches its largest possible value $E_0^2/\eta$ when both sine factors have unit magnitude. For integers $m,n$,
$$z=\frac{(2m+1)\pi}{4k}=\frac{\lambda}{8}+m\frac{\lambda}{4},\qquad t=\frac{(2n+1)\pi}{4\omega}=\frac{T}{8}+n\frac{T}{4}.$$
At these events,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}(-1)^{m+n}\hat{\mathbf z},$$
so even $m+n$ gives $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ flow and odd $m+n$ gives $-\hat{\mathbf z}$ flow. At any position with $\sin(2kz)\ne0$, the flow has temporal period $T/2$ and switches sign at $t=nT/4$. It therefore executes two complete reactive-flow oscillations during one field period $T$, with four sign changes over that field period; within each reactive-flow period it reverses direction twice. Its time average is
$$\boxed{\langle\mathbf S\rangle_t=\mathbf0},$$
because $\langle\sin(2\omega t)\rangle_t=0$. This cancellation does not make the instantaneous flux vanish. As an independent check, $\langle u\rangle_t=\epsilon E_0^2$ is independent of $z$, consistent with no net long-term energy accumulation or transport.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives the backward-wave magnetic-field sign and obtains the product-form standing fields.
Computes $\mathbf S$, $u$, and $\partial_tu$ and demonstrates pointwise cancellation using $k/\eta=\epsilon\omega$.
Identifies all flux maxima and directions and accurately distinguishes twice-frequency reactive oscillation from zero time-averaged transport.

commonErrors.description: Concluding that cancellation of the two waves' average powers makes the total instantaneous Poynting vector zero.
commonErrors.consequence: This removes the reactive energy exchange and prevents the pointwise Poynting balance from being demonstrated.

commonErrors.description: Assigning the backward wave a $+\hat{\mathbf y}$ magnetic field instead of the sign required by $(-\hat{\mathbf z})\times\hat{\mathbf x}=-\hat{\mathbf y}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The resulting fields do not represent oppositely directed plane waves and produce an incorrect energy flux and conservation check.

problems.flawedProof: Each traveling wave has average power magnitude $E_0^2/(2\eta)$, and their propagation directions are opposite. Their powers therefore cancel, so $\mathbf S(z,t)=\mathbf0$ everywhere. The source-free Poynting theorem then gives $\partial_tu=0$, proving that the standing wave stores a time-independent energy density and has no instantaneous energy motion.

problems.title: Unequal counterpropagating waves leave a standing-wave ratio and net power
problems.objective: Construct the partially standing field produced by unequal coherent counterpropagating waves, derive its envelope and net power, and recover both wave amplitudes from SWR and power measurements.
problems.statement:
A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, lossless medium fills all space, with $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$, $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$, $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$, and $k=\omega/v$. There are no free sources, interfaces, or imposed boundary conditions in the domain. Use right-handed coordinates, with $x$ polarization and positive flux through a plane $z=\mathrm{constant}$ defined by normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Phasors follow $\mathbf E=\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{-i\omega t})$.

Two coherent waves have positive peak electric amplitudes $E_+>E_->0$ and real fields
$$\mathbf E_+=E_+\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad \mathbf E_-=E_-\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
(a) Derive their magnetic fields and construct the complex electric envelope $A(z)=|\widetilde E_x(z)|$.
(b) Find every location of the envelope maxima and minima. Derive $A_{\max}$, $A_{\min}$, and the standing-wave ratio $\mathrm{SWR}=A_{\max}/A_{\min}$.
(c) Derive the instantaneous longitudinal Poynting flux and its time average, showing explicitly why interference terms do not alter the net average power.
(d) A measurement in a medium with $\eta=200\ \Omega$ gives $\mathrm{SWR}=3.00$ and net average flux $\langle S_z\rangle=8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$ in the $+z$ direction. Recover $E_+$ and $E_-$, including SI units, and check the measurements by substitution.
permittedResults: Linear superposition and the source-free Maxwell curl equations.
For the stated phasor convention, the relation derived from Faraday's law between a plane wave's electric field, wave vector, and magnetic field.
The identities $|a+be^{i\phi}|^2=a^2+b^2+2ab\cos\phi$ and $\langle\cos^2(\omega t+\phi)\rangle=1/2$.
problems.strategy: Represent the electric field by a two-term phasor and square its magnitude to expose the spatial envelope. Use the propagation direction to obtain opposite magnetic signs, multiply the total electric and magnetic fields before averaging, and then invert the measured SWR and power through the sum and difference of the two amplitudes.
hints: The electric phasor is proportional to $E_+e^{ikz}+E_-e^{-ikz}$; calculate its modulus squared before searching for extrema.
For the power calculation, the backward wave's magnetic field has the opposite sign. Multiplying the total $E_x$ and $H_y$ causes the two cross terms to cancel exactly.
Let $\Delta=E_+-E_-$. The SWR gives $E_++E_-=R\Delta$, while the measured power relates to the product $(E_++E_-)(E_+-E_-)$.
problems.solution:
Faraday's law in phasor form is $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B}$. The forward wave has wave vector $+k\hat{\mathbf z}$, whereas the backward wave has wave vector $-k\hat{\mathbf z}$. Consequently,
$$\mathbf B_+=\frac{E_+}{v}\cos(kz-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y},\qquad \mathbf B_-=-\frac{E_-}{v}\cos(kz+\omega t)\hat{\mathbf y}.$$
The total electric phasor is
$$\widetilde{\mathbf E}(z)=\left(E_+e^{ikz}+E_-e^{-ikz}\right)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
Its local peak envelope satisfies
$$A^2(z)=\left|E_+e^{ikz}+E_-e^{-ikz}\right|^2
=E_+^2+E_-^2+2E_+E_-\cos(2kz).$$
Because $E_+E_->0$, maxima occur when $\cos(2kz)=1$ and minima when $\cos(2kz)=-1$. Thus, for $m\in\mathbb Z$,
$$z_{\max}=\frac{m\pi}{k}=m\frac{\lambda}{2},\qquad A_{\max}=E_++E_-,$$
$$z_{\min}=\frac{(2m+1)\pi}{2k}=(2m+1)\frac{\lambda}{4},\qquad A_{\min}=E_+-E_-.$$
The difference is positive by hypothesis, so no absolute-value ambiguity remains. Therefore
$$\boxed{\mathrm{SWR}=\frac{E_++E_-}{E_+-E_-}}.$$

Set $C_+=\cos(kz-\omega t)$ and $C_-=\cos(kz+\omega t)$. Since $\mu v=\eta$, the total fields needed for the flux are
$$E_x=E_+C_++E_-C_-,$$
$$H_y=\frac{1}{\eta}\left(E_+C_+-E_-C_-\right).$$
Their product is
$$S_z=E_xH_y=\frac{1}{\eta}\left(E_+^2C_+^2-E_-^2C_-^2\right).$$
The interference cross terms cancel algebraically before any averaging because they enter with opposite signs. Averaging the remaining squared cosines gives
$$\boxed{\langle S_z\rangle=\frac{E_+^2-E_-^2}{2\eta}}.$$
This is positive because $E_+>E_-$ and has dimensions $(\mathrm{V/m})^2/\Omega=\mathrm{W/m^2}$.

For the inversion, write $R=\mathrm{SWR}$ and $\Delta=E_+-E_-$. The envelope result gives
$$E_++E_-=R\Delta.$$
The power measurement then becomes
$$\langle S_z\rangle=\frac{(E_++E_-)(E_+-E_-)}{2\eta}=\frac{R\Delta^2}{2\eta},$$
so
$$\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{2\eta\langle S_z\rangle}{R}}.$$
The individual amplitudes are half the sum and difference:
$$E_+=\frac{R+1}{2}\Delta,\qquad E_-=\frac{R-1}{2}\Delta.$$
With $R=3.00$, $\eta=200\ \Omega$, and $\langle S_z\rangle=8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}$,
$$\Delta=\sqrt{\frac{2(200\ \Omega)(8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2})}{3.00}}=32.66\ \mathrm{V/m}.$$
Hence
$$\boxed{E_+=65.3\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad E_-=32.7\ \mathrm{V/m}}.$$
The reconstructed envelope values are $A_{\max}=98.0\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $A_{\min}=32.7\ \mathrm{V/m}$, whose ratio is $3.00$. Also,
$$\frac{E_+^2-E_-^2}{2\eta}=\frac{(65.3\ \mathrm{V/m})^2-(32.7\ \mathrm{V/m})^2}{400\ \Omega}\approx8.00\ \mathrm{W/m^2}.$$
As limiting checks, $E_-\to0$ gives $\mathrm{SWR}\to1$ and the usual single-wave flux $E_+^2/(2\eta)$, while $E_-\to E_+$ gives zero net power and a divergent SWR because the envelope minima approach zero.
rubricCriteria: Derives the phasor envelope, its extrema and locations, and the stated SWR using $E_+>E_-$.
Uses the correct backward-wave magnetic sign to obtain $\langle S_z\rangle=(E_+^2-E_-^2)/(2\eta)$ and explains cross-term cancellation.
Correctly inverts the numerical SWR and power data to obtain both amplitudes with units and checks both measured quantities.

commonErrors.description: Giving the backward wave the same magnetic-field sign as the forward wave and therefore adding rather than subtracting their directed powers.
commonErrors.consequence: The derived net flux is proportional to $E_+^2+E_-^2$ and fails the equal-amplitude standing-wave limit.

commonErrors.description: Treating the measured SWR as the traveling-wave amplitude ratio $E_+/E_-$ instead of the envelope ratio $(E_++E_-)/(E_+-E_-)$.
commonErrors.consequence: The reconstructed amplitudes do not reproduce the measured envelope maxima and minima.

problems.flawedProof: The SWR directly compares the two traveling-wave amplitudes, so $E_+/E_-=3$. Both waves contribute positive average intensity regardless of direction, giving $8.00=(E_+^2+E_-^2)/(2\eta)$. With $\eta=200\ \Omega$, this yields $E_-=\sqrt{320}\ \mathrm{V/m}=17.9\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $E_+=53.7\ \mathrm{V/m}$.

problems.title: Orthogonally polarized counterpropagating waves hide a spatial polarization texture
problems.objective: Demonstrate that uniform time-averaged scalar observables can conceal a spatially varying polarization ellipse in a superposition of orthogonally polarized counterpropagating waves.
problems.statement:
A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, lossless medium fills all space and has real positive constants $\varepsilon$ and $\mu$. Let $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$, $\eta=\sqrt{\mu/\varepsilon}$, and $k=\omega/v$. Using Cartesian unit vectors with $\hat{\mathbf{x}}\times\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, consider equal-amplitude waves
$$\mathbf{E}_1=E_0\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cos(kz-\omega t),\qquad \mathbf{E}_2=E_0\hat{\mathbf{y}}\cos(kz+\omega t).$$
The first wave travels in $+z$ and the second in $-z$. The phasor convention is $\mathbf{E}=\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}e^{-i\omega t}\}$. There are no free charges, currents, boundaries, losses, or dispersion. (a) Derive the corresponding magnetic fields from Maxwell's equations. (b) At each fixed $z$, determine the polarization ellipse of $\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{E}_1+\mathbf{E}_2$. Identify all planes of linear and circular polarization over one spatial period and describe the intervening states. (c) Compute the instantaneous Poynting vector, its time-averaged flux through a plane $z=\text{constant}$ with normal $+\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, and the time-averaged electromagnetic energy density. (d) Explain precisely why the absence of fringes in a scalar observable proportional to $\langle |\mathbf{E}|^2\rangle$ does not make the vector field spatially uniform. Verify local energy conservation as an independent check.
permittedResults: The source-free Maxwell curl equations in a homogeneous linear medium
The plane-wave dispersion relation $k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}$, if re-established in the solution
Standard trigonometric identities and averages such as $\langle\cos^2\omega t\rangle=1/2$
problems.strategy: First use the propagation direction, rather than a fixed $+z$ rule, to obtain each magnetic field. Resolve the total electric field along axes rotated by $45^\circ$ so that its fixed-$z$ trajectory becomes an ellipse immediately. Compute energy and Poynting quantities before time averaging, which also permits a direct check of Poynting's theorem.
hints: For a phasor proportional to $e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$, Faraday's law gives $\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}=(1/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}$; the sign of $\hat{\mathbf{k}}$ matters.

Introduce $\hat{\mathbf{u}}=(\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\hat{\mathbf{y}})/\sqrt{2}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}}=(\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}})/\sqrt{2}$, then express the two components using $\cos(\omega t\mp kz)$.
Keep the two traveling-wave amplitudes separate when forming $\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}$; the result is the difference of their instantaneous directional fluxes.
problems.solution:
With the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law is $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf{B}}$. For a plane-wave factor $e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}}$,
$$\widetilde{\mathbf{H}}=\frac{1}{\omega\mu}\mathbf{k}\times\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=\frac{1}{\eta}\hat{\mathbf{k}}\times\widetilde{\mathbf{E}},$$
because $k/(\omega\mu)=\sqrt{\varepsilon/\mu}=1/\eta$. Thus
$$\mathbf{H}_1=\frac{E_0}{\eta}\hat{\mathbf{y}}\cos(kz-\omega t),\qquad \mathbf{H}_2=\frac{E_0}{\eta}\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cos(kz+\omega t).$$
The positive $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ direction of $\mathbf{H}_2$ follows from $(-\hat{\mathbf{z}})\times\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}$.

Set $q=\omega t$, $a=kz$, and define
$$\hat{\mathbf{u}}=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{x}}+\hat{\mathbf{y}}}{\sqrt{2}},\qquad \hat{\mathbf{v}}=\frac{\hat{\mathbf{x}}-\hat{\mathbf{y}}}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
The components along these axes are
$$E_u=\sqrt{2}E_0\cos a\cos q,\qquad E_v=\sqrt{2}E_0\sin a\sin q.$$
When both coefficients are nonzero, the fixed-$z$ trajectory therefore satisfies
$$\frac{E_u^2}{2E_0^2\cos^2(kz)}+\frac{E_v^2}{2E_0^2\sin^2(kz)}=1.$$
Its principal axes are fixed along $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$, but its semiaxes are $\sqrt{2}E_0|\cos kz|$ and $\sqrt{2}E_0|\sin kz|$. Hence the polarization is linear when
$$z=\frac{m\lambda}{4},\qquad m\in\mathbb{Z},$$
with successive linear states directed along $\hat{\mathbf{u}}$ and $\hat{\mathbf{v}}$. It is circular when
$$z=\frac{(2m+1)\lambda}{8},$$
and is elliptic elsewhere. The temporal rotation reverses whenever the sign of $\sin(kz)\cos(kz)$ changes, so adjacent circular planes have opposite senses of rotation.

Write $E_1=E_0\cos(kz-\omega t)$ and $E_2=E_0\cos(kz+\omega t)$. Then
$$\mathbf{E}=E_1\hat{\mathbf{x}}+E_2\hat{\mathbf{y}},\qquad \mathbf{H}=\frac{1}{\eta}(E_2\hat{\mathbf{x}}+E_1\hat{\mathbf{y}}),$$
so
$$\mathbf{S}=\mathbf{E}\times\mathbf{H}=\frac{E_1^2-E_2^2}{\eta}\hat{\mathbf{z}}=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}\sin(2\omega t)\sin(2kz)\hat{\mathbf{z}}.$$
Therefore the net average flux through the surface with normal $+\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ is
$$\langle S_z\rangle=0.$$
Individually, the two waves carry average fluxes $+E_0^2/(2\eta)$ and $-E_0^2/(2\eta)$; their directional irradiances add to $E_0^2/\eta$, but their signed fluxes cancel.

The instantaneous energy density is
$$u=\frac{\varepsilon E^2}{2}+\frac{\mu H^2}{2}=\varepsilon(E_1^2+E_2^2)=\varepsilon E_0^2\left[1+\cos(2\omega t)\cos(2kz)\right].$$
Thus
$$\langle u\rangle=\varepsilon E_0^2,$$
with equal average electric and magnetic contributions $\varepsilon E_0^2/2$. The SI dimensions are correct: $E_0^2/\eta$ is in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$, while $\varepsilon E_0^2$ is in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$.

There are no time-averaged scalar electric fringes because the polarizations are orthogonal:
$$\langle |\mathbf{E}|^2\rangle=\langle E_1^2+E_2^2\rangle=E_0^2.$$
Nevertheless, the phasor
$$\widetilde{\mathbf{E}}=E_0\left(\hat{\mathbf{x}}e^{ikz}+\hat{\mathbf{y}}e^{-ikz}\right)$$
has a relative component phase $-2kz$, which generates the spatial sequence of linear, elliptic, and circular states. Constant phasor norm therefore does not imply constant vector polarization.

Finally,
$$\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}=-2\omega\varepsilon E_0^2\sin(2\omega t)\cos(2kz),$$
while
$$\frac{\partial S_z}{\partial z}=\frac{2kE_0^2}{\eta}\sin(2\omega t)\cos(2kz)=2\omega\varepsilon E_0^2\sin(2\omega t)\cos(2kz),$$
because $k/\eta=\omega\varepsilon$. Hence $\partial u/\partial t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf{S}=0$, independently checking the signs and amplitudes.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives the opposite-direction magnetic field signs and obtains the fixed-$z$ ellipse with its linear and circular planes.
Correctly computes the instantaneous and average Poynting fluxes and the uniform time-averaged total energy density.
Explains the distinction between constant scalar intensity and spatially varying relative phase, and verifies local energy conservation.

commonErrors.description: Uses $\mathbf{H}=(1/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{E}$ for both waves, ignoring that the second wave propagates in $-z$.
commonErrors.consequence: Assigns the second wave the wrong magnetic-field sign and incorrectly makes both average energy fluxes point in $+z$.

commonErrors.description: Infers from constant $\langle |\mathbf{E}|^2\rangle$ that the total vector field has a fixed polarization everywhere.
commonErrors.consequence: Misses the $-2kz$ relative phase and the resulting spatial sequence of linear, elliptic, and circular polarization.

problems.flawedProof:
For either wave, take $\mathbf{H}=(1/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{E}$. This gives $\mathbf{H}_1=(E_1/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{y}}$ and $\mathbf{H}_2=-(E_2/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{x}}$. Therefore
$$\mathbf{S}=\frac{E_1^2+E_2^2}{\eta}\hat{\mathbf{z}},$$
so $\langle\mathbf{S}\rangle=(E_0^2/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{z}}$. Both waves consequently transport their energy in $+z$ even though the phase of the second wave moves toward decreasing $z$.

problems.title: Two nearby frequencies beat without dispersive envelope distortion
problems.objective: Construct and quantitatively analyze a two-frequency electromagnetic beat pattern, separating carrier oscillations, signed field envelope, energy-flux beats, and genuine dispersive effects.
problems.statement: A homogeneous, linear, isotropic, nonmagnetic dielectric fills all space. It is lossless and nondispersive over the relevant band, with refractive index $n=1.50$, so $\varepsilon=n^2\varepsilon_0$, $\mu=\mu_0$, $v=c/n$, and $\eta=\eta_0/n$. Two infinite plane waves travel in $+z$, are polarized along $+\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, and have equal electric amplitudes $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$ and frequencies $f_1=200.0\ \mathrm{THz}$ and $f_2=200.2\ \mathrm{THz}$. Use $\hat{\mathbf{x}}\times\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, the phasor convention $e^{-i\omega t}$, and $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. There are no interfaces or reflections. (a) Superpose the fields and factor the result into a carrier and a signed envelope. (b) Derive the carrier-resolved average Poynting flux through a plane normal to $+\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, using an averaging interval long compared with a carrier period but short compared with a beat period. Distinguish the signed-envelope period from the observable energy-beat period. (c) Calculate the carrier period and wavelength, the energy-beat period and length, and the minimum, maximum, and beat-cycle mean flux. (d) Determine the velocities of the carrier and envelope and explain why the beats do not represent group-velocity dispersion or envelope broadening.
permittedResults: The trigonometric identity $\cos A+\cos B=2\cos[(A-B)/2]\cos[(A+B)/2]$
For a forward plane wave in the stated medium, $\mathbf{H}=(1/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{E}$, if its use is explained
Carrier-scale averaging with $\langle\cos^2\phi\rangle=1/2$
problems.strategy: Introduce mean and difference frequencies and wave numbers before factoring the field. Average only the rapid carrier factor, leaving the slowly varying difference phase intact. Determine temporal and spatial beat scales from the period of the energy term rather than from the signed cosine envelope, and use the linear relation $k=\omega/v$ to compare propagation velocities.
hints: Let $\bar{\omega}=(\omega_1+\omega_2)/2$, $\Delta\omega=\omega_2-\omega_1$, and define $\bar{k}$ and $\Delta k$ similarly before applying the cosine-sum identity.

Because both waves propagate in $+z$ and the impedance is frequency independent, their total magnetic field is $\mathbf{H}=(E_x/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. Average the square of the carrier factor while retaining the difference phase.
The signed envelope changes sign after one energy-beat cycle; its sign change is equivalent to a $\pi$ shift of the carrier and does not double the spacing between energy maxima.
problems.solution:
For $j=1,2$, let $\omega_j=2\pi f_j$ and $k_j=\omega_j/v$. The electric and magnetic fields are
$$\mathbf{E}_j=E_0\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cos(k_jz-\omega_jt),\qquad \mathbf{H}_j=\frac{E_0}{\eta}\hat{\mathbf{y}}\cos(k_jz-\omega_jt).$$
The magnetic direction follows from $\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\hat{\mathbf{x}}=\hat{\mathbf{y}}$. Define
$$\bar{\omega}=\frac{\omega_1+\omega_2}{2},\quad \Delta\omega=\omega_2-\omega_1,
\qquad \bar{k}=\frac{k_1+k_2}{2},\quad \Delta k=k_2-k_1.$$
The total electric field factors as
$$\mathbf{E}=2E_0\hat{\mathbf{x}}\cos\left(\frac{\Delta k\,z-\Delta\omega\,t}{2}\right)\cos(\bar{k}z-\bar{\omega}t).$$
The second cosine is the carrier. The first is a signed field envelope; its sign can be absorbed into a $\pi$ shift of the carrier.

Since $\mathbf{H}=(E_x/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{y}}$, the instantaneous flux is $\mathbf{S}=(E_x^2/\eta)\hat{\mathbf{z}}$. Let
$$\Phi=\Delta k\,z-\Delta\omega\,t.$$
Averaging over a window satisfying $1/\bar f\ll\tau\ll1/\Delta f$ gives
$$\langle\mathbf{S}\rangle_{\mathrm{car}}=\frac{2E_0^2}{\eta}\cos^2\left(\frac{\Phi}{2}\right)\hat{\mathbf{z}}=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}\left[1+\cos\Phi\right]\hat{\mathbf{z}}.$$
Thus the energy-flux beat period is
$$T_{\mathrm{beat}}=\frac{2\pi}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{1}{\Delta f},$$
and the energy-beat length is
$$L_{\mathrm{beat}}=\frac{2\pi}{\Delta k}=\frac{v}{\Delta f}.$$
By contrast, the signed field-envelope cosine requires $4\pi$ change in $\Phi$ to return to the same sign, so its signed period and length are twice these values. Its magnitude and all quadratic energy observables repeat after $2\pi$.

Numerically,
$$\bar f=200.1\ \mathrm{THz},\qquad \Delta f=0.200\ \mathrm{THz}=2.00\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Hz},$$
$$v=\frac{c}{n}=1.99861639\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad \eta=\frac{376.730\ \Omega}{1.50}=251.15\ \Omega.$$
The carrier scales are
$$T_{\mathrm{car}}=\frac{1}{\bar f}=4.9975\ \mathrm{fs},$$
$$\lambda_{\mathrm{car}}=\frac{v}{\bar f}=9.988\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}=0.9988\ \mu\mathrm{m}.$$
The observable beat scales are
$$T_{\mathrm{beat}}=5.000\ \mathrm{ps},$$
$$L_{\mathrm{beat}}=9.993\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m}=0.9993\ \mathrm{mm}.$$
The carrier-averaged flux ranges from zero to
$$S_{\max}=\frac{2E_0^2}{\eta}=114.7\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}},$$
while its average over a complete beat cycle is
$$S_{\mathrm{mean}}=\frac{E_0^2}{\eta}=57.34\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}.$$
This equals the sum of the separate-wave averages, each $28.67\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. The flux units follow from $E_0^2/\eta=(\mathrm{V/m})^2/\Omega=\mathrm{W/m^2}$.

A surface of constant carrier phase obeys $\bar{k}z-\bar{\omega}t=\text{constant}$, so
$$v_{\mathrm{carrier}}=\frac{\bar{\omega}}{\bar{k}}=v.$$
A surface of constant envelope phase obeys $\Delta k\,z-\Delta\omega t=\text{constant}$, giving
$$v_{\mathrm{envelope}}=\frac{\Delta\omega}{\Delta k}=v,$$
because $k(\omega)=\omega/v$. Indeed, both factors depend only on $z/v-t$, so the entire two-frequency pattern translates without changing shape. Also $d\omega/dk=v$ and $d^2k/d\omega^2=0$; there is no frequency-dependent group delay and hence no group-velocity dispersion. The slow modulation at a fixed detector is interference between two coherent frequencies, not distortion of a propagating envelope.

As an energy check, carrier averaging gives
$$\langle u\rangle_{\mathrm{car}}=\varepsilon E_0^2(1+\cos\Phi),$$
and $\langle S_z\rangle_{\mathrm{car}}=v\langle u\rangle_{\mathrm{car}}$ because $v\varepsilon=1/\eta$. In the limit $\Delta f\to0$, the beat period and length diverge while the fields approach one wave of amplitude $2E_0$, whose average flux is $2E_0^2/\eta$, agreeing with the constructive limit above.
rubricCriteria: Correctly factors the two-frequency field and distinguishes the rapid carrier, signed field envelope, and quadratic energy-beat modulation.
Correctly derives and numerically evaluates the carrier and beat scales and the minimum, maximum, and mean carrier-averaged fluxes.
Uses the nondispersive relation $k=\omega/v$ to show equal carrier and envelope velocities and clearly distinguishes beating from group-velocity dispersion.

commonErrors.description: Uses the full signed-cosine envelope period as the observable beat period.
commonErrors.consequence: Reports $10.0\ \mathrm{ps}$ and approximately $2.00\ \mathrm{mm}$, both twice the energy-flux beat scales.

commonErrors.description: Uses the vacuum speed $c$ for the beat length or attributes the modulation to unequal group velocities.
commonErrors.consequence: Obtains the wrong spatial beat length and incorrectly claims dispersive envelope distortion in a medium with linear $k(\omega)$.

problems.flawedProof:
The envelope is $2E_0\cos[(\Delta k z-\Delta\omega t)/2]$. A cosine returns to its original value after its argument changes by $2\pi$, so the beat period is
$$T=\frac{4\pi}{\Delta\omega}=\frac{2}{\Delta f}=10.0\ \mathrm{ps}.$$
Likewise, the beat length is
$$L=\frac{4\pi}{\Delta k}=\frac{2v}{\Delta f}=1.999\ \mathrm{mm}.$$
These are the temporal and spatial separations between successive measured intensity maxima.

problems.title: A perfect conductor reverses tangential electric field but not magnetic field
problems.objective: Derive the reflected-field signs at a vacuum–PEC boundary, construct the resulting standing wave, and connect the magnetic boundary field to surface current and radiation pressure.
problems.statement:
Vacuum occupies $z<0$ and an ideal perfect electric conductor occupies $z>0$, with interface $z=0$. The oscillatory fields inside the PEC vanish. The outward unit normal from the conductor into vacuum is $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use SI units, $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf F}e^{-i\omega t}\}$ phasors, $k=\omega/c$, and $Z_0=\sqrt{\mu_0/\epsilon_0}$. A normally incident wave propagates in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ with peak electric amplitude $E_0$ and polarization $\hat{\mathbf x}$.

(a) Starting from Faraday's law for a plane wave, establish the relation between $\mathbf E$, $\mathbf B$, and the propagation direction. Impose the PEC condition $\mathbf E_t=0$ at $z=0$ to derive the reflected electric and magnetic fields, including their signs.

(b) Construct the total real standing-wave fields in $z<0$ and identify the electric and magnetic nodes at the surface.

(c) Use the magnetic boundary condition to calculate the induced surface-current density $\mathbf K=\mathbf n\times\mathbf H_{\mathrm{out}}$.

(d) Using the average of the magnetic fields immediately on the two sides of the current sheet, find its instantaneous and time-averaged force per unit area. State the force direction and independently check the average pressure using incident-wave momentum flux.
permittedResults: Vacuum Maxwell equations and the PEC condition that the oscillatory interior fields vanish
The magnetic jump condition obtained from an infinitesimal Ampère loop
The Lorentz surface-force density evaluated with the mean field across an ideal sheet
problems.strategy: First derive the magnetic orientation of each traveling wave rather than assigning it by analogy with the electric reflection coefficient. Apply the tangential electric boundary condition to determine the reflected amplitude, combine the two waves with trigonometric identities, and then use the fixed conductor-outward normal in the magnetic jump condition. For the force, exclude the sheet's self-field by averaging the fields on its two sides and compare the result with twice the incident momentum flux.
hints: For a phasor proportional to $e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}$, insert $\nabla\to i\mathbf k$ into Faraday's law. Apply the resulting cross product separately to $\mathbf k_i=+k\hat{\mathbf z}$ and $\mathbf k_r=-k\hat{\mathbf z}$.
At $z=0$, the incident and reflected electric phases coincide. After finding the reflection coefficient, use $\cos(a-b)-\cos(a+b)$ and $\cos(a-b)+\cos(a+b)$ to expose the standing-wave nodes.
The magnetic field acting on an infinitesimally thin surface current is $\big(\mathbf B_{\mathrm{out}}+\mathbf B_{\mathrm{in}}\big)/2$. The identity $1/(Z_0c)=\epsilon_0$ simplifies the pressure.
problems.solution:
With the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law is $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$. For a plane-wave phasor this gives
$$
i\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\widetilde{\mathbf B},
\qquad
\widetilde{\mathbf B}=\frac{1}{\omega}\mathbf k\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=\frac{1}{c}\hat{\mathbf k}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}.
$$
Thus the prescribed incident real fields are
$$
\mathbf E_i=E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\cos(kz-\omega t),
\qquad
\mathbf B_i=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(kz-\omega t),
$$
because $\hat{\mathbf z}\times\hat{\mathbf x}=\hat{\mathbf y}$.

Let the reflected electric amplitude be $rE_0\hat{\mathbf x}$. At the surface both electric waves have the same time factor, so $\mathbf E_t(0,t)=0$ requires $1+r=0$, hence $r=-1$. Therefore
$$
\mathbf E_r=-E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\cos(kz+\omega t).
$$
The reflected wave propagates along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$, so its magnetic field must be calculated with that direction:
$$
\mathbf B_r=\frac{1}{c}(-\hat{\mathbf z})\times(-E_0\hat{\mathbf x})\cos(kz+\omega t)
=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(kz+\omega t).
$$
Hence the tangential electric field reverses sign on reflection, while the magnetic field does not.

Adding the waves gives the standing fields in $z<0$:
$$
\mathbf E=2E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\sin(kz)\sin(\omega t),
\qquad
\mathbf B=\frac{2E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(kz)\cos(\omega t).
$$
At $z=0$, the electric field has a node and the magnetic field has an antinode:
$$
\mathbf E(0,t)=0,
\qquad
\mathbf H_{\mathrm{out}}(0,t)=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(\omega t),
$$
where $\mathbf H=\mathbf B/\mu_0$ and $Z_0=\mu_0c$.

The conductor-outward normal is $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$, and the interior magnetic field vanishes. The magnetic jump condition therefore gives
$$
\mathbf K=\mathbf n\times\mathbf H_{\mathrm{out}}
=(-\hat{\mathbf z})\times\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(\omega t)
=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\hat{\mathbf x}\cos(\omega t).
$$
Its units are $(\mathrm{V/m})/\Omega=\mathrm{A/m}$, as required.

The field acting on the ideal sheet is the mean of the limiting fields. Since $\mathbf B_{\mathrm{in}}=0$,
$$
\mathbf B_{\mathrm{act}}=\frac{\mathbf B_{\mathrm{out}}}{2}
=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(\omega t).
$$
There is no surface-charge force here because the electric field is purely tangential and vanishes at the surface. The magnetic surface force density is
$$
\mathbf f_s=\mathbf K\times\mathbf B_{\mathrm{act}}
=2\epsilon_0E_0^2\cos^2(\omega t)\hat{\mathbf z},
$$
where $1/(Z_0c)=\epsilon_0$. Thus the force is always in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, into the conductor and opposite its outward normal. Time averaging gives
$$
\langle\mathbf f_s\rangle=\epsilon_0E_0^2\hat{\mathbf z}.
$$
As an independent check, the incident average intensity is $I_i=E_0^2/(2Z_0)$. Reversal of the normal electromagnetic momentum gives pressure $2I_i/c=E_0^2/(Z_0c)=\epsilon_0E_0^2$, agreeing in magnitude and direction.
rubricCriteria: Correctly obtains a negative electric reflection coefficient but a positive magnetic amplitude by applying $\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E$ to the reflected wave.
Constructs the standing fields with an electric node and magnetic antinode at $z=0$, then uses $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$ to obtain $\mathbf K=(2E_0/Z_0)\hat{\mathbf x}\cos\omega t$.
Uses the mean magnetic field across the sheet to obtain the $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ pressure and verifies $\langle p\rangle=2I_i/c=\epsilon_0E_0^2$.

commonErrors.description: Assigning the reflected magnetic field the same negative reflection coefficient as the tangential electric field without applying the propagation-direction cross product.
commonErrors.consequence: The magnetic fields are incorrectly made to cancel at the PEC, producing zero surface current and zero radiation pressure.

commonErrors.description: Using $\mathbf H\times\mathbf n$ instead of the fixed-normal relation $\mathbf K=\mathbf n\times\mathbf H_{\mathrm{out}}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The induced current and the resulting magnetic force are reversed even though the standing-field magnitudes are correct.

problems.flawedProof: The PEC reverses every field component of the incident wave, so $\mathbf E_r=-E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\cos(kz+\omega t)$ and $\mathbf B_r=-(E_0/c)\hat{\mathbf y}\cos(kz+\omega t)$. At $z=0$ both total fields vanish. Consequently $\mathbf H_{\mathrm{out}}=0$, the induced surface current is $\mathbf K=0$, and the perfect mirror experiences no electromagnetic pressure.

problems.title: Oblique PEC reflection determines surface charge and current together
problems.objective: Synthesize plane-wave transversality, PEC reflection, electromagnetic boundary conditions, and local charge conservation to determine coupled surface charge and current at oblique incidence.
problems.statement:
Vacuum occupies $z<0$ and an ideal PEC occupies $z>0$, with interface $z=0$ and conductor-outward normal $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$. The plane of incidence is the $xz$ plane, and the incidence angle $\theta$ is measured from $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use SI units and the phasor convention $\operatorname{Re}\{\widetilde{\mathbf F}e^{-i\omega t}\}$. A p-polarized wave of peak electric amplitude $E_0$ has
$$
\hat{\mathbf k}_i=\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}+\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
\hat{\mathbf e}_i=\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z}.
$$
Assume the oscillatory fields inside the PEC vanish.

(a) Derive the reflected propagation direction and both components of its electric polarization by imposing transversality and $\mathbf E_t=0$. Derive the incident and reflected magnetic fields from Faraday's law.

(b) Construct the total real fields in $z<0$ and evaluate their limiting values at $z=0^-$. From the normal electric field and tangential magnetic field, determine the time-dependent surface charge density $\sigma(x,t)$ and surface current density $\mathbf K(x,t)$.

(c) Verify the local surface-continuity equation $\partial\sigma/\partial t+\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K=0$ point by point.

(d) For $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $\theta=35.0^\circ$, calculate the peak magnitudes of the normal surface electric field, $\sigma$, and $\mathbf K$. Check the normal-incidence limit.
permittedResults: Vacuum Maxwell equations and plane-wave transversality
Electric and magnetic PEC boundary conditions derived from infinitesimal pillboxes and loops
The local surface charge-conservation equation
problems.strategy: Resolve the p-polarized electric field into tangential and normal components. The tangential PEC condition fixes the reflected tangential component, while orthogonality to the reflected wave vector fixes its normal component. Add the waves before applying the pillbox and loop boundary conditions. Finally, retain the shared surface phase when differentiating the charge and current so that local, rather than merely global, conservation is tested.
hints: Specular reflection preserves the $x$ component of the wave vector and reverses its $z$ component. If $\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=A\hat{\mathbf x}+C\hat{\mathbf z}$, use both $A=-E_0\cos\theta$ and $\mathbf k_r\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=0$.
Define $\psi=kx\sin\theta-\omega t$. At the surface, the incident and reflected phases both reduce to $\psi$, so their normal electric components add even though their tangential components cancel.
Write $\sigma=\sigma_0\cos\psi$ and $\mathbf K=K_0\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf x}$. In the continuity check, use $k=\omega/c$ and $1/(cZ_0)=\epsilon_0$.
problems.solution:
Specular reflection preserves the phase variation parallel to the surface and reverses the normal wave-vector component. Thus
$$
\hat{\mathbf k}_r=\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z}.
$$
Let the reflected electric amplitude be $A\hat{\mathbf x}+C\hat{\mathbf z}$. Cancellation of the tangential electric field at $z=0$ requires $A=-E_0\cos\theta$. Plane-wave transversality then gives
$$
0=\hat{\mathbf k}_r\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=A\sin\theta-C\cos\theta,
$$
so $C=A\tan\theta=-E_0\sin\theta$. Therefore
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf E}_r=-E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z}).
$$
For the stated phasor convention, Faraday's law gives $\widetilde{\mathbf B}=\hat{\mathbf k}\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}/c$. Direct cross products yield
$$
\widetilde{\mathbf B}_i=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y},
\qquad
\widetilde{\mathbf B}_r=\frac{E_0}{c}\hat{\mathbf y}.
$$
The magnetic amplitudes therefore add at the conductor.

Define
$$
\psi=kx\sin\theta-\omega t,
\qquad
a=kz\cos\theta.
$$
The real incident and reflected electric fields are
$$
\mathbf E_i=E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z})\cos(\psi+a),
$$
$$
\mathbf E_r=-E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}+\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z})\cos(\psi-a).
$$
Adding them gives, for $z<0$,
$$
\mathbf E=-2E_0\cos\theta\sin\psi\sin a\,\hat{\mathbf x}
-2E_0\sin\theta\cos\psi\cos a\,\hat{\mathbf z},
$$
while the magnetic field is
$$
\mathbf B=\frac{2E_0}{c}\cos\psi\cos a\,\hat{\mathbf y}.
$$
At $z=0^-$, where $a=0$,
$$
\mathbf E_{out}=-2E_0\sin\theta\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf z},
\qquad
\mathbf H_{out}=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf y}.
$$
The tangential electric field vanishes as required, but the normal electric field generally does not.

A Gaussian pillbox with normal $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$ gives, because the interior field vanishes,
$$
\sigma=\mathbf n\cdot\epsilon_0\mathbf E_{out}
=2\epsilon_0E_0\sin\theta\cos(kx\sin\theta-\omega t).
$$
The magnetic jump condition gives
$$
\mathbf K=\mathbf n\times\mathbf H_{out}
=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}\cos(kx\sin\theta-\omega t)\,\hat{\mathbf x}.
$$
Thus the traveling surface-charge modulation and the current have the same phase.

Let $q=k\sin\theta$. Their derivatives are
$$
\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial t}
=2\epsilon_0E_0\omega\sin\theta\sin(qx-\omega t),
$$
$$
\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K
=\frac{\partial K_x}{\partial x}
=-\frac{2E_0q}{Z_0}\sin(qx-\omega t).
$$
Since $q=k\sin\theta=(\omega/c)\sin\theta$ and $1/(cZ_0)=\epsilon_0$,
$$
\nabla_s\cdot\mathbf K
=-2\epsilon_0E_0\omega\sin\theta\sin(qx-\omega t)
=-\frac{\partial\sigma}{\partial t}.
$$
Local surface charge conservation is therefore satisfied point by point.

For $E_0=120\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $\theta=35.0^\circ$, using $\sin35.0^\circ=0.573576$, $\epsilon_0=8.85419\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$, and $Z_0=376.730\ \Omega$, the peak normal electric field is
$$
E_{n,\mathrm{pk}}=2E_0\sin\theta=137.7\ \mathrm{V/m}.
$$
The peak surface charge density is
$$
\sigma_{\mathrm{pk}}=2\epsilon_0E_0\sin\theta
=1.22\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C/m^2},
$$
and the peak surface current density is
$$
K_{\mathrm{pk}}=\frac{2E_0}{Z_0}=0.637\ \mathrm{A/m}.
$$
The dimensions follow from $\epsilon_0E$ giving $\mathrm{C/m^2}$ and $E/Z_0$ giving $\mathrm{A/m}$. In the limit $\theta\to0$, the normal electric field and $\sigma$ vanish, while $K_{\mathrm{pk}}\to2E_0/Z_0$, reproducing normal-incidence PEC reflection.
rubricCriteria: Derives $\hat{\mathbf k}_r$ and the reflected polarization using both tangential-field cancellation and transversality, including the fact that the two reflected electric components have negative amplitudes in the chosen basis.
Obtains the correct phase-dependent boundary fields and uses $\mathbf n=-\hat{\mathbf z}$ to find $\sigma=2\epsilon_0E_0\sin\theta\cos\psi$ and $\mathbf K=(2E_0/Z_0)\cos\psi\,\hat{\mathbf x}$.
Verifies local surface continuity with the spatial derivative of $K_x$, reports the three numerical peak values with units, and recovers zero surface charge at normal incidence.

commonErrors.description: Reversing the entire incident electric vector on reflection instead of fixing the tangential component first and using transversality for the reflected normal component.
commonErrors.consequence: The normal electric fields are made to cancel, incorrectly eliminating the induced surface charge and producing a reflected field that is not transverse.

commonErrors.description: Claiming charge conservation from the absence of net accumulated charge while omitting the surface divergence $\partial K_x/\partial x$.
commonErrors.consequence: The pointwise continuity equation is not tested, and an inconsistent phase or amplitude between surface charge and current can go unnoticed.

problems.flawedProof: A PEC simply sends back the negative of the incident electric vector, so the reflected amplitude is $-E_0(\cos\theta\,\hat{\mathbf x}-\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf z})$. Its tangential component cancels the incident field, and its normal component cancels the incident normal component as well. Hence $\sigma=0$. The magnetic fields still add, giving $\mathbf K=(2E_0/Z_0)\cos(kx\sin\theta-\omega t)\hat{\mathbf x}$. Surface continuity is satisfied because $\partial\sigma/\partial t=0$.

problems.title: Maxwell stress reproduces oblique radiation pressure
problems.objective: Derive the force on an obliquely illuminated perfect mirror both from intercepted momentum and from the Maxwell stress traction, including the projected-area factor and polarization independence.
