problems.strategy: Represent the slab field by independent forward and backward amplitudes, eliminate those amplitudes in favor of the boundary state $(E_x,H_y)^T$, and use the inverse propagation matrix to connect the incident side to the outgoing load. Derive the same answer from interface coefficients and a round-trip geometric series. Finish with a Poynting-flux identity and a phase-thickness calculation.
hints: For $E_x=E^+e^{ikz}+E^-e^{-ikz}$, the backward contribution to $H_y$ has the opposite sign. Express $E^\pm$ in terms of $E_x$ and $H_y$ at one plane before translating them by $d$.
At $z=d$, the absence of an incoming wave gives $(E_x,H_y)=(t,t/\eta_1)$. Apply the right-to-left slab matrix and then add and subtract the resulting equations for $1+r$ and $1-r$.

If $\rho=(\eta_2-\eta_1)/(\eta_2+\eta_1)$, each complete internal round trip contributes two internal reflection factors and a phase $e^{2i\delta}$. For the energy check, compare the squared denominator with $4+(q-q^{-1})^2\sin^2\delta$, where $q=\eta_2/\eta_1$.
problems.solution:
Inside the slab, write
$$E_x(z)=E^+e^{ik_2z}+E^-e^{-ik_2z},\qquad H_y(z)=\frac{E^+}{\eta_2}e^{ik_2z}-\frac{E^-}{\eta_2}e^{-ik_2z}.$$
The minus sign in the backward-wave magnetic field follows because its Poynting vector points along $-\hat{\mathbf z}$. Solving at $z=0$ gives $E^+=(E_x+\eta_2H_y)/2$ and $E^-=(E_x-\eta_2H_y)/2$. Translation to $z=d$ therefore yields
$$\begin{pmatrix}E_x(d)\\H_y(d)\end{pmatrix}=P_2(d)\begin{pmatrix}E_x(0)\\H_y(0)\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_2(d)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\delta&i\eta_2\sin\delta\\i\eta_2^{-1}\sin\delta&\cos\delta\end{pmatrix}.$$
Thus the right-to-left transfer matrix is
$$M_2(d)=P_2(d)^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\delta&-i\eta_2\sin\delta\\-i\eta_2^{-1}\sin\delta&\cos\delta\end{pmatrix}.$$
Both matrices have determinant $\cos^2\delta+\sin^2\delta=1$. Their upper-right entries have units of ohms and their lower-left entries have units of siemens, so each row has the units of the state component it produces.

At $z=0$, continuity gives $E_x=1+r$ and $H_y=(1-r)/\eta_1$. At $z=d$, the outgoing transmitted wave gives $E_x=t$ and $H_y=t/\eta_1$. With $c=\cos\delta$, $s=\sin\delta$, and $q=\eta_2/\eta_1$, application of $M_2$ gives
$$1+r=t(c-iqs),\qquad 1-r=t(c-iq^{-1}s).$$
Adding and subtracting these equations produces
$$t=\frac{2}{2c-i(q+q^{-1})s},\qquad r=\frac{-i(q-q^{-1})s}{2c-i(q+q^{-1})s}.$$

For an independent multiple-reflection derivation, define the electric-field reflection coefficient from medium 1 into medium 2 by
$$\rho=\frac{\eta_2-\eta_1}{\eta_2+\eta_1}.$$
The corresponding interface coefficients are $t_{12}=1+\rho$, $t_{21}=t_{23}=1-\rho$, and $r_{21}=r_{23}=-\rho$. A complete slab round trip therefore contributes
$$r_{21}r_{23}e^{2i\delta}=\rho^2e^{2i\delta}.$$
Summing every transmitted path gives
$$t=t_{12}t_{23}e^{i\delta}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(\rho^2e^{2i\delta})^m=\frac{(1-\rho^2)e^{i\delta}}{1-\rho^2e^{2i\delta}}.$$
The reflected field is the direct reflection plus every path that enters the slab, reflects at $z=d$, and eventually exits at $z=0$:
$$r=\rho+t_{12}r_{23}t_{21}e^{2i\delta}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}(\rho^2e^{2i\delta})^m=\frac{\rho(1-e^{2i\delta})}{1-\rho^2e^{2i\delta}}.$$
Substitution of $\rho=(q-1)/(q+1)$ reduces these expressions to the matrix results.

For unequal impedances, $r=0$ exactly when $\sin\delta=0$, hence
$$\delta=m\pi,\qquad d=\frac{m\lambda_2}{2},\qquad m=1,2,3,\ldots.$$
At such a resonance, $t=(-1)^m$ and $|t|=1$. If $q=1$, both interfaces are impedance matched and $r=0$ for every $d$, with $t=e^{i\delta}$.

Because the exterior media are identical, the incident, reflected, and transmitted fluxes have the same impedance factor, so $R=|r|^2$ and $T=|t|^2$. The common squared denominator is
$$D=4c^2+(q+q^{-1})^2s^2.$$
Therefore
$$R=\frac{(q-q^{-1})^2s^2}{D},\qquad T=\frac{4}{D}.$$
Using
$$4+(q-q^{-1})^2s^2=4c^2+(q+q^{-1})^2s^2$$
gives $R+T=1$. This also checks the signs in the transfer matrix and internal-reflection product.

For the numerical slab, $n_2=\sqrt{\epsilon_{r2}}=2.4$, $\eta_2=\eta_0/2.4$, and
$$\lambda_2=\frac{c_0}{fn_2}=1.0409460\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{m}.$$
Successive resonant thicknesses differ by $\lambda_2/2=5.204730\,\mathrm{mm}$. The smallest one strictly above $10.0\,\mathrm{mm}$ has $m=2$:
$$d_{\mathrm{res}}=\lambda_2=10.40946\,\mathrm{mm}.$$
An added $0.400\,\mathrm{mm}$ changes the phase by
$$\Delta\delta=\frac{2\pi(0.400\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m})}{\lambda_2}=0.24144.$$
With $q=1/2.4$ and $\delta=2\pi+0.24144$, the exact flux formulas give
$$R=0.05323,\qquad T=0.94677.$$
They sum to unity within rounding, while the zero-offset result is $R=0$ and $T=1$.
rubricCriteria: Derives the dimensionally consistent forward and inverse $(E_x,H_y)$ transfer matrices with the correct backward-wave magnetic-field sign and determinant one.
Obtains the exact $r$ and $t$, reproduces them with the correctly signed internal-round-trip series, and identifies both half-wave resonances and the matched-impedance exception.
Verifies $R+T=1$ from Poynting flux and correctly finds $d_{\mathrm{res}}=10.40946\,\mathrm{mm}$, $R=0.05323$, and $T=0.94677$ after the stated offset.

commonErrors.description: Assigning $H_y=+E_x/\eta_2$ to both forward and backward slab waves.
commonErrors.consequence: The propagation matrix has incorrect off-diagonal signs, and the resulting amplitudes generally violate the Poynting-flux identity.

commonErrors.description: Using a round-trip reflection factor $-\rho^2e^{2i\delta}$ instead of $+\rho^2e^{2i\delta}$.
commonErrors.consequence: The geometric series predicts spurious quarter-wave transmission resonances rather than the correct half-wave resonances.

problems.flawedProof:
Let $\rho=(\eta_2-\eta_1)/(\eta_2+\eta_1)$. One internal reflection contributes $-\rho$ at the right interface, while the reflection at the left interface contributes $+\rho$, so a round trip contributes $-\rho^2e^{2i\delta}$. Hence
$$t=\frac{(1-\rho^2)e^{i\delta}}{1+\rho^2e^{2i\delta}}.$$
The denominator is smallest when $e^{2i\delta}=-1$, so exact transmission occurs at $\delta=(m+\tfrac12)\pi$. Thus every lossless dielectric slab is perfectly transmitting at odd quarter-wave thicknesses.

problems.title: A quarter-wave impedance transformer is broader than one coating formula
problems.objective: Prove the quarter-wave impedance-transformation theorem, quantify its leading detuning sensitivity, and show why impedance matching cannot generally be replaced by a refractive-index rule in magnetic media.
problems.statement:
Media 1, 2, and 3 occupy $z<0$, $0<z<d$, and $z>d$, respectively. Each is linear, homogeneous, isotropic, nondispersive over the frequency interval considered, and lossless, with real positive $\epsilon_j$, $\mu_j$, intrinsic impedance $\eta_j=\sqrt{\mu_j/\epsilon_j}$, and wavenumber $k_j=\omega\sqrt{\mu_j\epsilon_j}$. There are no free surface charges or surface currents. Use $e^{-i\omega t}$ phasors, $\mathbf E\parallel\hat{\mathbf x}$, forward propagation along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, and $\mathbf H\parallel\hat{\mathbf y}$. Interface normals point along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Medium 3 is semi-infinite, so only a forward wave is present there. Let $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=E_x(0)/H_y(0)$ looking into layer 2 from medium 1 and let $\delta=k_2d$. (a) Derive the layer transfer matrix and prove
$$Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{\eta_3\cos\delta-i\eta_2\sin\delta}{\cos\delta-i(\eta_3/\eta_2)\sin\delta}.$$
Check the zero-thickness limit. (b) At an odd quarter wave, $\delta=(2m+1)\pi/2$, prove that zero reflection occurs if and only if $\eta_2=\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}$. (c) For the fundamental quarter wave, impose this matching condition and set $\delta=\pi/2+\Delta$ with real $|\Delta|\ll1$. Derive the first nonzero term in the complex reflection amplitude and in the reflected power fraction. Express the latter in terms of $(\omega-\omega_0)/\omega_0$ when $d$ is exactly quarter-wave at $\omega_0$. (d) Verify exact power transmission at the design frequency even when the transmitted electric amplitude is not unity. (e) Explain precisely when the familiar rule $n_2=\sqrt{n_1n_3}$ follows, where $n_j=c_0\sqrt{\mu_j\epsilon_j}$, and provide a concrete magnetic-media counterexample showing that refractive index alone does not determine the transformer condition.
permittedResults: Tangential $E_x$ and $H_y$ are continuous across an interface with no free surface current.
A forward plane wave in a lossless isotropic medium obeys $H_y=E_x/\eta$, while a backward wave obeys $H_y=-E_x/\eta$.

The reflection amplitude at a load impedance $Z$ viewed from a medium of impedance $\eta_1$ is $r=(Z-\eta_1)/(Z+\eta_1)$, provided this relation is also derived from the incident and reflected fields.
For a transmitted traveling wave, the time-averaged normal power flux is $|E|^2/(2\eta)$.
problems.strategy: Propagate the field state from the outgoing load in medium 3 back through layer 2, form the ratio $E_x/H_y$, and then relate that ratio to the incident-side reflection coefficient. At the matched quarter wave, simplify the exact reflection amplitude before expanding in phase detuning. Finally separate the material combinations $\mu/\epsilon$ and $\mu\epsilon$ that control impedance and refractive index.
hints: At $z=d$, the outgoing-wave condition fixes $E_x/H_y=\eta_3$. Apply the right-to-left layer matrix to the state $(\eta_3H_y,H_y)^T$ before taking the ratio at $z=0$.

At a quarter wave, $\cos\delta=0$ and $\sin\delta=\pm1$. For detuning, first impose $\eta_2^2=\eta_1\eta_3$ in the exact expression for $r$; only then expand $\cos(\pi/2+\Delta)$ and $\sin(\pi/2+\Delta)$.

Impedance depends on the ratio $\mu/\epsilon$, whereas refractive index depends on the product $\mu\epsilon$. To construct a counterexample, choose media 1 and 3 with equal indices but reciprocal electric and magnetic relative parameters.
problems.solution:
For layer 2, the forward and backward waves are
$$E_x(z)=E^+e^{ik_2z}+E^-e^{-ik_2z},\qquad H_y(z)=\frac{E^+}{\eta_2}e^{ik_2z}-\frac{E^-}{\eta_2}e^{-ik_2z}.$$
Eliminating $E^\pm$ gives the right-to-left matrix
$$\begin{pmatrix}E_x(0)\\H_y(0)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\delta&-i\eta_2\sin\delta\\-i\eta_2^{-1}\sin\delta&\cos\delta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}E_x(d)\\H_y(d)\end{pmatrix}.$$
The upper-right entry has units of impedance and the lower-left entry has units of admittance. Since medium 3 contains only a forward wave, $E_x(d)=\eta_3H_y(d)$. Writing $c=\cos\delta$ and $s=\sin\delta$ then gives
$$E_x(0)=H_y(d)(\eta_3c-i\eta_2s),$$
$$H_y(0)=H_y(d)\left(c-i\frac{\eta_3}{\eta_2}s\right).$$
Consequently,
$$Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{\eta_3c-i\eta_2s}{c-i(\eta_3/\eta_2)s}.$$
This expression has units of ohms. In the limit $d\to0$, $c\to1$ and $s\to0$, so $Z_{\mathrm{in}}\to\eta_3$, as required when the layer disappears.

At $z=0$, let the incident electric amplitude be one and the reflected amplitude be $r$. Then
$$E_x(0)=1+r,\qquad H_y(0)=\frac{1-r}{\eta_1}.$$
Thus $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_1(1+r)/(1-r)$, which solves to
$$r=\frac{Z_{\mathrm{in}}-\eta_1}{Z_{\mathrm{in}}+\eta_1}.$$
At any odd quarter wave, $c=0$ and $s=\pm1$, so
$$Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\frac{-i\eta_2s}{-i(\eta_3/\eta_2)s}=\frac{\eta_2^2}{\eta_3}.$$
Zero reflection is equivalent to $Z_{\mathrm{in}}=\eta_1$. Since all impedances are positive,
$$r=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \eta_2^2=\eta_1\eta_3\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \eta_2=\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}.$$
This proves both necessity and sufficiency.

For detuning, impose the matching condition and define
$$p=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_3},\qquad \frac{\eta_2}{\eta_3}=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}=\sqrt p.$$
Applying the transfer matrix directly to incident, reflected, and transmitted amplitudes gives the exact matched-layer reflection coefficient
$$r=\frac{(1-p)\cos\delta}{(1+p)\cos\delta-i2\sqrt p\sin\delta}.$$
For $\delta=\pi/2+\Delta$,
$$\cos\delta=-\Delta+O(\Delta^3),\qquad \sin\delta=1-\frac{\Delta^2}{2}+O(\Delta^4).$$
Therefore the first nonzero reflected amplitude is
$$r=i\frac{p-1}{2\sqrt p}\Delta+O(\Delta^2)=i\frac{\eta_1-\eta_3}{2\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}}\Delta+O(\Delta^2).$$
The exact reflected fraction under the matching condition is
$$R=|r|^2=\frac{(1-p)^2\cos^2\delta}{(1+p)^2\cos^2\delta+4p\sin^2\delta},$$
so its first nonzero term is quadratic:
$$R=\frac{(\eta_1-\eta_3)^2}{4\eta_1\eta_3}\Delta^2+O(\Delta^4).$$
For a nondispersive layer whose fundamental quarter-wave condition holds at $\omega_0$, $k_2d=(\pi/2)(\omega/\omega_0)$. Hence
$$\Delta=\frac{\pi}{2}\frac{\omega-\omega_0}{\omega_0},$$
and
$$R=\frac{\pi^2}{16}\frac{(\eta_1-\eta_3)^2}{\eta_1\eta_3}\left(\frac{\omega-\omega_0}{\omega_0}\right)^2+O\!\left(\left|\frac{\omega-\omega_0}{\omega_0}\right|^4\right).$$
If $\eta_1=\eta_3$, the matching condition also gives $\eta_2=\eta_1$; all interfaces are impedance matched and reflection vanishes for every phase thickness, so the displayed detuning coefficient correctly vanishes.

At the design frequency, let $t$ be the transmitted electric amplitude at $z=d$. With $\delta=\pi/2$, the two boundary equations reduce under the matching condition to
$$1+r=-it\frac{\eta_2}{\eta_3},\qquad 1-r=-it\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_2}.$$
The two impedance ratios are equal, so $r=0$ and
$$t=i\sqrt{\frac{\eta_3}{\eta_1}}.$$
The transmitted-to-incident power ratio is therefore
$$T=\frac{|t|^2/(2\eta_3)}{1/(2\eta_1)}=\frac{\eta_1}{\eta_3}|t|^2=1.$$
Thus electric amplitude need not be unity for power transmission to be complete.

Finally, impedance and index encode different material combinations:
$$\eta_j=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_j}{\epsilon_j}},\qquad n_j=c_0\sqrt{\mu_j\epsilon_j}.$$
The general transformer condition is
$$\frac{\mu_2}{\epsilon_2}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_1\mu_3}{\epsilon_1\epsilon_3}},$$
not an index condition. If all three permeabilities are fixed at the same value, then $\eta_j$ is proportional to $1/n_j$, and $\eta_2=\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}$ becomes
$$n_2=\sqrt{n_1n_3}.$$
Without the common-permeability assumption this implication fails. For example, choose relative parameters
$$\epsilon_{r1}=4,\quad \mu_{r1}=1;\qquad \epsilon_{r3}=1,\quad \mu_{r3}=4.$$
Then $n_1=n_3=2$, but $\eta_1=\eta_0/2$ and $\eta_3=2\eta_0$. A layer with
$$\epsilon_{r2}=3,\qquad \mu_{r2}=3$$
has $\eta_2=\eta_0=\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}$ and therefore gives exact quarter-wave matching, while $n_2=3\ne\sqrt{n_1n_3}=2$. Its physical thickness must be set by $k_2d=\pi/2$, independently of the impedance condition.
rubricCriteria: Derives the dimensionally correct transfer matrix and input impedance, checks $Z_{\mathrm{in}}\to\eta_3$ as $d\to0$, and proves the quarter-wave matching condition as an if-and-only-if statement.
Obtains the leading complex amplitude $r=i(\eta_1-\eta_3)\Delta/(2\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3})$ and the quadratic reflected-power and frequency-detuning laws.

Separates the roles of $\mu/\epsilon$ and $\mu\epsilon$, verifies unit power transmission despite nonunit electric amplitude, and supplies a valid magnetic-media counterexample to the geometric-index rule.

commonErrors.description: Replacing the impedance condition by $n_2=\sqrt{n_1n_3}$ without requiring a common permeability across all media.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed layer can have the correct optical thickness but the wrong wave impedance, leaving a nonzero design-frequency reflection.

commonErrors.description: Treating the first-order reflection amplitude as though it were the reflected power fraction.
commonErrors.consequence: The detuning loss is incorrectly predicted to be linear and possibly signed, whereas $R=|r|^2$ is nonnegative and begins quadratically.

problems.flawedProof:
At a quarter wave the layer must have the geometric-mean refractive index, because intrinsic impedance is always $\eta=\eta_0/n$. Thus $\eta_2^2=\eta_1\eta_3$ implies $n_2=\sqrt{n_1n_3}$ even when the permeabilities differ. For a small phase error, expanding the reflection coefficient gives
$$r\approx i\frac{\eta_1-\eta_3}{2\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}}\Delta.$$
Therefore the reflected power fraction to first order is
$$R\approx \frac{\eta_1-\eta_3}{2\sqrt{\eta_1\eta_3}}\Delta,$$
so the coating loses power linearly on either side of its design frequency.

problems.title: An oblique multilayer matrix preserves flux through a weighted determinant
problems.objective: Derive the s-polarized transfer matrix of an oblique lossless layer, prove its unimodular and flux-preserving structure, compose two layers, and verify energy conservation numerically.
problems.statement:
Plane interfaces have normal $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, the plane of incidence is the $xz$ plane, and all media are homogeneous, isotropic, linear, and lossless with real positive $\epsilon_j,\mu_j$. Use phasors with physical fields $\operatorname{Re}[\widetilde{\mathbf E}e^{-i\omega t}]$ and a common tangential wavenumber $k_x$. The incident wave is s polarized, so $\widetilde{\mathbf E}=\hat{\mathbf y}\widetilde E_y(z)e^{ik_xx}$. There are no free surface charges or currents. Let $Z_{\rm ref}>0$ be a fixed real reference impedance and define
$$k_{zj}=\sqrt{\omega^2\epsilon_j\mu_j-k_x^2},\qquad Y_j=\frac{k_{zj}}{\omega\mu_j},\qquad y_j=Z_{\rm ref}Y_j,$$
using $k_{zj}>0$ for propagation and $k_{zj}=i\kappa_j$ with $\kappa_j>0$ for evanescence. Define the state
$$\Psi(z)=\begin{pmatrix}\widetilde E_y(z)\\-Z_{\rm ref}\widetilde H_x(z)\end{pmatrix}.$$
(a) Starting from Maxwell's curl equations, derive the matrix $M_j(d_j)$ satisfying $\Psi(z+d_j)=M_j(d_j)\Psi(z)$ for a layer of thickness $d_j$.
(b) Prove $\det M_j=1$ and prove the weighted flux identity $M_j^\dagger JM_j=J$, where $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Explain why this preserves the time-averaged normal Poynting flux, including for an evanescent lossless layer.
(c) For two successive layers, with layer 1 encountered first, calculate $M=M_2M_1$ explicitly and prove that it has the same two invariants.
(d) Numerically audit energy conservation for nonmagnetic media using $Z_{\rm ref}=Z_0$, vacuum wavelength $\lambda_0=600\,\mathrm{nm}$, incidence angle $30.0^\circ$, indices $n_0=1.00$, $n_1=1.50$, $n_2=2.00$, and $n_s=1.20$. Choose each layer to have phase thickness $\delta_j=k_{zj}d_j=\pi/2$. For unit incident electric amplitude, determine $d_1,d_2$, the amplitude coefficients $r,t$, and the power coefficients $R,T$, and verify $R+T=1$ to numerical precision.
permittedResults: The phasor Maxwell equations $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\mu\widetilde{\mathbf H}$ and $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}=-i\omega\epsilon\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ may be used.
At an interface without free surface current, tangential components of $\widetilde{\mathbf E}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf H}$ are continuous.
The time-averaged Poynting vector is $\langle\mathbf S\rangle=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde{\mathbf E}\times\widetilde{\mathbf H}^*)$.
problems.strategy: Resolve each layer into forward and backward s-polarized amplitudes, express the electric and scaled magnetic components at the two faces, and eliminate the amplitudes. Interpret the resulting indefinite quadratic form as normal flux. For the numerical audit, exploit the diagonal two-layer matrix produced by two quarter-phase layers.
hints: For a forward s wave, Maxwell's curl equation gives $-\widetilde H_x=Y_j\widetilde E_y$; the sign reverses for the backward wave.
Write the layer matrix using $c_j=\cos\delta_j$ and $s_j=\sin\delta_j$. In a propagating layer, direct multiplication of $M_j^\dagger JM_j$ reduces to $c_j^2+s_j^2=1$.
At the left boundary use $\Psi_L=(1+r,\,y_0(1-r))^T$, while at the substrate use $\Psi_R=(t,\,y_st)^T$. Power transmission is weighted by $y_s/y_0$.
problems.solution:
Let a local coordinate in layer $j$ have its origin at the left face. The electric field is
$$\widetilde E_y(z)=Ae^{ik_{zj}z}+Be^{-ik_{zj}z}.$$
For this polarization, the $x$ component of $\nabla\times\widetilde{\mathbf E}=i\omega\mu_j\widetilde{\mathbf H}$ is $-\partial_z\widetilde E_y=i\omega\mu_j\widetilde H_x$. Hence
$$-Z_{\rm ref}\widetilde H_x=y_j\left(Ae^{ik_{zj}z}-Be^{-ik_{zj}z}\right).$$
The omitted component is fixed consistently by $\widetilde H_z=k_x\widetilde E_y/(\omega\mu_j)$. Eliminating $A,B$ between the two faces gives, with $\delta_j=k_{zj}d_j$,
$$\Psi(z+d_j)=M_j\Psi(z),\qquad M_j=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\delta_j&i\sin\delta_j/y_j\\i y_j\sin\delta_j&\cos\delta_j\end{pmatrix}.$$
The mixed matrix entries have the correct dimensions because both state components have electric-field units. Its determinant is
$$\det M_j=\cos^2\delta_j-\left(\frac{i\sin\delta_j}{y_j}\right)\left(i y_j\sin\delta_j\right)=\cos^2\delta_j+\sin^2\delta_j=1.$$
For a propagating lossless layer, $y_j$ and $\delta_j$ are real. Setting $c=\cos\delta_j$ and $s=\sin\delta_j$, direct multiplication gives
$$M_j^\dagger JM_j=\begin{pmatrix}c&-iys\\-is/y&c\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}iys&c\\c&is/y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&c^2+s^2\\c^2+s^2&0\end{pmatrix}=J.$$
For an evanescent layer, write $y_j=i\eta$ and $\delta_j=i\alpha$ with real positive $\eta,\alpha$. Then
$$M_j=\begin{pmatrix}\cosh\alpha&i\sinh\alpha/\eta\\-i\eta\sinh\alpha&\cosh\alpha\end{pmatrix},$$
and the same multiplication now uses $\cosh^2\alpha-\sinh^2\alpha=1$, again yielding $M_j^\dagger JM_j=J$.
The normal Poynting flux is
$$\langle S_z\rangle=-\frac12\operatorname{Re}(\widetilde E_y\widetilde H_x^*)=\frac{1}{2Z_{\rm ref}}\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\widetilde E_y[-Z_{\rm ref}\widetilde H_x]^*\right)=\frac{1}{4Z_{\rm ref}}\Psi^\dagger J\Psi.$$
Thus the weighted identity preserves normal flux. An isolated evanescent exponential has zero average normal flux, while a superposition can carry a nonzero interference flux; the same invariant covers both cases.
For two layers, let $c_j=\cos\delta_j$ and $s_j=\sin\delta_j$. Since layer 1 is encountered first,
$$M=M_2M_1=\begin{pmatrix}c_2c_1-(y_1/y_2)s_2s_1&i(c_2s_1/y_1+s_2c_1/y_2)\\i(y_2s_2c_1+c_2y_1s_1)&c_2c_1-(y_2/y_1)s_2s_1\end{pmatrix}.$$
Multiplicativity gives $\det M=(\det M_2)(\det M_1)=1$. Moreover,
$$M^\dagger JM=M_1^\dagger(M_2^\dagger JM_2)M_1=M_1^\dagger JM_1=J.$$
For the numerical case, conservation of tangential phase gives $k_x=k_0\sin30^\circ$. Because every medium is nonmagnetic,
$$y_j=Z_0Y_j=\sqrt{n_j^2-\sin^2 30^\circ}.$$
Therefore
$$y_0=0.8660254,\quad y_1=1.4142136,\quad y_2=1.9364917,\quad y_s=1.0908712.$$
Since $k_{zj}=k_0y_j$ and $\delta_j=\pi/2$,
$$d_j=\frac{\lambda_0}{4y_j},\qquad d_1=106.07\,\mathrm{nm},\qquad d_2=77.46\,\mathrm{nm}.$$
Each quarter-phase matrix is off-diagonal, so
$$M=M_2M_1=\begin{pmatrix}-y_1/y_2&0\\0&-y_2/y_1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-0.7302967&0\\0&-1.3693064\end{pmatrix}.$$
Tangential-field continuity gives
$$\begin{pmatrix}t\\y_st\end{pmatrix}=M\begin{pmatrix}1+r\\y_0(1-r)\end{pmatrix}.$$
Writing $a=y_1/y_2$ and $d=y_2/y_1$, these equations yield
$$r=\frac{d y_0-y_sa}{d y_0+y_sa}=0.196314,\qquad t=-a(1+r)=-0.873664.$$
The incident and reflected waves occupy the same medium, whereas the transmitted flux has the admittance factor $y_s/y_0$. Thus
$$R=|r|^2=0.0385390,\qquad T=\frac{y_s}{y_0}|t|^2=0.961461,$$
so
$$R+T=1.000000.$$
This is also an independent numerical check of the flux-preserving matrix identity. The ratio $y_s/y_0$ is dimensionless, and the calculated thicknesses have length units as required.
rubricCriteria: Derives the s-polarized admittance $Y_j=k_{zj}/(\omega\mu_j)$, the sign in the scaled magnetic state, and the complete layer matrix from Maxwell's equations.
Proves both $\det M_j=1$ and $M_j^\dagger JM_j=J$, connects the latter to normal Poynting flux, and addresses the evanescent lossless case.
Composes $M_2M_1$ in the correct order and obtains the stated quarter-phase thicknesses, amplitudes, admittance-weighted $T$, and numerical identity $R+T=1$.

commonErrors.description: Uses the p-polarized admittance $Y=\omega\epsilon/k_z$ for the specified s polarization or assigns the wrong sign to $-H_x$ for the forward wave.
commonErrors.consequence: The boundary state and numerical layer matrix describe the wrong polarization, so the calculated reflection coefficient is not the requested one.

commonErrors.description: Sets $T=|t|^2$ even though the incident and substrate wave admittances differ.
commonErrors.consequence: The numerical audit falsely gives $R+T\ne1$ despite a lossless stack.

problems.flawedProof: For s polarization take the layer admittance to be $Y_j=\omega\epsilon_j/k_{zj}$. The quarter-phase matrices then have the same off-diagonal form, so their product has determinant one. Solving the boundary equations gives electric amplitudes $r$ and $t$. Since power is proportional to the square of electric amplitude, define $R=|r|^2$ and $T=|t|^2$. Therefore any discrepancy between $R+T$ and unity is merely rounding error.

problems.title: A finite nondispersive pulse carries energy at the material wave speed
problems.objective: Derive the electromagnetic fields and energy transport of an arbitrary finite traveling pulse, prove that its center of energy moves at the material wave speed, and evaluate an exact Gaussian energy integral.
problems.statement:
A homogeneous, isotropic, source-free medium fills all space and obeys $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, where $\epsilon>0$ and $\mu>0$ are real constants independent of frequency. This is an ideal lossless nondispersive approximation. Coordinates are right-handed, and the pulse propagates along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Fields are real; no phasor convention is used. Let
$$\mathbf E(z,t)=\hat{\mathbf x}f(\xi),\qquad \xi=z-vt,$$
where $f$ is real, piecewise continuously differentiable, and of finite support. Require all fields to vanish outside the pulse.
(a) Use Maxwell's equations to derive $v$, $\mathbf B$, and $\mathbf H$, including their directions and signs. Verify the divergence equations.
(b) Derive the total electromagnetic energy density $u$ and Poynting vector $\mathbf S$. Prove both local energy conservation and $\mathbf S=v u\hat{\mathbf z}$.
(c) Because the transverse plane is infinite, define energy per transverse area by $\mathcal U=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u\,dz$. Prove that $\mathcal U$ is constant. Define the center of energy $z_C=\mathcal U^{-1}\int zu\,dz$ and prove $dz_C/dt=v$ without assuming that $f$ is symmetric.
(d) Extend the convergent integral result to the square-integrable, noncompact Gaussian profile
$$f(\xi)=E_0e^{-\xi^2/(2\sigma^2)}$$
with $E_0=120\,\mathrm{V/m}$ and $\sigma=0.400\,\mathrm m$ in a medium with $\epsilon_r=4.00$ and $\mu_r=1.00$. Derive the exact Gaussian integral rather than quoting it, then calculate $\mathcal U$ and the pulse speed. Use $\epsilon_0=8.8541878128\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{F/m}$ and $c=299792458\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
permittedResults:
The source-free Maxwell equations $
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B$, $
abla	imes\mathbf H=\partial_t\mathbf D$, $
abla\cdot\mathbf D=0$, and $
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0$ may be used.
In a linear lossless medium, electromagnetic energy density and Poynting vector are $u=\tfrac12(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf B\cdot\mathbf H)$ and $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$.
Ordinary changes of variables and polar coordinates in convergent integrals may be used.
problems.strategy: Insert the traveling coordinate into both curl equations and use the requirement that the fields vanish outside the pulse to eliminate integration constants. Show that the electric and magnetic energy densities are equal, then use a translation of the energy integral to isolate all time dependence of its first moment. Derive the Gaussian integral by squaring it and converting the resulting plane integral to polar coordinates.
hints: The only nonzero magnetic component can be along $\hat{\mathbf y}$. If $B_y=b f(\xi)$, Faraday's law determines $b$ and its sign.
After using $v^2=1/(\mu\epsilon)$, compare $B^2/(2\mu)$ with $\epsilon E^2/2$ before simplifying $u$ and $\mathbf S$.
In the first energy moment substitute $z=\xi+vt$. For the Gaussian integral, square $I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-q^2}dq$ and evaluate $I^2$ over the plane.
problems.solution:
Write a prime for differentiation with respect to $\xi$. The electric curl is
$$\nabla\times\mathbf E=\hat{\mathbf y}f'(\xi).$$
Let $\mathbf B=\hat{\mathbf y}B_y(\xi)$. Faraday's law gives
$$f'(\xi)=-\partial_tB_y(\xi)=vB_y'(\xi).$$
Integration yields $B_y=f/v+C$. Since every field must vanish outside the finite pulse, $C=0$, and therefore
$$\mathbf B=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{f(\xi)}{v},\qquad \mathbf H=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{f(\xi)}{\mu v}.$$
The orientation is correct because $\hat{\mathbf x}\times\hat{\mathbf y}=\hat{\mathbf z}$. Ampere-Maxwell's law has the $x$ component
$$-\partial_zH_y=\partial_tD_x,$$
so
$$-\frac{f'}{\mu v}=-\epsilon v f'.$$
For a nonconstant pulse this requires
$$v^2=\frac{1}{\mu\epsilon},\qquad v=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}},$$
where the positive root is selected by propagation in the $+z$ direction. Both $\mathbf D$ and $\mathbf B$ are transverse and depend only on $z$, so $\nabla\cdot\mathbf D=\nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0$.
The electric and magnetic energy densities are equal because
$$\frac{B^2}{2\mu}=\frac{f^2}{2\mu v^2}=\frac{\epsilon f^2}{2}.$$
Consequently,
$$u=\frac12\epsilon f^2+\frac{B^2}{2\mu}=\epsilon f^2(\xi).$$
The Poynting vector is
$$\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H=\hat{\mathbf z}\frac{f^2}{\mu v}=\hat{\mathbf z}\epsilon v f^2=\hat{\mathbf z}v u.$$
This gives the local conservation check directly:
$$\partial_tu=-2\epsilon vff',\qquad \partial_zS_z=2\epsilon vff',\qquad \partial_tu+\partial_zS_z=0.$$
The energy per transverse area is
$$\mathcal U(t)=\epsilon\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f^2(z-vt)\,dz.$$
With $\xi=z-vt$ and $dz=d\xi$,
$$\mathcal U=\epsilon\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f^2(\xi)\,d\xi,$$
which is finite and independent of time. The total energy is infinite only because the ideal plane pulse has infinite transverse area.
For the center of energy,
$$z_C(t)=\frac{\epsilon\int zf^2(z-vt)\,dz}{\mathcal U}=\frac{\epsilon\int(\xi+vt)f^2(\xi)\,d\xi}{\mathcal U}.$$
Defining the time-independent intrinsic center
$$\bar\xi=\frac{\int\xi f^2(\xi)\,d\xi}{\int f^2(\xi)\,d\xi},$$
one obtains
$$z_C(t)=\bar\xi+vt,\qquad \frac{dz_C}{dt}=v.$$
No symmetry of $f$ was used.
The Gaussian is not compactly supported, but it and its first energy moment are absolutely integrable, so the preceding change-of-variable argument extends to it. To derive the required integral, set
$$I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-q^2}\,dq.$$
The integrand is positive, and squaring the integral gives
$$I^2=\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dx\,dy=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\phi=2\pi\left[ -\frac12e^{-r^2}\right]_0^\infty=\pi.$$
Thus $I=\sqrt\pi$. Since $f^2=E_0^2e^{-\xi^2/\sigma^2}$, the substitution $q=\xi/\sigma$ gives
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f^2(\xi)\,d\xi=E_0^2\sigma\sqrt\pi.$$
Here $\epsilon=4\epsilon_0$, so
$$\mathcal U=4\epsilon_0E_0^2\sigma\sqrt\pi=4(8.8541878128\times10^{-12})(120)^2(0.400)\sqrt\pi=3.62\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{J/m^2}.$$
The SI dimensions are $[\epsilon E_0^2\sigma]=\mathrm{F\,V^2/m^2}=\mathrm{J/m^2}$. Finally,
$$v=\frac{c}{\sqrt{\epsilon_r\mu_r}}=\frac{c}{2}=1.49896229\times10^8\,\mathrm{m/s}.$$
As an independent limit, setting $\epsilon=\epsilon_0$ and $\mu=\mu_0$ recovers $v=c$, $B=E/c$, and $S=cu$ for a vacuum pulse.
rubricCriteria: Uses both curl equations and the vanishing-field condition to derive the positive-$z$ fields $\mathbf B=\hat{\mathbf y}f/v$, $\mathbf H=\hat{\mathbf y}f/(\mu v)$, and $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$.

Includes both electric and magnetic contributions to obtain $u=\epsilon f^2$, proves $\mathbf S=vu\hat{\mathbf z}$ and local conservation, and derives $z_C=\bar\xi+vt$ with the correct $f^2$ weighting.
Derives $\int e^{-q^2}dq=\sqrt\pi$ by a two-dimensional polar integral and obtains the stated Gaussian energy, speed, units, and vacuum-limit check.

commonErrors.description: Retains only the electric contribution $\epsilon f^2/2$ when calculating the pulse energy.
commonErrors.consequence: The energy per area is too small by a factor of two and the derived ratio between energy flux and energy density is inconsistent with $v$.

commonErrors.description: Defines the pulse center using $f$ rather than the physical energy weight $f^2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed center can depend on field sign or become undefined for a bipolar pulse and is not the center transported by the Poynting flux.

problems.flawedProof: Faraday's and Ampere's laws give $B_y=f/v$ and $v=1/\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}$. The pulse energy is purely electric, so $u=\epsilon f^2/2$ and $\mathcal U=(\epsilon/2)\int f^2dz$. Its location should follow the field envelope itself; hence define $z_C=\int zf(z-vt)dz/\int f(z-vt)dz$. Substituting $\xi=z-vt$ gives $z_C=vt+\int\xi f(\xi)d\xi/\int f(\xi)d\xi$, proving that this electric-field center is the transported energy center.

problems.title: A pulse at an impedance step partitions energy without changing its shape
problems.objective: Derive the exact time-domain partition of an arbitrary finite plane-wave pulse at a lossless impedance discontinuity, including amplitudes, spatial widths, energies, conservation, and detector arrival times.
problems.statement:
Two homogeneous, isotropic, linear, lossless, nondispersive media meet at $z=0$. Medium 1 occupies $z<0$, medium 2 occupies $z>0$, and the interface normal from 1 to 2 is $\hat{\mathbf n}=+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Their constitutive laws are $\mathbf D_j=\epsilon_j\mathbf E_j$ and $\mathbf B_j=\mu_j\mathbf H_j$, with $\epsilon_j,\mu_j>0$, no conductivity, and no free surface charge or current. Define $v_j=(\mu_j\epsilon_j)^{-1/2}$ and $Z_j=(\mu_j/\epsilon_j)^{1/2}$. Edge diffraction is neglected, and energies are evaluated through a common transverse area $A$.

An $x$-polarized pulse approaches normally from medium 1:
$$\mathbf E_I(z,t)=\hat{\mathbf x}F(t-z/v_1),$$
where $F(s)$ is real, square-integrable, and supported on $0\le s\le\tau$. The leading edge reaches the interface at $t=0$.

(a) Starting from Maxwell's curl equations and the tangential interface conditions, derive the magnetic fields and show that the reflected and transmitted electric fields have the form
$$\mathbf E_R=\hat{\mathbf x}\,rF(t+z/v_1),\qquad \mathbf E_T=\hat{\mathbf x}\,t_EF(t-z/v_2).$$
Determine $r$ and $t_E$.

(b) Determine the longitudinal spatial widths of all three pulses. Explain precisely in what sense the pulse shape is unchanged even when $v_1\ne v_2$.

(c) Derive the pulse energies $U_I,U_R,U_T$ by integrating the electromagnetic energy density. Obtain the energy fractions $R=U_R/U_I$ and $T=U_T/U_I$, and prove $U_R+U_T=U_I$.

(d) Evaluate a magnetic-dielectric case with $\epsilon_{r1}=4$, $\mu_{r1}=1$, $\epsilon_{r2}=9$, $\mu_{r2}=4$, $A=2.00\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, and
$$F(s)=\begin{cases}(120\ \mathrm{V/m})\sin(\pi s/\tau),&0\le s\le\tau,\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad \tau=12.0\ \mathrm{ns}.$$
Use $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $Z_0=376.7303\ \Omega$. Find the impedances, speeds, amplitude coefficients, spatial widths, and three energies. Track the incident and reflected time windows at $z=-1.20\ \mathrm m$ and the transmitted time window at $z=+0.300\ \mathrm m$, retaining the convention that the incident leading edge reaches $z=0$ at $t=0$.
permittedResults: Maxwell's curl equations in source-free linear media
The electromagnetic energy density $u=(\epsilon E^2+\mu H^2)/2$
Tangential $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ are continuous when the interface carries no surface current or singular magnetic flux
problems.strategy: First establish the sign-sensitive relation between $\mathbf E$ and $\mathbf H$ for waves traveling in the two opposite directions. Apply the two tangential boundary conditions pointwise in the arbitrary waveform $F$. Treat temporal duration and spatial width separately. For energy, integrate the full electric-plus-magnetic density and change variables from position to the retarded pulse coordinate; this exposes the necessary impedance factor. Finish by checking the algebraic conservation identity and then applying the result to the magnetic-dielectric data and detector geometry.
hints: For any transverse profile traveling in direction $\hat{\mathbf k}$, use Faraday's law to test the relation $\mathbf H=Z^{-1}\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E$. The reflected magnetic field therefore has the opposite tangential sign from the incident magnetic field.

At $z=0$, write one equation from tangential $E_x$ continuity and a second from tangential $H_y$ continuity. Because the equations hold for every value of the arbitrary function $F(t)$, solve directly for the two constant amplitude coefficients.

For a traveling wave, show that its electric and magnetic energy densities are equal. In $U=A\int u\,dz$, change variables from $z$ to the waveform argument; the speed appearing in $dz$ cancels the speed contained in $u$ but leaves an impedance.
problems.solution:
For a $+z$-traveling field $\mathbf E=\hat{\mathbf x}G(t-z/v)$, Faraday's law $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\partial\mathbf B/\partial t$ gives $\mathbf B=\hat{\mathbf y}G/v$. Hence
$$\mathbf H=\frac{\mathbf B}{\mu}=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{G}{\mu v}=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{G}{Z},$$
because $\mu v=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}=Z$. Reversing the propagation direction reverses the magnetic-field sign. Thus
$$\mathbf H_I=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{F(t-z/v_1)}{Z_1},\qquad \mathbf H_R=-\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{rF(t+z/v_1)}{Z_1},$$
$$\mathbf H_T=\hat{\mathbf y}\frac{t_EF(t-z/v_2)}{Z_2}.$$

At $z=0$, tangential-field continuity gives
$$1+r=t_E,\qquad \frac{1-r}{Z_1}=\frac{t_E}{Z_2}.$$
Solving,
$$r=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1},\qquad t_E=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_1+Z_2}.$$
These coefficients are independent of time and frequency under the stated nondispersive assumptions, so every value of $F$ is multiplied by the same constant.

The support of $F(t-z/v_1)$ at fixed $t$ spans a $z$ interval of length $v_1\tau$. The reflected argument has the opposite $z$ orientation but the same scale, while the transmitted argument uses $v_2$. Therefore
$$L_I=L_R=v_1\tau,\qquad L_T=v_2\tau.$$
At a fixed detector, all pulses retain the temporal waveform $F$ and duration $\tau$. As spatial profiles, the reflected pulse is reversed in propagation direction and the transmitted pulse is rescaled longitudinally by $v_2/v_1$; neither is distorted.

For any one of these plane waves, $H=E/Z$, so
$$u=\frac{\epsilon E^2}{2}+\frac{\mu H^2}{2}=\frac{\epsilon E^2}{2}+\frac{\mu E^2}{2Z^2}=\epsilon E^2=\frac{E^2}{Zv},$$
where $Z^2=\mu/\epsilon$ and $Zv=1/\epsilon$. For the incident pulse, changing variables from $z$ to $s=t-z/v_1$ gives $|dz|=v_1ds$ and
$$U_I=\frac{A}{Z_1}\int_0^\tau F(s)^2\,ds.$$
The separated reflected and transmitted pulse energies are therefore
$$U_R=\frac{Ar^2}{Z_1}\int_0^\tau F(s)^2\,ds,$$
$$U_T=\frac{At_E^2}{Z_2}\int_0^\tau F(s)^2\,ds.$$
Consequently,
$$R=r^2=\left(\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1}\right)^2,$$
$$T=\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}t_E^2=\frac{4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}.$$
Their sum is
$$R+T=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2+4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}=1,$$
which proves $U_R+U_T=U_I$. The impedance factor in $T$ is essential: an electric-field amplitude exceeding the incident amplitude need not imply excess transmitted energy.

For the numerical media,
$$v_1=\frac{c}{2}=1.49896\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s},\qquad Z_1=\frac{Z_0}{2}=188.365\ \Omega,$$
$$v_2=\frac{c}{6}=4.99654\times10^7\ \mathrm{m/s},\qquad Z_2=\frac{2Z_0}{3}=251.154\ \Omega.$$
Thus
$$r=\frac17=0.142857,\qquad t_E=\frac87=1.14286,$$
$$R=\frac1{49}=0.0204082,
\qquad T=\frac{48}{49}=0.979592.$$
The peak reflected and transmitted electric fields are $17.14\ \mathrm{V/m}$ and $137.14\ \mathrm{V/m}$, respectively. The widths are
$$L_I=L_R=v_1\tau=1.79875\ \mathrm m,$$
$$L_T=v_2\tau=0.599585\ \mathrm m.$$

For the half-sine pulse,
$$\int_0^\tau F(s)^2ds=(120\ \mathrm{V/m})^2\frac{\tau}{2}=8.64\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{V^2s/m^2}.$$
Hence
$$U_I=9.174\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm J,$$
$$U_R=\frac{U_I}{49}=1.872\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm J,$$
$$U_T=\frac{48U_I}{49}=8.986\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm J.$$
Their numerical sum is $9.174\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm J$ to the stated precision. Dimensionally, $AE^2\tau/Z$ has units $\mathrm{V^2s/\Omega}=\mathrm J$.

At $z=-1.20\ \mathrm m$, the one-way propagation time to the interface is
$$\frac{1.20\ \mathrm m}{v_1}=8.00554\ \mathrm{ns}.$$
The incident condition $0\le t-z/v_1\le\tau$ gives the detector window
$$-8.00554\ \mathrm{ns}\le t\le3.99446\ \mathrm{ns}.$$
The reflected condition $0\le t+z/v_1\le\tau$ gives
$$8.00554\ \mathrm{ns}\le t\le20.0055\ \mathrm{ns}.$$
At $z=+0.300\ \mathrm m$, $z/v_2=6.00415\ \mathrm{ns}$, so the transmitted window is
$$6.00415\ \mathrm{ns}\le t\le18.0042\ \mathrm{ns}.$$

As an independent limit check, if $Z_2=Z_1$, then $r=0$, $t_E=1$, and all energy is transmitted even if $v_2\ne v_1$; the transmitted spatial width can change without changing its energy or detector-time waveform.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives the propagation-direction-dependent magnetic fields and obtains $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$ and $t_E=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$ from both tangential boundary conditions.
Correctly distinguishes duration from spatial width and derives the impedance-weighted energies, including $T=(Z_1/Z_2)t_E^2$ and an explicit proof that $R+T=1$.
Accurately evaluates the magnetic-dielectric coefficients, pulse widths, energies, and all three detector time windows with consistent SI units and at least one physical limit check.

commonErrors.description: Treating transmitted energy as proportional only to $t_E^2$ and omitting the factor $Z_1/Z_2$.
commonErrors.consequence: The proposed energy fractions fail to sum to unity and incorrectly interpret a transmitted electric amplitude larger than the incident amplitude as energy gain.

commonErrors.description: Assigning the transmitted pulse the spatial width $v_1\tau$ merely because its detector-time waveform is unchanged.
commonErrors.consequence: This confuses invariant temporal duration with longitudinal compression or expansion caused by the transmitted speed $v_2$.

problems.flawedProof: The boundary equations give $r=(Z_2-Z_1)/(Z_2+Z_1)$ and $t_E=2Z_2/(Z_1+Z_2)$. Since wave energy is proportional to electric amplitude squared, the reflected and transmitted fractions are $R=r^2$ and $T=t_E^2$. In the numerical case this gives $R=1/49$ and $T=64/49$. Also, because the pulse shape does not change, all three spatial widths equal $v_1\tau=1.79875\ \mathrm m$. Thus the transmitted pulse keeps both the original width and an energy larger than the incident energy.

problems.title: Polarization-varying pulses require a vector energy ledger
problems.objective: Construct and analyze a finite-energy pulse with independently varying orthogonal Jones envelopes, deriving its detector-local polarization ellipse and a cross-term-free vector energy ledger.
problems.statement:
A homogeneous, isotropic, linear, lossless, nondispersive medium has $\mathbf D=\epsilon\mathbf E$, $\mathbf B=\mu\mathbf H$, speed $v=(\mu\epsilon)^{-1/2}$, and impedance $Z=(\mu/\epsilon)^{1/2}$. A plane pulse propagates in $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ and is sampled over detector area $A$ in a plane whose normal is $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Use the phasor convention that physical fields are the real parts of complex fields proportional to $e^{-i\omega_0t}$.

Let $u=t-z/v$ and construct the finite-energy field
$$\mathbf E(z,t)=\operatorname{Re}\left\{\left[\hat{\mathbf x}a(u)+\hat{\mathbf y}b(u)e^{i\delta}\right]e^{-i\omega_0u}\right\},$$
where $a(u)$ and $b(u)$ are distinct real, slowly varying envelopes and $|a'|,|b'|\ll\omega_0\max(|a|,|b|)$. The slow-envelope condition is needed only to assign a polarization ellipse during one carrier cycle; propagation of the displayed waveform is exact in a nondispersive medium.

(a) Derive the associated magnetic field directly from Maxwell's equations. At a detector $z=L$, freeze the envelopes over one carrier cycle and eliminate the carrier phase to obtain the time-dependent polarization ellipse. Derive its orientation angle and semiaxis lengths for general $a$, $b$, and $\delta$.

(b) Derive the instantaneous longitudinal Poynting flux and prove that orthogonal Jones components produce no $E_xE_y$ interference term. Obtain the cycle-averaged detector power and integrated cycle-averaged pulse energy.

(c) Determine the exact integrated energy of the real carrier-resolved field for the Gaussian pair
$$a(u)=E_0e^{-u^2/(2\sigma_x^2)},\qquad b(u)=\beta E_0e^{-(u-\Delta)^2/(2\sigma_y^2)}.$$
Compare it with the cycle-averaged result.

(d) Evaluate the concrete case $\epsilon_r=4$, $\mu_r=1$, $L=1.50\ \mathrm m$, $A=1.00\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, $E_0=100\ \mathrm{V/m}$, $\beta=0.700$, $\sigma_x=8.00\ \mathrm{ns}$, $\sigma_y=12.0\ \mathrm{ns}$, $\Delta=10.0\ \mathrm{ns}$, $f_0=\omega_0/(2\pi)=20.0\ \mathrm{GHz}$, and $\delta=\pi/3$. Find the two envelope-peak arrival times, the cycle-averaged total energy, and representative ellipse data at $u=0$, $u=10.0\ \mathrm{ns}$, and the dominant time at which $a=b$. Take $c=2.99792458\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s}$ and $Z_0=376.7303\ \Omega$. Gaussian pulses are not compactly supported but have finite integrated energy.
permittedResults: Maxwell's curl equations in a source-free linear medium
The Poynting vector $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$
The elementary Gaussian integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-q^2/\sigma^2}dq=\sqrt{\pi}\sigma$
problems.strategy: Express both polarization components using the same retarded coordinate and derive the magnetic field as a vector relation. For the local ellipse, regard the two envelopes as constants over one carrier period, eliminate the carrier phase, and diagonalize the resulting two-dimensional shape matrix. Compute power using the vector triple-product identity rather than squaring a scalar sum. Integrate the two orthogonal contributions separately, then evaluate the carrier-resolved Gaussian corrections to verify the cycle-averaged approximation quantitatively.
hints: At $z=L$, write $E_x=a\cos\theta$ and $E_y=b\cos(\theta-\delta)$ with $\theta=\omega_0(t-L/v)$. Eliminating $\sin\theta$ produces a quadratic equation in $E_x/a$ and $E_y/b$.

The squared semiaxes are the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix with entries $a^2$, $b^2$, and $ab\cos\delta$. For energy, first use $\mathbf E\times(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E)$ before performing any carrier average.

For the exact Gaussian energy, replace each $\cos^2$ by $(1+\cos2\theta)/2$. Shift the integration variable to the center of each Gaussian; the oscillatory correction contains $e^{-\omega_0^2\sigma^2}$.
problems.solution:
Write the real field as
$$E_x=a(u)\cos(\omega_0u),\qquad E_y=b(u)\cos(\omega_0u-\delta).$$
Each Cartesian component is an arbitrary function of $u=t-z/v$. Applying Faraday's law componentwise gives the exact plane-wave relation
$$\mathbf H(z,t)=\frac{1}{Z}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E(z,t).$$
Thus $H_x=-E_y/Z$ and $H_y=E_x/Z$.

At $z=L$, define $u_d=t-L/v$ and $\theta=\omega_0u_d$. Over one carrier cycle, freeze $a=a(u_d)$ and $b=b(u_d)$. With
$$X=\frac{E_x}{a}=\cos\theta,\qquad Y=\frac{E_y}{b}=\cos(\theta-\delta),$$
one has $Y=X\cos\delta+\sin\theta\sin\delta$. Eliminating $\sin\theta$ gives
$$X^2+Y^2-2XY\cos\delta=\sin^2\delta.$$
Equivalently,
$$\frac{E_x^2}{a^2}+\frac{E_y^2}{b^2}-\frac{2E_xE_y\cos\delta}{ab}=\sin^2\delta.$$
This ellipse changes with detector time because $a(u_d)/b(u_d)$ changes. It degenerates to a line when $\sin\delta=0$ or one envelope vanishes.

A parametric form is
$$\begin{pmatrix}E_x\\E_y\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\cos\delta\end{pmatrix}\cos\theta+\begin{pmatrix}0\\b\sin\delta\end{pmatrix}\sin\theta.$$
The squared semiaxes are the eigenvalues of the corresponding shape matrix
$$M=\begin{pmatrix}a^2&ab\cos\delta\\ab\cos\delta&b^2\end{pmatrix}.$$
Therefore
$$s_\pm^2=\frac{a^2+b^2\pm\sqrt{(a^2-b^2)^2+4a^2b^2\cos^2\delta}}{2},$$
where $s_+$ is the major semiaxis. The major-axis angle $\psi$, measured from $+x$, is fixed with the correct quadrant by
$$2\psi=\operatorname{atan2}(2ab\cos\delta,a^2-b^2).$$
For $a,b>0$ and $0<\delta<\pi$, the field moves from $+x$ toward $+y$ as time increases when it passes the positive-$x$ extremum.

Using the vector magnetic-field relation,
$$\mathbf S=\frac{1}{Z}\mathbf E\times(\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E).$$
Because $\mathbf E\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=0$, the vector triple-product identity gives
$$\mathbf S=\hat{\mathbf z}\frac{\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf E}{Z}=\hat{\mathbf z}\frac{E_x^2+E_y^2}{Z}.$$
There is no $E_xE_y$ term: the two field components are geometrically orthogonal, even though they share a carrier frequency and overlap in time. Freezing the envelopes during a cycle and using $\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=1/2$ gives
$$\langle S_z\rangle=\frac{a(u_d)^2+b(u_d)^2}{2Z},$$
$$\overline P(t)=\frac{A}{2Z}\left[a(u_d)^2+b(u_d)^2\right].$$
The integrated cycle-averaged energy is
$$\overline U=\frac{A}{2Z}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[a(u)^2+b(u)^2\right]du.$$
For the Gaussian pair,
$$\int a^2du=E_0^2\sqrt{\pi}\sigma_x,\qquad \int b^2du=\beta^2E_0^2\sqrt{\pi}\sigma_y,$$
so
$$\overline U=\frac{AE_0^2\sqrt{\pi}}{2Z}\left(\sigma_x+\beta^2\sigma_y\right).$$

The exact carrier-resolved energy is
$$U=\frac{A}{Z}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[E_x(u)^2+E_y(u)^2\right]du.$$
Using $\cos^2q=(1+\cos2q)/2$, shifting each Gaussian to its center, and completing the square in the Gaussian Fourier integral gives
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-q^2/\sigma^2}\cos(2\omega_0q)dq=\sqrt{\pi}\sigma e^{-\omega_0^2\sigma^2}.$$
The odd sine integral vanishes. Hence
$$U=\frac{AE_0^2\sqrt{\pi}}{2Z}\left\{\sigma_x\left[1+e^{-\omega_0^2\sigma_x^2}\right]+\beta^2\sigma_y\left[1+e^{-\omega_0^2\sigma_y^2}\cos(2\omega_0\Delta-2\delta)\right]\right\}.$$
Thus the cycle-averaged result differs only by exponentially small carrier-edge corrections when $\omega_0\sigma_x$ and $\omega_0\sigma_y$ are large. Orthogonal additivity remains exact even before averaging.

For the numerical medium,
$$v=\frac{c}{2}=1.49896\times10^8\ \mathrm{m/s},\qquad Z=\frac{Z_0}{2}=188.365\ \Omega.$$
The propagation delay to the detector is
$$\frac{L}{v}=10.0069\ \mathrm{ns}.$$
The $x$ envelope peaks at
$$t_x=10.0069\ \mathrm{ns},$$
and the delayed $y$ envelope peaks at
$$t_y=20.0069\ \mathrm{ns}.$$
The cycle-averaged energy is
$$\overline U=\frac{(1.00\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m^2})(100\ \mathrm{V/m})^2\sqrt{\pi}}{2(188.365\ \Omega)}\left[8.00+0.700^2(12.0)\right]\mathrm{ns},$$
$$\overline U=6.53\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm J=65.3\ \mathrm{pJ}.$$
Here $AE_0^2\sigma/Z$ has units $\mathrm{V^2s/\Omega}=\mathrm J$. Also, $\omega_0\sigma_x\approx1005$ and $\omega_0\sigma_y\approx1508$, so both exact correction factors are smaller than $e^{-10^6}$; $U$ and $\overline U$ agree to far more than the displayed precision.

At $u=0$,
$$a=100\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad b=70e^{-100/288}\ \mathrm{V/m}=49.5\ \mathrm{V/m}.$$
With $\delta=\pi/3$, the major-axis orientation is
$$\psi=\frac12\operatorname{atan2}(ab,a^2-b^2)\approx16.6^\circ.$$
At $u=10.0\ \mathrm{ns}$,
$$a=100e^{-100/128}\ \mathrm{V/m}=45.8\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad b=70.0\ \mathrm{V/m},$$
and
$$\psi\approx65.6^\circ.$$
The major axis has therefore rotated toward $+y$ as the delayed, broader envelope becomes dominant.

The equality $a=b$ requires
$$\ln\left(\frac1\beta\right)-\frac{u^2}{2\sigma_x^2}+\frac{(u-\Delta)^2}{2\sigma_y^2}=0.$$
Its roots are approximately $u=-23.0\ \mathrm{ns}$ and $u=7.04\ \mathrm{ns}$. The latter is the dominant overlap event, occurring at detector time
$$t\approx17.05\ \mathrm{ns},$$
with $a=b\approx67.9\ \mathrm{V/m}$. At this time $\psi=45^\circ$, and because $\cos\delta=1/2$,
$$s_+=a\sqrt{\frac32}\approx83.2\ \mathrm{V/m},\qquad s_-=a\sqrt{\frac12}\approx48.0\ \mathrm{V/m}.$$
The axial ratio is $s_+/s_-=\sqrt3$. As an independent check, setting $b=0$ reduces both the ellipse and the power formulas to those of a single linearly polarized pulse.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives $\mathbf H=Z^{-1}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E$ and the detector-local ellipse, including its semiaxes and quadrant-correct orientation from the time-dependent envelope amplitudes.
Uses the vector Poynting calculation to demonstrate the absence of an $E_xE_y$ term and derives both the cycle-averaged energy and the exact carrier-resolved Gaussian correction.

Accurately evaluates the material delay, envelope-peak times, total energy, evolving ellipse orientations, and the dominant equal-envelope ellipse with consistent SI units and a valid approximation check.

commonErrors.description: Replacing the transverse vector field by the scalar sum $E_x+E_y$ before calculating power.
commonErrors.consequence: Squaring the scalar sum creates a spurious phase-dependent $2E_xE_y$ interference term that is absent from $\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf E$ for orthogonal directions.

commonErrors.description: Treating the relative envelope amplitude $b/a$ as the constant $\beta$ despite the different Gaussian widths and delay.
commonErrors.consequence: The solution incorrectly assigns one fixed polarization ellipse and misses the detector-time rotation and equal-envelope events.

problems.flawedProof: The total electric field amplitude is $E_x+E_y$, so the averaged power is $A\langle(E_x+E_y)^2\rangle/Z$. Therefore $\overline P=A[a^2+b^2+2ab\cos\delta]/(2Z)$, and the pulse energy depends on the relative Jones phase through an interference term. Since the second Jones amplitude is $\beta$ times the first, the ellipse keeps the same orientation throughout the pulse; for $\beta=0.700$ and $\delta=\pi/3$ it is one fixed ellipse merely multiplied by a common Gaussian envelope.

problems.title: Multiple pulse echoes sum to the exact slab energy
problems.objective: Derive the signed electric-field amplitudes and energies of every temporally resolved echo from a finite lossless slab, sum the resulting geometric series, and verify exact energy conservation and numerical convergence.
problems.statement: Three homogeneous, isotropic, linear, lossless, nondispersive media occupy $z<0$, $0<z<L$, and $z>L$. Their positive real wave impedances are $Z_1,Z_2,Z_3$, and the slab wave speed is $v_2$. Use $+\hat{\mathbf z}$ from medium 1 toward medium 3 as the reference normal. A normally incident, $x$-polarized pulse has boundary value $\mathbf E_i(0,t)=E_0f(t)\hat{\mathbf x}$, where $f$ is real, dimensionless, supported on $0\le t\le\tau$, and $I_f=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(t)^2dt<\infty$. There are no free surface charges or currents. For propagation in direction $s\hat{\mathbf z}$, $s=\pm1$, take $\mathbf H=(s/Z)\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E$. If Fourier components are used, adopt the $e^{-i\omega t}$ phasor convention. (a) Derive the single-interface signed electric-field coefficients $r_{ab}$ and $t_{ab}$ for incidence from medium $a$ into medium $b$. (b) Let $T=2L/v_2$ and $q=r_{21}r_{23}$. Derive the waveform, signed amplitude, arrival time, and energy fraction of the prompt reflection, every delayed reflected echo, and every transmitted echo. State a sufficient temporal-separation condition. (c) Sum all echo energies and prove that the total reflected and transmitted energy fractions satisfy $\mathcal R+\mathcal T=1$. Do not sum field amplitudes before computing energy. (d) For $Z_1=377\ \Omega$, $Z_2=250\ \Omega$, $Z_3=500\ \Omega$, $L=0.600\ \mathrm m$, $v_2=2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, and $\tau=2.00\ \mathrm{ns}$, verify separation, evaluate the relevant amplitude and energy ratios, compute $\mathcal R$ and $\mathcal T$, and bound the omitted energy after retaining the terms $n=0,1,2$ in each delayed geometric sequence.
permittedResults: The source-free tangential boundary conditions are continuity of $\mathbf E_\parallel$ and $\mathbf H_\parallel$.
The Poynting vector is $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$.
problems.strategy: First derive the signed coefficients at one interface, taking special care that $r_{ba}=-r_{ab}$. Trace one ray path for each family of echoes and identify the round-trip amplitude multiplier. Convert each resolved pulse amplitude into an energy fraction using its propagation-medium impedance, then sum energy—not field—geometric series. Express the conservation proof through single-interface energy coefficients and use the numerical round-trip energy factor to quantify convergence.
hints: At an $a$-$b$ interface, continuity gives $1+r_{ab}=t_{ab}$ and $(1-r_{ab})/Z_a=t_{ab}/Z_b$.
After the first traversal, every additional slab round trip multiplies an electric-field amplitude by $q=r_{21}r_{23}$ and its energy by $q^2$.
Introduce $A=r_{12}^2$ and $B=r_{23}^2$. The interface transmission energy fractions are $1-A$ and $1-B$, while one complete internal round trip retains the energy fraction $AB$.
problems.solution:
For a wave traveling in $s\hat{\mathbf z}$, the stated magnetic field gives $\mathbf S=s|\mathbf E|^2\hat{\mathbf z}/Z$. At an interface from $a$ to $b$, tangential-field continuity therefore gives
$$1+r_{ab}=t_{ab},\qquad \frac{1-r_{ab}}{Z_a}=\frac{t_{ab}}{Z_b}.$$
Solving,
$$r_{ab}=\frac{Z_b-Z_a}{Z_a+Z_b},\qquad t_{ab}=\frac{2Z_b}{Z_a+Z_b}.$$
Thus $r_{ba}=-r_{ab}$. Notice that $t_{ab}$ is an electric-field amplitude coefficient and need not be less than one.

Let
$$T=\frac{2L}{v_2},\qquad q=r_{21}r_{23}.$$
At $z=0$, the prompt reflected pulse is
$$\mathbf E_{R,\mathrm p}(0,t)=E_0r_{12}f(t)\hat{\mathbf x}.$$
The pulse first transmitted into the slab has amplitude $t_{12}E_0$. It reflects at $z=L$, returns to $z=0$, and partially exits through that boundary. Hence the delayed reflected echoes are
$$\mathbf E_{R,n}(0,t)=E_0t_{12}r_{23}t_{21}q^n f\bigl(t-(n+1)T\bigr)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.$$
At $z=L$, the transmitted echoes are
$$\mathbf E_{T,n}(L,t)=E_0t_{12}t_{23}q^n f\left(t-\frac{(2n+1)L}{v_2}\right)\hat{\mathbf x},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.$$
Successive members of either delayed family are separated by $T$. Because propagation is nondispersive, their duration remains $\tau$. A sufficient nonoverlap condition, including separation of the prompt reflection from the first delayed reflection, is
$$\tau<T=\frac{2L}{v_2}.$$

For a pulse with electric waveform $aE_0f$, its fluence in impedance $Z$ is
$$\frac UA=\int |S_z|dt=\frac{a^2E_0^2I_f}{Z}.$$
The incident fluence is $U_i/A=E_0^2I_f/Z_1$. Since the reflected pulses are all in medium 1, their energy fractions are
$$R_{\mathrm p}=r_{12}^2,$$
$$R_n=\bigl(t_{12}t_{21}r_{23}\bigr)^2q^{2n}.$$
The transmitted pulses propagate in medium 3, so
$$T_n=\frac{Z_1}{Z_3}\bigl(t_{12}t_{23}\bigr)^2q^{2n}.$$
The factor $Z_1/Z_3$ is required because an electric-field amplitude alone is not an energy fraction.

For a single interface define
$$R_{ab}=r_{ab}^2,
\qquad T_{ab}=\frac{Z_a}{Z_b}t_{ab}^2.$$
Direct substitution gives
$$T_{ab}=\frac{4Z_aZ_b}{(Z_a+Z_b)^2}=1-R_{ab}=T_{ba}.$$
Set $A=R_{12}$ and $B=R_{23}$. The prompt reflected fraction is $A$. A delayed reflected path first transmits through interface 12, reflects at interface 23, and transmits back through interface 21, so
$$R_n=(1-A)^2B(AB)^n.$$
A transmitted path exits through interface 23 instead, giving
$$T_n=(1-A)(1-B)(AB)^n.$$
These agree with the amplitude formulas because $q^2=AB$. Since finite positive impedances give $0\le A,B<1$, the series converge. Their sums are
$$\mathcal R=A+\frac{(1-A)^2B}{1-AB},$$
$$\mathcal T=\frac{(1-A)(1-B)}{1-AB}.$$
Combining them,
$$\mathcal R+\mathcal T
=A+\frac{(1-A)\bigl[(1-A)B+1-B\bigr]}{1-AB}
=A+\frac{(1-A)(1-AB)}{1-AB}=1.$$
Thus the lossless slab redistributes, but neither creates nor destroys, pulse energy.

For the numerical data,
$$T=\frac{2(0.600\ \mathrm m)}{2.00\times10^8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}}=6.00\ \mathrm{ns}>2.00\ \mathrm{ns},$$
so the echoes are resolved. The slab data are dimensionally consistent with $\mu_2=Z_2/v_2=1.25\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$ and $\epsilon_2=1/(Z_2v_2)=2.00\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$. The coefficients are
$$r_{12}=-0.202552,\quad t_{12}=0.797448,\quad r_{21}=0.202552,$$
$$t_{21}=1.202552,\quad r_{23}=0.333333,\quad t_{23}=1.333333.$$
Therefore
$$q=r_{21}r_{23}=0.0675173,$$
so consecutive signed echo amplitudes are smaller by a factor $0.0675173$. The prompt reflected amplitude is $-0.202552E_0$; the first delayed reflected and transmitted amplitudes are respectively
$$t_{12}r_{23}t_{21}E_0=0.319658E_0,$$
$$t_{12}t_{23}E_0=1.06326E_0.$$
The corresponding interface energy quantities are
$$A=r_{12}^2=0.0410272,\qquad B=r_{23}^2=0.111111,$$
$$AB=q^2=0.00455858.$$
Hence each additional round trip reduces an echo's energy by a factor about $1/219.4$. The total fractions are
$$\mathcal R=0.14368,\qquad \mathcal T=0.85632,$$
which sum to one within rounding. If terms $n=0,1,2$ are retained in both delayed families, their combined omitted fraction is
$$\Delta_2=(1-A)(AB)^3=9.08\times10^{-8}.$$
As an independent limit check, if $Z_1=Z_2=Z_3$, then all reflection coefficients vanish, only the direct transmitted pulse remains, and $\mathcal R=0$, $\mathcal T=1$.
rubricCriteria: Correctly derives the direction-sensitive interface coefficients and every signed echo amplitude, delay, and impedance-weighted energy fraction.
Sums the two energy geometric series and proves algebraically that the complete reflected and transmitted fractions total exactly one.
Verifies the numerical separation condition, coefficients, total fractions, and the $n=2$ truncation bound with correct SI units.

commonErrors.description: Treats the transmitted electric-field factor $t_{ab}^2$ as an energy fraction without multiplying by $Z_a/Z_b$.
commonErrors.consequence: The transmitted pulse energy and the final conservation ledger are wrong whenever the exterior impedances differ.

commonErrors.description: Adds the amplitudes of temporally separated echoes as a coherent geometric series and squares the result.
commonErrors.consequence: Spurious cross terms are introduced between pulses with disjoint temporal support, producing an incorrect reflected or transmitted energy.

problems.flawedProof:
The total reflected field amplitude is the coherent sum of the prompt reflection and all delayed reflections,
$$\frac{E_R}{E_0}=r_{12}+\frac{t_{12}r_{23}t_{21}}{1-q},$$
and the total transmitted amplitude is
$$\frac{E_T}{E_0}=\frac{t_{12}t_{23}}{1-q}.$$
Therefore the slab energy fractions are
$$\mathcal R=\left(r_{12}+\frac{t_{12}r_{23}t_{21}}{1-q}\right)^2,\qquad
\mathcal T=\frac{Z_1}{Z_3}\left(\frac{t_{12}t_{23}}{1-q}\right)^2.$$
Substitution of the interface coefficients proves that these are the complete reflected and transmitted energies of the separated pulse train.

problems.title: Arbitrary transverse pulses obey a frequency-independent interface theorem
problems.objective: Prove in the time domain that a source-free interface between two lossless nondispersive media scatters every finite-energy transverse waveform by the same constant coefficients, with exact energy and Maxwell-stress momentum ledgers.
problems.statement: Two homogeneous, isotropic, linear, lossless, nondispersive media occupy $z<0$ and $z>0$, with constant real parameters $\epsilon_j>0$, $\mu_j>0$, wave speeds $v_j=(\epsilon_j\mu_j)^{-1/2}$, and impedances $Z_j=(\mu_j/\epsilon_j)^{1/2}$ for $j=1,2$. The interface is stationary at $z=0$, its reference normal is $+\hat{\mathbf z}$, and it carries no free surface charge or current. Let $\mathbf e\in L^2(\mathbb R;\mathbb R^2)$ be any real transverse waveform, where $\mathbf e\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}=0$. The incident field is $\mathbf E_i(z,t)=\mathbf e(t-z/v_1)$. If Fourier analysis is used, take $\widetilde{\mathbf e}(\omega)=\int\mathbf e(t)e^{i\omega t}dt$, with inverse components proportional to $e^{-i\omega t}$. (a) Starting from Maxwell's equations and the source-free interface conditions, prove that the reflected and transmitted fields are $\mathbf E_r(z,t)=r\mathbf e(t+z/v_1)$ and $\mathbf E_t(z,t)=t\mathbf e(t-z/v_2)$ with constants independent of frequency and waveform. Determine $r$ and $t$, and justify the result for all $L^2$ waveforms rather than only differentiable pulses. (b) Prove that the time-integrated Poynting fluxes and the corresponding spatial pulse-energy integrals exist and obey an exact energy ledger. (c) Using the macroscopic Maxwell stress $\mathsf T=\mathbf E\mathbf D+\mathbf H\mathbf B-\tfrac12(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf H\cdot\mathbf B)\mathsf I$ and momentum density $\mathbf g=\mathbf D\times\mathbf B$, derive the exact normal momentum-flux ledger, including the impulse per area delivered to the interface. (d) Audit the impedance-matched and perfect-electric-conductor limits. State precisely which conclusions cease to hold if dispersion, loss, or imposed surface sources are introduced, without developing theories of those effects.
permittedResults: The macroscopic Maxwell equations in each source-free homogeneous region may be used in differential or integral form.
The Poynting vector and energy density are $\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf H$ and $u=(\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf D+\mathbf H\cdot\mathbf B)/2$.
Translation is an isometry on $L^2(\mathbb R)$, and smooth compactly supported functions are dense in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.
problems.strategy: Prove the claim first for a smooth transverse waveform by deriving the magnetic field of each traveling pulse and applying both tangential boundary conditions pointwise. Because the resulting coefficients are scalar constants, extend the construction to arbitrary $L^2$ data by density. Use $L^2$ norms to establish finite fluence and spatial energy. For momentum, keep the field ledger distinct from the mechanical interface impulse and evaluate both from the Maxwell stress.
hints: For $\mathbf E=\mathbf e(t-sz/v)$ with $s=\pm1$, Maxwell's curl equations require $\mathbf H=(s/Z)\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E$.
At $z=0$, the two vector boundary equations reduce to $(1+r)\mathbf e=t\mathbf e$ and $(1-r)\mathbf e/Z_1=t\mathbf e/Z_2$ in the $L^2$ sense.

For a traveling pulse, $U/A=\int S_zdt=I/Z$ and its Maxwell-stress momentum magnitude is $U/v$. The incident and reflected stresses add at the interface because their electric and magnetic interference terms cancel in $T_{zz}$.
problems.solution:
First suppose that $\mathbf e$ is smooth and compactly supported. For propagation in direction $s\hat{\mathbf z}$, define
$$\mathbf E(z,t)=\mathbf e\left(t-\frac{sz}{v}\right),\qquad
\mathbf H(z,t)=\frac{s}{Z}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E(z,t).$$
Using $1/v=\sqrt{\epsilon\mu}$ and $Z=\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}$ gives
$$\frac{\mu}{Z}=\frac1v,\qquad \frac1{vZ}=\epsilon.$$
Direct differentiation then verifies $\nabla\times\mathbf E=-\mu\partial_t\mathbf H$ and $\nabla\times\mathbf H=\epsilon\partial_t\mathbf E$. The fields are transverse, so the divergence equations also hold.

An infinitesimal rectangular Faraday loop crossing the interface gives continuity of tangential $\mathbf E$. An analogous Ampere-Maxwell loop, with no imposed surface current, gives continuity of tangential $\mathbf H$. Write the candidate scattered fields as
$$\mathbf E_r(z,t)=r\mathbf e(t+z/v_1),\qquad
\mathbf E_t(z,t)=t\mathbf e(t-z/v_2).$$
Their magnetic fields are
$$\mathbf H_i=\frac1{Z_1}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E_i,\qquad
\mathbf H_r=-\frac1{Z_1}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E_r,\qquad
\mathbf H_t=\frac1{Z_2}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf E_t.$$
At $z=0$, boundary continuity gives
$$1+r=t,
\qquad \frac{1-r}{Z_1}=\frac{t}{Z_2}.$$
Therefore
$$r=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1},\qquad
t=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_2+Z_1}.$$
Both coefficients are real constants because $\epsilon_j$ and $\mu_j$ are real and frequency independent. They multiply every transverse component equally, so arbitrary time-dependent linear, elliptical, or changing polarization is preserved without cross-polarization.

For general $\mathbf e\in L^2$, choose smooth compactly supported $\mathbf e_n\to\mathbf e$ in $L^2$. Translation, multiplication by $r$ or $t$, and the map $\mathbf e\mapsto\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf e$ are bounded on $L^2$. The corresponding fields therefore converge in $L^2$ at every fixed plane. Maxwell's equations and the boundary equalities pass to the distributional, or weak, limit. This constructs the unique outgoing finite-energy scattering solution for every $L^2$ waveform. Equivalently, Plancherel's theorem applies the same $r$ and $t$ to almost every Fourier component; because they contain no $\omega$, inverse transformation gives constant time-domain multiplication rather than convolution.

Let
$$I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\mathbf e(t)|^2dt<\infty.$$
For a forward wave, $\mathbf S=|\mathbf E|^2\hat{\mathbf z}/Z$; for a backward wave its sign reverses. Thus the positive pulse fluences are
$$\frac{U_i}{A}=\frac I{Z_1},\qquad
\frac{U_r}{A}=\frac{r^2I}{Z_1},\qquad
\frac{U_t}{A}=\frac{t^2I}{Z_2}.$$
They exist because $|\mathbf e|^2\in L^1$. For one traveling pulse, its electric and magnetic energy densities are equal, so
$$u=\frac12\left(\epsilon|\mathbf E|^2+\mu|\mathbf H|^2\right)=\epsilon|\mathbf E|^2.$$
At fixed time, substitution of $\xi=t-sz/v$ gives
$$\frac WA=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u\,dz
=\epsilon v\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\mathbf e(\xi)|^2d\xi
=\frac I Z,$$
because $\epsilon v=1/Z$. Thus the spatial pulse energy equals the time-integrated flux and is finite.

The energy coefficients obey
$$\frac{U_r}{U_i}=r^2,
\qquad \frac{U_t}{U_i}=\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}t^2.$$
Substitution gives
$$r^2+\frac{Z_1}{Z_2}t^2
=\frac{(Z_2-Z_1)^2+4Z_1Z_2}{(Z_1+Z_2)^2}=1.$$
Therefore
$$U_i=U_r+U_t.$$
The factor $Z_1/Z_2$ is essential. Its SI audit is consistent: $I/Z$ has units $\mathrm{V^2m^{-2}s/\Omega}=\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}}$.

For momentum, use the stress and momentum density specified in the problem. For a single traveling wave,
$$\mathbf g=\mathbf D\times\mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf S}{v^2}.$$
Integrating over the pulse's spatial extent gives the signed field momentum per area
$$\frac{\mathbf P}{A}=s\frac{U/A}{v}\hat{\mathbf z}.$$
Define the positive directional magnitudes
$$\Pi_i=\frac{U_i}{Av_1},\qquad
\Pi_r=\frac{U_r}{Av_1},\qquad
\Pi_t=\frac{U_t}{Av_2}.$$
At the interface, the total fields on side 1 are
$$\mathbf E_1=(1+r)\mathbf e,
\qquad \mathbf H_1=\frac{1-r}{Z_1}\hat{\mathbf z}\times\mathbf e.$$
Because both fields are transverse,
$$T_{zz}=-\frac12\left(\epsilon|\mathbf E|^2+\mu|\mathbf H|^2\right).$$
Using $\mu_1/Z_1^2=\epsilon_1$, the incident-reflected interference terms cancel:
$$-T_{zz}^{(1)}=\epsilon_1(1+r^2)|\mathbf e|^2.$$
On side 2,
$$-T_{zz}^{(2)}=\epsilon_2t^2|\mathbf e|^2.$$
The stress discontinuity therefore delivers to the interfacial matter the impulse per area
$$\frac{J_z}{A}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[-T_{zz}^{(1)}+T_{zz}^{(2)}\right]dt
=\left[\epsilon_1(1+r^2)-\epsilon_2t^2\right]I.$$
Since $1/(Zv)=\epsilon$, this is equivalently
$$\frac{J_z}{A}=\frac{U_i+U_r}{Av_1}-\frac{U_t}{Av_2}.$$
Hence the exact normal momentum-flux ledger is
$$\Pi_i+\Pi_r=\Pi_t+\frac{J_z}{A}.$$
The sign of $J_z$ is measured along $+\hat{\mathbf z}$. Its units are $\epsilon I=\mathrm{N\,s\,m^{-2}}$, as required for impulse per area. This explicitly stated Maxwell-stress ledger avoids incorrectly assuming that field momentum alone must be continuous across a material interface.

If $Z_2=Z_1$, then $r=0$ and $t=1$. Energy is transmitted exactly: $U_t=U_i$. The momentum impulse is
$$\frac{J_z}{A}=\frac{U_i}{A}\left(\frac1{v_1}-\frac1{v_2}\right).$$
Thus impedance matching eliminates reflection, but it eliminates interface impulse only if the wave speeds also match. For identical media, both reflection and impulse vanish.

A perfect electric conductor is a boundary limit rather than a second ordinary lossless propagation medium. Its condition is $\mathbf E_\parallel(0,t)=0$, giving
$$r=-1,
\qquad U_r=U_i,
\qquad U_t=0.$$
The momentum ledger gives
$$\frac{J_z}{A}=\frac{2U_i}{Av_1},$$
the expected reversal of the pulse's normal field momentum. Formally, the electric reflection coefficient approaches this result as $Z_2\to0$.

If the media are dispersive, $\epsilon$, $\mu$, $Z$, $r$, and $t$ generally depend on frequency. Reflection and transmission then act as time-domain filters rather than constant multipliers, and the simple nondispersive energy-density and pulse-momentum formulas require additional medium-energy terms. If loss is present, material absorption adds a nonnegative volume term to the energy ledger, transmitted fields attenuate with distance, and momentum is transferred throughout the lossy region. If imposed surface charge or current is present, the homogeneous jumps are replaced by source terms such as $\hat{\mathbf z}\times(\mathbf H_2-\mathbf H_1)=\mathbf K_s$; the surface can absorb or supply power and impulse, so the source-free coefficients and closed field-energy ledger no longer follow. None of these changes invalidates the theorem under its stated constant, lossless, source-free assumptions.
rubricCriteria: Derives the constant waveform-independent coefficients from Maxwell traveling-wave relations and source-free boundary conditions, including a valid extension from smooth pulses to all transverse $L^2$ waveforms.
Establishes finite temporal and spatial energy integrals and proves the impedance-weighted identity $U_i=U_r+U_t$.
Derives the Maxwell-stress momentum ledger with the correct interface impulse and correctly audits matched, identical-medium, PEC, dispersion, loss, and surface-source cases.

commonErrors.description: Equates electric-field amplitude squares directly with energy fractions and asserts $r^2+t^2=1$.
commonErrors.consequence: Energy conservation is falsely violated or falsely claimed whenever $Z_1\ne Z_2$ because transmitted fluence requires the factor $Z_1/Z_2$.

commonErrors.description: Assumes the normal electromagnetic momentum flux is continuous and sets the interface impulse to zero merely because the interface has no free surface sources.
commonErrors.consequence: The momentum ledger fails for unequal wave speeds and gives an immediate contradiction in the PEC limit, where the reflected pulse reverses its momentum.

problems.flawedProof:
The boundary conditions give
$$r=\frac{Z_2-Z_1}{Z_2+Z_1},\qquad t=\frac{2Z_2}{Z_2+Z_1},$$
so the same constants apply to all frequencies. The correct impedance factor also gives $U_i=U_r+U_t$. Because there are no free surface charges or currents, no force can act at the interface and the normal stress must be continuous. Hence the interface impulse is zero and momentum conservation requires
$$\frac{U_i}{v_1}+\frac{U_r}{v_1}=\frac{U_t}{v_2}.$$
This proves that the electromagnetic momentum flux alone is conserved across every source-free material interface.
